News.title: Ecclestone stopped by police for taking shotgun into Portugal
News.content:
Former Formula 1 boss Bernie Ecclestone has denied being arrested at an airport in Portugal after arriving with a shotgun he intended to use in a clay pigeon shooting competition.

Ecclestone, 95, said he was stopped and questioned by four police officers and customs officials at the Tires Aerodrome in Cascais on Monday after arriving from Switzerland.

The British businessman told the Press Association he had to "surrender" the weapon he travelled with as he did not have the right documents to correctly import it.

Ecclestone, who was in charge of F1 for nearly 40 years until 2017, said the Portuguese police were "very helpful" and rejected reports he had been arrested.

"I was going to take part in a clay pigeon shooting competition in Portugal," said Ecclestone.

"I went to see the police and said, 'What can I do for you?' And they said, 'We would like some information on this gun you brought in'."

Ecclestone added he had already taken his shotgun from England to Switzerland and said he anticipated no problems as the airport officials know him "very well".

However, on arrival he was questioned by police for about an hour and was asked to hand over the weapon as he did not have the official documents to bring it into the country.

The incident marks the second time Ecclestone has encountered airport issues regarding firearms. In 2022, he was arrested in Brazil for illegally carrying a gun while boarding a private plane to Switzerland and was ordered to pay 6,000 Brazilian reals (Â£1,000) to the local authorities.

News.title: Plans for major overhaul of councils halted
News.content:
Plans for a major shake-up of local government are on hold, after the government launched a review in light of new legal advice.

Proposals to merge smaller councils to form larger authorities in Essex, Hampshire, Norfolk and Suffolk have been withdrawn.

Meanwhile, plans for 14 other areas will also be reviewed and paused.

Reorganisation in Surrey, where councillors for two new unitary authorities were elected in May, will not be affected by the review.

The government confirmed local elections in May 2027 would go ahead on existing council boundaries.

Confirming the review in Parliament, Local Government Secretary Angela Rayner told MPs that "in light of legal advice, I want to satisfy myself firstly that the right process is in place, that it is robust, and of course complies with the law".

She added: "And secondly, I want to fully test whether our proposals for local government reorganisation meet the priorities of a new administration and a new prime minister and any additional considerations."

Rayner acknowledged the announcement was "disappointing" but insisted the government was "determined more than ever to devolve power closer to the people we represent" - a key priority of new PM Andy Burnham.

The plans originated under Sir Keir Starmer's government, when Rayner was also local government secretary, before she was replaced by Steve Reed.

The government was already facing legal challenges over proposals to reorganise councils in Essex, Hampshire, Norfolk and Suffolk.

In June, Reform-led councils in Essex, Norfolk and Suffolk launched judicial reviews against the plans, while the Conservative-led administration in Hampshire did the same.

Reform UK leader Nigel Farage said: "Reform UK not only argued that this government's plans for local government reorganisation were an unmitigated disaster, but we once again put our money where our mouth is."

He added: "Thanks to our judicial reviews in affected Reform-led councils, the government has backed down on their plans yet again."

Conservative shadow local government minister David Simmonds said it was a "humiliation" for the government.

He said: "Ministers are only backing off because they have been found out in the face of relentless Conservative opposition to their gerrymandering."

Liberal Democrat local government spokeswoman ZÃ¶e Franklin said: "This is an embarrassing and chaotic climbdown, which has resulted in already cash-strapped councils wasting huge sums on plans the government told them were legally watertight."

Sean Matthews, from the County Councils Network, welcomed the move, adding: "Many of our members will be relieved that the decisions they viewed as damaging to local services and financially unsustainable have been withdrawn or are being reviewed."

A spokesperson for the Local Government Association, which represents councils, said that while local authorities hold different views on the reorganisation plans "there is no excuse for the government's mishandling of this process".

The spokesperson added that Rayner's announcement "will have caused significant uncertainty, after councils have invested scarce public money and countless hours" in the reorganisation programme.

Local government in England is currently covered by a complicated patchwork of arrangements.

In some places, responsibility for local services is shared between county councils, which manage areas including social care and education; and district councils, which cover smaller areas and are responsible for services such as bin collections.

Some areas, particularly larger towns and some cities, have "unitary" authorities responsible for both - while the regions surrounding big cities are increasingly covered by regional mayors and multi-council "combined" authorities, with greater powers in areas such as transport policy, planning and housing.

In late 2024, as local government secretary, Rayner announced plans to move towards unitary councils across all of England, with council boundaries redrawn and smaller district councils abolished.

The government argued the proposals would make the system simpler and produce savings by making the delivery of services more efficient, while also handing new powers from Westminster to regions across the country.

However, critics said the plans would not save money, while diverting resources from front-line services and leaving councils more remote from their communities.

Under Sir Keir, the government had been pushing ahead with the proposals.

In July â just days before Burnham became prime minister â Rayner's successor as secretary of state, Reed, had announced plans for new councils in 14 areas.

News.title: Chancellor calls for 'confidence about Britain' despite 'historic high' borrowing costs
News.content:
Asked about the impact of higher borrowing costs, which have surged this month, the Chancellor said that the government was responding to "extreme pressures in the wider market," and reiterated that he wanted to "bring down welfare costs."

Earlier, in his first major speech as chancellor, Healey said his mission was to "make Great Britain growth Britain" again.

Speaking at the Manufacturing Technology Centre (MTC) in Coventry, he said,

"My defining mission as chancellor is growth, good growth in every postcode. And I've set out today the way this government will set about it: more devolution, more public leadership and control, more investment, more innovation, more jobs."

Healey said he is in "lockstep" with Prime Minister Andy Burnham about the need for fiscal discipline and having a buffer in the government's spending plans "against the sort of uncertainty that the JLR decision locally has shown".

It came as Healey offered an upbeat view of the state of the UK economy ahead of the Budget, building on a recent uptick in consumer and business confidence.

Speaking in Coventry, he set out a "new story" of the economy not just turning a corner but being resilient, optimistic and "ready to seize the opportunities of new technologies and ideas".

With seven weeks until the Budget, Healey said the government will stick to Labour's manifesto pledge, made under Sir Keir Starmer and former Chancellor Rachel Reeves, to not "increase taxes on working people".

He repeatedly refused to comment on possible tax rises or spending cuts ahead of 28 October, stating only: "Staying true to our values means being honest about the need to control government spending."

Conservative Shadow Chancellor Andrew Griffith, said: "Healey failed to end uncertainty by ruling out more tax rises."

He added that Healey "sounds increasingly like continuity Rachel Reeves".

In his speech from the Manufacturing Technology Centre in the Midlands, Healey described the UK as "turning the corner" and said greater devolution would spread economic growth more evenly across the UK.

But recent ructions in government debt markets have piled fresh pressure on already-stretched public finances, with the Treasury needing to fill possible multi-billion pound gaps caused by rising borrowing costs and the need to fund higher defence spending.

News.title: Murder arrest after two people found dead at house
News.content:
A man has been arrested on suspicion of murder after two people were found dead in a house in Blackburn.

Lancashire Police said the bodies of a man and woman were found at the home in Hardman Street in the town at about 08:20 BST, and a man aged in his 40s had been arrested.

The man and woman, who have not been named, were both pronounced dead at the scene.

Police said they were unable to confirm the victims' ages but local residents told the BBC they were elderly.

Police said a dedicated team of officers had been assigned to the case, and were carrying out CCTV, house-to-house and forensic inquiries.

News.title: Barrister jailed over revenge plot with client
News.content:
A barrister from West Yorkshire who plotted a revenge attack with her "career criminal" client has been jailed for more than three years.

Samreen Akhtar had represented Tabish Ali, who had been shot and injured in Blacker Road in Huddersfield on 14 September 2021.

The following day, the 38-year-old barrister, of Sufton Street, Huddersfield, was recorded on a telephone call to Ali putting forward a plan to find the person responsible for the shooting so they could be caused serious injuries, according to West Yorkshire Police.

Akhtar was convicted of encouraging or assisting the commission of an indictable offence, namely inflicting grievous bodily harm with intent.

At Manchester Crown Court on Monday, she was given a prison term of three years and three months.

Police said Ali was part of a drugs gang and was later charged with the murder of Jamal Nedd.

Nedd had been shot and killed outside his Huddersfield home as he was driving his mother to work on 19 December 2020.

Ali, of Clare Road, Cleckheaton, was charged with his murder in 2021 and later convicted and given a life sentence along with two other men in July 2022.

News.title: Murder arrests over baby girl's death in woodland
News.content:
Four people have been arrested on suspicion of murder after a baby was found dead while camping with her family in Staffordshire.

The three-month-old girl died after emergency services were called to reports of a child in cardiac arrest in woodland off Strawberry Lane, near Cheslyn Hay, at 08:45 BST on Saturday.

The people arrested were a 42-year-old man and 30-year-old woman from south Staffordshire, a 20-year-old woman from Wolverhampton and an 18-year-old man from Walsall.

All four were detained at the scene and have since been bailed while inquiries continue, Staffordshire Police said.

Det Insp Josh Lee said officers were working to gather further evidence around the circumstances of the girl's death and were "keeping an open mind".

He said it was being treated as an isolated incident and urged people not to share "unconfirmed and speculative" claims online.

News.title: Man, 102, with dementia died after being pushed in pub, inquest told
News.content:
A 102-year-old man with dementia who was allegedly pushed at a Cwmbran pub died nearly two weeks later, an inquest has heard.

Philip Ormerod, from Cwmbran, Torfaen, was taken to hospital in a critical condition following an incident at the Crows Nest pub in the town on 1 August.

He is understood to have been visiting the pub for a drink when he went on to a stage in the venue to complain about the volume of the music.

A 56-year-old man from Llanelli, Carmarthenshire, was arrested on suspicion of inflicting grievous bodily harm, and remains on bail under investigation.

The senior coroner Caroline Saunders said the former design engineer "sustained a fall at the pub", adding that it happened "following an allegation that he was pushed".

The inquest heard he was taken to the Grange hospital with a fractured hip, however his condition deteriorated and he died on the 12 August.

The coroner said Ormerod's death was being investigated by police and that a forensic post mortem examination had taken place.

An inquest was opened but adjourned while a police investigation is carried out.

The coroner said that the inquest would not be resumed if there was a criminal prosecution, however should there be a need for a conclusion, it would take place on 26 May 2027.

Philip Ormerod's son Robert previously said his father was a "pub character" and that he wanted justice for him.

Following Ormerod's death, Det Ch Insp Shelley Comley, senior investigating officer for Gwent Police, said a criminal investigation is ongoing and urged people to "consider the impact that inaccurate or speculative comments" including "online commentary" could have.

The force is urging anyone who was at the pub between 22:00 and 23:00 BST on the night of the incident to contact them.

News.title: Next wins key appeal to overturn £30m equal pay ruling
News.content:
Next has won an appeal allowing it to keep paying warehouse workers a higher hourly rate than shop floor staff in a long running battle over equal pay.

The Employment Appeal Tribunal has overturned a key part of a landmark ruling in 2024 which found the retailer was wrong to pay its warehouse staff higher basic pay than shop floor workers for jobs of equal value.

More than 3,500 current and former employees, mainly women, had been set to share potentially more than Â£30m in back pay as a result of that judgement.

After Next's appeal, the law firm Leigh Day, which represents store workers, described the conclusion on basic pay as "disappointing" and said it will appeal the decision.

The tribunal accepted that Next was justified in paying higher rates because of recruitment and retention pressures for warehouse workers.

Next described the decision as a "landmark victory" succeeding on the "key issue of basic pay".

In a statement, it said: "The importance of this decision is that the Appeal Tribunal has confirmed that it was justifiable for Next to rely on market forces to distinguish between different groups of employees, where there was a good rationale to pay one group more than the other.

"In this case, Next had to pay a higher market rate to warehouse operatives because of recruitment and retention pressures, which did not apply to the workforce in its stores. Next believes this element of the judgment is not only correct in law, but also a victory for common sense.

"The judgment affirms a principle at the heart of any effective employment market - that employers must be able to pay what is necessary to recruit the people they need; and that doing so does not oblige them to raise the pay of other employees where there is no reason to do so."

Leigh Day said judges did uphold 2024 findings on night-time premiums, overtime premiums and paid rest breaks.

Next said it will now seek permission to appeal these decisions.

Both the original Employment Tribunal and the Appeal Tribunal found there was no direct sex discrimination in Next's pay rates. Shop floor staff are predominantly women while warehouse workers are predominantly male.

Questions are now being asked about if this result could set a precedent across the industry. Tesco, Asda, Morrisons, and Sainbury's are all involved in similar long running claims and will be studying the findings closely.

Last year, thousands of female workers at Birmingham City Council heard how much money they will receive in a long-awaited equal pay settlement. Brighton and Hove City Council is also facing over 1,000 equal pay cases.

News.title: Jorja Smith, Chase & Status and Sam Smith to head up Radio 1's Live Lounge month
News.content:
Sam Smith, Chase & Status and Jorja Smith are among the artists who have been revealed for BBC Radio 1's Live Lounge month.

Indie band Blossoms, singer-songwriter Rachel Chinouriri and US rappers Anderson .Paak and Cordae will also take to the studio in October.

Each Live Lounge guest traditionally performs an acoustic version of one of their own songs, plus a cover of a track by a different artist.

The sessions will air on Radio 1's Live Lounge show, which will now be fronted by Charlie Hedges and Jeremiah Asiamah.

The recordings will go out throughout October on Mondays, Wednesdays and Fridays at midday on the pair's new show.

A performance from Stockport-formed band Blossoms on 5 October will kick off the run.

Rock band Nothing But Thieves, US rising star Stella Lefty, Brit-nominated singer Beabadoobee and London-based artist Odeal are also among the artists on the line-up.

Brighton duo Royal Blood will close out this year's sessions on 30 October, but a surprise artist, who will perform just before them, is still to be announced.

West Midlands superstar Jorja Smith will be performing following on from the release of her third album, What Are The Odds.

The Brit Award winner's latest album received largely positive reviews, with Rolling Stone UK describing it as her "best album yet". , external

Electronic heavyweights Chase & Status will also take to the studio after they headlined Reading and Leeds Festival last month.

And Oscar-winner Sam Smith will be rolling out their vocals following on from the release of their fifth album, Hazel Eyes, last month.

News.title: Far-right anti-migrant protests escalate amid fears of wider mobilisation
News.content:

Police officers were injured and vehicles damaged when a second major anti-migrant protest turned violent as fears grow over further far-right unrest and disorder across the UK.

Less than 48 hours after masked vigilantes blockaded roads in Dover, around 200 black-clad activists descended on Portsmouth, where a small boat with 140 asylum seekers on board was intercepted off the coast.

In an ensuing standoff with police, some of the protesters, who were trying to stop the newly arrived migrants from being driven away, attacked officers and vehicles.

On Monday, the Home Office strongly condemned the “intimidating and thuggish behaviour”. However, politicians and campaigners raised fears of further unrest across the UK, particularly along the southern coast, with 625 people crossing the English Channel illegally over the past seven days.

Concerns have also been raised that traffickers could be shifting their desired destinations across England’s coast.

Local Patriot groups, thought to be part of a national Patriot Platform network led by Tommy Robinson associate Daniel Thomas, urged their members to be on standby to react to more migrant boats arriving at ports such as Bournemouth, Poole and Portsmouth.

But crime and policing minister Sarah Jones vowed “disorder of any kind will never be tolerated”, warning that crossing the line from a “peaceful protest into illegality will face the full force of the law”.

Giving a statement in the Commons on Monday afternoon, she said: “Peaceful protest is a fundamental part of our democracy, and it must be defended. But so too is the right of other citizens to go about their lives without undue interference, and there can be no excuse for threatening behaviour or serious disruption.

“Let me therefore make clear to the House and to the country that disorder of any kind will never be tolerated ... illegality will face the full force of the law.”

open image in gallery A standoff between police and protesters in Portsmouth after more than 100 migrants were rescued from the English Channel and landed nearby ( PA )

But she added: “None of this is to in any way minimise the very valid concerns that people have when they see vile criminal gangs exploiting our nation's generosity and people making illegal and unnecessary journeys to reach this country.”

Andy Burnham told Labour MPs and peers at a closed-doors meeting on Monday the party must work to stop the “politics of poison seeping into our streets” after the scenes of unrest.

The prime minister said the party’s mission must be to counter “fear with positivity and hope”.

“We’ve got a fantastic opportunity in our hands to change this country for the better. We go into the autumn, in really good heart, with a spring in our step,” Mr Burnham told the Parliamentary Labour Party (PLP).

“There’s a lot at stake and it requires us to counter fear with positivity and hope. We have a responsibility in the times that we’re living in. It’s a solemn responsibility to prevent the politics of poison seeping into our streets.

“We are here to speak to the politics of hope and of positivity.”

It comes after Nick Lowles, chief executive of anti-racism charity HOPE, said any failings to act on threats of mobilisation could mean “things will only get worse from here”. The group later warned that the events should be a “wake-up call for authorities to take this type of threat seriously”.

Lord Walney, who was Keir Starmer’s Independent Adviser on Political Violence and Disruption, told The Independent that the protest in Portsmouth highlighted the need for police and political leaders to “respond firmly”. He said: “Politicians who excuse extreme protestors of either right or left because they sympathise with the cause risk fanning a wave of unrest and disorder across the UK.”

Reform UK leader Nigel Farage said the country was “on the edge of serious civil disturbance”, warning the movement of small boats across the Channel was getting out of control. “I predicted an invasion, and boy is it happening,” he said.

However, he said protesters dressed in paramilitary-style uniforms were not going to solve the issue.

open image in gallery Daniel Thomas, known as Danny Tommo, live streams during the operation to rescue the migrants in Portsmouth ( PA )

So far this year, 16,513 people have been detected crossing the English Channel in small boats, which is the lowest for five years, when the same figure at this point in 2021 was 12,647.

On Monday afternoon, a press conference arranged by Reform UK home affairs spokesperson Zia Yusuf on the coast in Portsmouth was interrupted by Mr Thomas, a leading figure behind the protest in Dover.

Mr Thomas said there was no violence in Dover and, when questioned about his Patriot Platform group’s masks and attire being intimidating, said: “The reason people felt potentially intimidated was because of the faces covered. I’ve made that point very clear. The only reason they’ve done that is because no one wants to be labelled far right.”

He claimed the group members were creating an “infrastructure of men” to create a voting bloc to back “the most suitable party that is able to bring this country back into order”.

Across both incidents in Dover and Portsmouth at the weekend, neither Kent nor Hampshire and Isle of Wight forces made any arrests. However, an investigation has been launched to identify those who attacked officers and vehicles in Portsmouth.

open image in gallery Daniel Thomas interrupts Reform UK home affairs spokesman Zia Yusuf’s press conference ( PA )

Footage shared on social media from Sunday night showed protesters blocking roads in an attempt to stop the migrants being taken by coach to Kent. Mr Thomas, also known as Danny Tommo, livestreamed himself running on the beach toward the coaches, threatening those preparing to help the migrants: “If you don’t stop right now I’m calling 1,000 men to come to this place.”

The migrants’ dinghy was met by lifeboats from the Isle of Wight when it reached UK waters, having set off from the Cherbourg area. It is thought to have made one of the longest journeys of any small boat, and landings as far west as Hampshire are rare.

It is understood that the government currently has no evidence to suggest there has been a change in people smuggler tactics.

However, Mihnea Cuibus, senior researcher at the University of Oxford’s Migration Observatory, said people traffickers could change targeted landings along England’s southern coast to avoid the patrolled Calais to Dover route.

open image in gallery Local resident Sue Dewey, 68, collects some of the discarded life jackets following Sunday night's operation in Portsmouth. Local leaders say the city is not suited for such landings. ( PA )

“It’s much harder to leave by boat from around the Calais area because of all of the patrols, drones in the air, and more boots on the ground, so they're just trying to find ways to avoid that,” he told The Independent.

Donna Jones, Conservative police and crime commissioner for Hampshire and Isle of Wight, said that places such as Portsmouth are “not set up” for the arrival of migrants. Portsmouth’s Liberal Democrat council leader Steve Pitt said the city was an “unsuitable” disembarking location for the boats.

A Home Office spokesperson said: “The right to peaceful protest is fundamental to our democracy, but it must never cross a line into disorder. We thank the emergency services who safely managed this situation.

“This government is doing the hard and necessary work of bearing down on small boat crossings, with the lowest number of June to August arrivals since 2020.”

Patients with asthma using the weight loss and diabetes drug semaglutide may experience fewer attacks, a new study suggests.

The connection to reduced asthma or chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD) flare-ups was stronger among those receiving higher doses of semaglutide.

Researchers also noted that individuals with "more pronounced" asthma appeared to benefit the most.

Semaglutide acts as the key active ingredient in diabetes treatment Ozempic and weight management drug Wegovy.

It is part of a group of drugs called GLP-1 receptor agonists, also known as GLP-1s, which help to lower blood sugar levels and slow down digestion, helping people stay fuller for longer.

open image in gallery Boxes containing Wegovy (semaglutide) tablets. Semaglutide acts as the key active ingredient in Ozempic and Wegovy ( Reuters )

“GLP-1 receptor agonists are widely used to treat type 2 diabetes and obesity. Previous research suggests that they may have anti-inflammatory effects and may improve lung-related outcomes, however, asthma and COPD outcomes have not been included as outcomes in GLP-1 drug trials,” said study lead Professor Chloe Bloom, clinical associate professor in respiratory epidemiology at the National Heart and Lung Institute at Imperial College London.

“We wanted to use real-world health records to investigate whether people with asthma or COPD who started GLP-1 receptor agonists had fewer acute respiratory attacks.”

The study, presented to the European Respiratory Society Congress in Barcelona, Spain, examined whether a number of treatments were linked to a reduction in exacerbations.

Experts examined UK medical records of tens of thousands of people who started GLP-1s.

Prof Bloom said: “The effect was strongest with semaglutide especially in people with asthma, where use of semaglutide appears to be associated with nearly 40 per cent reduction in asthma attacks.

“Semaglutide also led to a 20 per cent reduction in COPD flare-ups.”

She added: “The findings from this study are encouraging, but they should not change treatment decisions on their own.

“People with asthma or COPD should not start GLP-1 receptor agonists specifically for their lung condition outside current prescribing guidance.

“While the findings suggest that some people taking GLP-1 receptor agonists may experience fewer respiratory attacks, this needs confirmation in clinical trials.”

Commenting on the study, Dr Alexander Mathioudakis, chairman of the European Respiratory Society’s Group on Airway Pharmacology and Treatment, said: “This is one of the largest real-world studies to investigate GLP-1 receptor agonists and airways disease, and one of the first to examine whether effects differ between individual GLP-1 receptor agonists.

open image in gallery Researchers noted individuals with "more pronounced" asthma appeared to benefit the most from the drug ( Getty/iStock )

“It highlights the need to consider metabolic health as part of respiratory care.

“It also supports the case for including respiratory outcomes, such as asthma attacks and COPD exacerbations, in future trials of metabolic therapies.”

Dr Samantha Walker, director of research and innovation at Asthma + Lung UK, said: “This promising study indicates that people already taking semaglutide for diabetes or obesity experience a significant reduction in asthma attacks and COPD flare ups. The positive effects of semaglutide were significant for patients with asthma and COPD compared with other GLP-1 agnostics but stronger in asthma.

“These exciting findings build on research funded by Asthma + Lung UK, using existing health data to improve our understanding of lung health treatments.

“For people with asthma living with conditions like diabetes or obesity, this is a promising step forward in helping to treat their lung health.

“Cutting edge research like this is vital to improve the health and lives of people with lung conditions but funding for lung health research is on life support. While lung conditions remain the third biggest cause of death in the UK, we need urgent action to boost research investment and improve health outcomes.”

Sandra Bullock and Nicole Kidman view “Practical Magic” very differently today than they did when they made it 28 years ago.

In 1998, the film received mixed reviews and had a modest box office performance. It has since become a cult favorite, embraced by a new generation who found the romantic comedy through social media clips. The two Oscar winners are returning to their roles of witchy sisters Sally and Gillian Owens in “Practical Magic 2,” in theaters on Sept. 10, giving them a chance to reckon with the original’s rocky reception and its unlikely second life.

Both films trace their roots to Alice Hoffman’s novels: “Practical Magic,” published in 1995, inspired the original film, while her 2021 novel “The Book of Magic” expands the Owens family’s story and provides inspiration for the sequel.

‘Maybe it needed to marinate’

Bullock recalls a promotional push for the original film that became memorable — for the wrong reasons.

“I had so much trauma from the press junket from the first one because it was brutal,” Bullock recalls. “We were not well-received because we were ‘too much,’ ‘too witchy,’ ‘too many women,’ ‘too many tones.’ I’m like, ‘Have you lived a day in a life as a woman?’ ”

“We didn’t stumble, but it stumbled, but it didn’t really stumble. Maybe it needed to marinate a little bit. We were marinating,” said Bullock. “But here we are, and how lucky are we that we’re still here to be able to go reap the benefits and the rewards of our work?”

The movie eventually found the audience it had missed in theaters, and Bullock said she realized there had been a reappraisal about six years ago.

“I was still harboring so much shame,” she said. “I was like, ‘Oh my god, the things that were said, I’m sorry, we thought we were doing something nice.’ And turns out we did. It was just 28 and change years too early.”

Reclaiming the witch

Part of that second life, Bullock believes, reflects a broader change in the way people have come to view the word “witch.”

“A witch has always been a negative connotation. It was presented that way. The word is being taken back, and there’s ownership of it from the community saying, ‘I’m a witch and I’m proud,’ ” Bullock said.

For Kidman, the film’s resurgence became personal.

“People started just coming into my life who would go, 'You want to know what my favorite film of yours is? ‘Practical Magic.’ And suddenly I was like, ‘What? Wow, OK,’ ” she said.

When it came time to make the sequel, Bullock sat down with her children and their friends to watch the original.

“I wanted fresh eyes,” she said. “Because we were embarking on the new chapter, the new baby witches coming in. I wanted to understand it from a point of view I didn’t have. I wanted to see what they had to say.”

Building the magic again

As producers, Bullock and Kidman also faced the practical realities of mounting a legacy sequel on a budget. Among the challenges was recreating one of the original film’s most recognizable elements: the Owens house.

The production rebuilt the house on a London back lot as a full structure, rather than the temporary exterior shell used for the original film.

“It was an incredibly tough fiscal time. We were hedging the dollar,” Bullock said. “We’re not a big superhero film, so you don’t get the luxury of a big price tag.”

Kidman added: “And we also knew the responsibility of bringing it in on a certain price because then you go, 'OK, we can breathe a bit,' ” she said. “I think when a budget blows out, you’re like, ‘Oh my gosh, the stress.’ And we don’t need any more stress in our lives. It’s stressful enough.”

A new generation of witches

The sequel continues the story of the younger generation of Owens women, with Joey King and Maisie Williams playing Kylie and Antonia Owens, the daughters of Sally.

“I really appreciate that it’s like a passing of the baton. I think it’s beautiful,” King said. “It just felt like we were stepping into their world and doing this with them, and it’s a real gift and honor to be considered the people who are taking the batons.”

Producer Denise Di Novi, who also produced the original and cast King in her first leading role in 2010's “Ramona and Beezus,” said the new characters could carry the story forward.

“We would love to make a third one, and I think there’s so much more to do with Kylie and Antonia," she said. “At the end of the movie, spoiler alert, but you kind of feel like the Sally and Gillian characters are kind of the elder aunts, you know, and Kylie and Antonia are the ones launching off into the world as witches.”

Williams is also hoping to expand on the younger Owens women’s story: “We’re so there for it. There’s so much more of ‘Book of Magic’ that we didn’t get to explore,” she said.

An Amazon cargo plane that killed five people when it overshot the runway and crashed in Miami on Sunday left behind a scene of “utter devastation,” according to the National Transportation Safety Board.

The crash spread jet fuel “everywhere” across the impact site, while a Ford van with seven people inside it was “torn apart” by the Boeing jet, NTSB chair Jennifer Homendy told reporters on Monday in Miami.

The destruction was “hard to see,” Homendy said.

“I’m sure it must’ve been very difficult for the responders as well,” she added.

The van, struck inside the grounds of the airport, was owned by a cleaning contractor, Professional Ocean Service Corporation, the NTSB said.

open image in gallery An Amazon cargo plane overshot the runway in Miami on Sunday and crashed, killing five people and leaving behind a scene of “utter devastation,” according to the National Transportation Safety Board, which has recovered the Boeing 737’s flight data and cockpit voice recorders for analysis ( Getty )

The plane hit another vehicle, a Toyota Corolla SUV, after bursting through an airport fence, part of a violent crash that left the jet roughly 1,300 feet past the end of the runway surface.

The NTSB did not comment on the health status of the two-person crew flying the Boeing 737-300, but Homendy said those killed in the crash were in the two automobiles.

Officials have recovered the plane’s flight data and cockpit voice recorders for analysis.

Interviews are being scheduled with any potential survivors of the crash and bystanders with relevant information.

A 32-person NTSB team is on site investigating the crash, and responders are working to gather perishable physical evidence, remove fuel from the crashed plane and recover victims.

The NTSB is expected to release more information and hold a press conference on Tuesday.

open image in gallery A 32-person NTSB team is on site investigating the crash ( Getty )

The agency is calling on the public to submit any relevant photos or videos of the crash.

A “key part” of the investigation will be whether an Engineered Material Arresting System, designed to stop planes that escape their runways, would’ve prevented more destruction, Homendy said.

Miami International Airport reportedly lacks such a system.

The flight, operated by contractor 21 Air, was on its third voyage of the day when it crashed.

It had previously flown from Cincinnati to Miami, then from Miami to San Juan, Puerto Rico. The crash occurred as the plane returned to Miami from San Juan.

The NTSB did not discuss any possible causes of the crash.

Video obtained by CNN shows the jet appearing to hover unusually above the runway as it flew over its landing zone, while its left rear landing gear bounced on the tarmac.

Policing minister Sarah Jones has blamed the Conservatives for "the frustration we see in our communities today" following a weekend of anti-migrant demonstrations in Dover and Portsmouth.

The unrest in Portsmouth overnight on Sunday resulted in damaged official vehicles and injuries to several police officers following a stand-off with masked demonstrators.

This followed actions on Saturday, where black-clad, masked crowds blocked access to the Port of Dover, drawing condemnation from all political parties.

Ms Jones warned that any protesters stepping "from peaceful protest into illegality will face the full force of the law".

She also labelled Patriot Platform, the group claiming to have organised the Dover event, as "far-right racist".

Addressing the Commons, she said approximately 120 migrants arrived by boat near the Isle of Wight on Sunday afternoon, after which more than 200 protesters tried to block three coaches transporting the arrivals for processing.

She told MPs on Monday: “Let us never forget that the frustration we see in our communities today is a product of chaos and crisis in the years that preceded the general election of 2024.

“Since then, this Government has taken action to fix the broken system we inherited and bear down on the people smugglers.”

open image in gallery More than 200 protesters then attempted to stop three coaches which were due to take the arrivals for processing ( Reuters )

Shadow home secretary Chris Philp hit back at her, saying: “If they’re serious about fixing this and ending public anger, they need to get serious about the measures – leave the ECHR (European Convention on Human Rights) and deport illegal immigrants as soon as they arrive.

“Then people won’t be so angry.”

And Suella Braverman, a former Conservative home secretary, said people in her Hampshire constituency “are terrified, they are furious and they are desperate – they are not far-right racists”.

Mrs Braverman, who is now the Reform UK MP for Fareham and Waterlooville, said the Government’s response to the arrival of small boats “has been frankly pathetic”, pointing to “leaflets to illegal migrants, asking them not to rape British girls and women”.

Hampshire and Isle of Wight Constabulary has started an investigation into potential assaults and criminal damage, but Ms Jones said no arrests have been made so far.

The chairman of Hampshire Police Federation, Spencer Wragg, described the scenes in Portsmouth as “merely criminal behaviour of assaults, damage and intimidation”.

He said officers “became the target for some of the protest” on Sunday, adding: “Thankfully, there are no serious injuries to officers, but the professionalism they showed in the face of provocation and immense pressure was admirable.

“Those scenes in that area of Portsmouth weren’t protests, they weren’t protests at all, it was clear that some people were intent on disorder and venting their frustrations.

“If people have a point to make, and an issue they want to legitimately protest about, that is not about assaulting officers, that is not about damaging vehicles or anything like that. That is just disorder.”

Patriot Platform founder Daniel Thomas, known as Danny Tommo – an associate of right-wing activist Tommy Robinson – confronted Reform UK’s Zia Yusuf, telling him his party leader Nigel Farage needs to be “careful with his words”.

Interrupting an interview the home affairs spokesperson was conducting, Mr Thomas accused Mr Farage of calling protesters at the Unite the Kingdom rally in London earlier in the year “knuckle-draggers”.

open image in gallery Patriot Platform founder Daniel Thomas confronted Reform UK’s Zia Yusuf, telling him his party leader Nigel Farage needs to be ‘careful with his words’ ( PA )

Mr Thomas was a leader of the Portsmouth protest on Sunday.

The demonstration at Dover appeared to have come as a surprise to the authorities, with Kent Police claiming it was “spontaneous”.

Questions have been raised over whether either the Kent or Hampshire force was prepared for the disorder.

Liberal Democrat home affairs spokesman Max Wilkinson pressed for a review of “why the police were caught off-guard”.

He said: “How is it that far-right thugs in balaclavas were able to close Britain’s busiest port without the police receiving any prior intelligence, and how is it that then an apparently separate group, with some commonalities, were then able to blockade another site the next evening?

Ms Jones replied: “It wouldn’t be appropriate for Government to comment on specific intelligence matters on these cases, but of course we are looking at all decisions that were taken, and we will learn any lessons.”

Kent Police assistant chief constable Nigel Brookes said the only criminal offence under investigation was damage to a road.

Ms Jones told MPs there has been a trend of migrants leaving France “to the western end”.

She added: “We have pushed some of that resource from the French police down the coastline, but of course, we will be monitoring all those things.”

Ms Jones continued: “Because we are making it harder for people to launch from their sort of traditional places, that people are starting to launch further west along the French coast.

“There’s no evidence to suggest that they want to particularly land anywhere other than to get to Manston (arrivals centre in Kent) and to go where they would normally go. But, of course, we will keep these things totally under review.”

The government is set to unveil a ban on the trade of goods and some services from Israeli settlements in the West Bank after promising to take a tougher stance in support of Gaza.

It is understood that foreign secretary Ed Miliband will make the announcement in the Commons on Tuesday as part of a reset of Britain’s relations with Israel.

The decision comes in response to controversial plans in the occupied West Bank, in which Israel issued tenders for 1,200 homes as part of the E1 settlement project.

Mr Miliband described the plans as an “unacceptable and destructive act” as he vowed to take action, with Israel warning it would retaliate to any response from the UK.

He said last month: “In the coming weeks we will set out a comprehensive set of measures to respond to Israeli government policies, protect the viability of the Palestinian state, target sanctions at those who participate in illegal settlement expansion and support a just and lasting peace for Israelis and Palestinians.”

Mr Miliband’s latest announcement is expected to draw strong criticism from the US, with the Trump administration set to issue a statement condemning the move, The Times reported.

open image in gallery Donald Trump’s administration is expected to attack the decision ( Getty/AP )

Andy Burnham is understood to have discussed the plans in a phone call with Donald Trump on Monday, with Downing Street saying the prime minister “set out the UK’s commitment to working towards peace and security in the region, stressing the importance of the two-state solution.”

It comes just days after the US president’s ambassador to Israel, Mike Huckabee, accused the British government of “Jew hate” after Mr Miliband said vital medicines on their way to Gaza were being blocked.

In a video describing what he had been told by people working in the area, the foreign secretary said: “Frankly, it was horrific, what is unfolding.

“The stories that people were telling me of medicines being blocked [and] children dying while waiting for vital life-saving treatment.”

Mr Huckabee hit back on X, writing: “The Brits have lost it. The Jew hate of their government knows no boundaries and knows no facts.”

open image in gallery Ed Miliband has promised to take a tougher stance on Israel ( PA Wire )

Israel promised earlier this month that it would respond if Britain imposed sanctions over its plans to expand West Bank settlements.

“If Britain acts against Israel, Israel will act against Britain,” foreign minister Gideon Saar said “If they act, I think they will be making a big mistake.”

Violence and land and water seizures by militant Jewish settlers have risen in the West Bank since the Hamas-led October 7 attacks on Israel.

Mr Miliband said the impact of settler violence “has been catastrophic for Palestinian communities.

“Settlement expansion and attempts to create irreversible divisions on the ground threaten peace, security and the prospects for a viable Palestinian state. Britain will not stand back and accept the destruction of the two-state solution.”

A YouGov survey found that 50 per cent of Britons would support a ban on trade with Israeli settlements in the West Bank, while only 16 per cent would oppose such a move.

KFC has appointed its first-ever global chief brand officer as the fast-food chain looks to make a comeback amid fierce competition.

Amy Ellis Durini — a longtime executive at KFC’s parent company, Yum Brands — was appointed to the role, effective November 1, the company said in a press release.

Durini will lead global brand strategy and oversee brand, loyalty, retail and new concept development and innovation. Her appointment to the role comes amid efforts to modernize the KFC brand and help improve the fried chicken chain’s positioning among competitors.

While the chain is successful overseas, its U.S. arm has been attempting a comeback, looking to rival competitor chicken chains like Raising Cane’s and Chick-fil-A. The chain announced a rebrand this June that includes new menu items and a new logo as part of an effort to lure back those customers.

The new logo features Colonel Sanders sandwiched between “KFC” in the shape of a chicken bucket.

open image in gallery KFC has appointed Amy Ellis Durini to become its first-ever global chief brand officer as the company looks to make a comeback ( AP )

The company said it was looking to make its logo feel “more relevant, more expressive, and more in tune with modern culture” while “keeping it’s “iconic ‘Finger Lickin’ Good’ ethos,” according to a statement.

The rebranding effort also included changes to stores and a revamped menu that features more boneless chicken, more than 20 new flavors of dipping sauces and a variety of drinks.

The new dips range includes flavors like include “Chimichurri Ranch” and “Hot Honey Habanero.”

open image in gallery KFC revamped some of its stores over the summer as part of its efforts to rebrand ( PA )

KFC, which has 34,000 locations globally, is also joining scores of other fast food restaurants in expanding its drink selection.

The new drink line, available under the sub-brand Kwench by KFC, includes “Boba Refreshers,” sparkling lemonades and iced coffees.

The offerings are already available in some U.K. and Ireland locations and will expand from a pilot program to permanent menu items in Australia and Canada sometime this year. It was not immediately clear when they would arrive in the U.S.

Establishing global chief brand and marketing officer roles is one way companies attempt to bring consistency to their operations, Restaurant Dive reports.

Valier Kubizniak has acted as KFC’s global chief marking officer since 2022 and has been working on KFC’s most recent overhaul, according to the report.

In addition to KFC’s revamp, Yum Brands just finished selling Pizza Hut for $2.7 billion, concluding years of struggles for the pizza chain.

Andy Burnham has urged Labour to halt the "politics of poison seeping into our streets” after a weekend of unrest at anti-migrant demonstrations.

Addressing MPs and peers in a private meeting on Monday, the Prime Minister stated that the party needs to focus on countering "fear with positivity and hope".

The comments follow a disruption on Saturday where groups of masked men obstructed roads to the Port of Dover.

Further confrontation occurred in Portsmouth on Sunday, resulting in damage to official vehicles and injuries to a small number of police officers.

“We’ve got a fantastic opportunity in our hands to change this country for the better. We go into the autumn, in really good heart, with a spring in our step,” the Prime Minister told the Parliamentary Labour Party (PLP).

“There’s a lot at stake and it requires us to counter fear with positivity and hope. We have a responsibility in the times that we’re living in. It’s a solemn responsibility to prevent the politics of poison seeping into our streets.

open image in gallery Any demonstrators who crossed the line from peaceful protest into illegality would ‘face the full force of the law’, policing minister Sarah Jones ( PA )

“We are here to speak to the politics of hope and of positivity.”

Setting the tone ahead of party conference in the autumn, the Prime Minister said his government would be “boldly, authentically, confidently Labour” and focus on making the public believe that politics can work to improve their lives.

“We have to fulfil our historic mission all over again and bring hope to a divided country. To lift people and make them feel that things are possible. That we can make people’s lives better,” he said.

“Never accept the narrative that there’s nothing we can do.”

More than 200 protesters attempted to stop coaches which were due to take migrants for processing after around 120 people arrived in a boat near the Isle of Wight in the early afternoon on Sunday.

Policing minister Sarah Jones warned earlier there was “no excuse” for threatening behaviour and any demonstrators who crossed the line from peaceful protest into illegality would “face the full force of the law”.

She told the Commons that Patriot Platform, the group which claims to have organised the demonstration in Dover, was “far-right racist”.

Responding, shadow home secretary Chris Philp said the right to protest “should never be violently exercised”, but criticised the Government’s record on migration.

open image in gallery Further confrontation occurred in Portsmouth on Sunday, resulting in damage to official vehicles and injuries to a small number of police officers ( PA )

“If they’re serious about fixing this and ending public anger, they need to get serious about the measures – leave the ECHR (European Convention on Human Rights) and deport illegal immigrants as soon as they arrive.

“Then people won’t be so angry,” he said.

The demonstration at Dover appeared to have come as a surprise to the authorities, with Kent Police claiming it was “spontaneous”.

Hampshire and Isle of Wight Constabulary has launched an investigation into potential assaults and criminal damage following the unrest in Portsmouth.

Labour MP for Dover and former migration minister Mike Tapp called on Mr Burnham to convene a Cobra meeting on what he described as a “national emergency” over the small boat crossings.

“We have to gain control of the borders, and of course we’ve made progress but by convening Cobra, all of the mechanisms of government can come behind this problem and we can do our best to solve it,” he told Sky’s The Cathy Newman Show.

“It’s uncontrolled borders, although we have gained some control.”

News.title: The Chancellor’s speech, as it happened
News.content:
John Healey failed to rule out tax rises at next month’s Budget in his first major speech as Chancellor.

Mr Healey also sought to blame Liz Truss and her mini-Budget in 2022 for the high borrowing costs being paid by the Treasury.

During a speech in Coventry, the Chancellor said he would be “honest” about the need to control public spending during his time in Number 11.

He was speaking days after the cost of government borrowing hit its highest level since 2007.

It was also overshadowed by Jaguar Land Rover announcing plans to cut 4,000 jobs in the face of “intense competition and ongoing geopolitical uncertainty”.

Read our report on the Chancellor’s speech.

News.title: Maitland-Niles’ last-gasp debut goal salvages Everton’s miserable week
News.content:
At the final whistle, the first song the stadium DJ played was Spirit of the Blues and how those relieved Evertonians lapped it up after a week of angst.

Their team had been on the precipice of a defeat that would have exacerbated all the frustrations that bubbled away following the chaotic conclusion to the transfer window. Indeed, it was 10 seconds over the allotted five minutes of added time when the ball fell to Ainsley Maitland-Niles.

It had been three years since the former Arsenal full-back had played in the Premier League – his last goal in England was on October 30, 2019, in an EFL Cup tie with Liverpool at Anfield that ended 5-5 – and he would not have joined Everton if their attempt to sign Kenny Tete from Fulham had not failed.

But here he was 30 yards from goal, with no need to break his stride as Manchester United’s backtracking defenders presented him with an invitation to shoot. So that’s what he did. With one perfectly timed swish of his right foot, an unlikely hero transformed the mood of a club.

News.title: Arsenal teach Chelsea a lesson in how to be champions
News.content:
This is how champions are supposed to play and, although the Arsenal home support have not seen a team defend their place at the apex of English league football for two decades, they knew it when they saw it.

The chase was on for Mikel Arteta’s team within two minutes when Morgan Rogers, the man who might have moved to Arsenal this summer, put his new club Chelsea in the lead. So unfolded a thrilling 100 minutes of Premier League competition. Arsenal were the better team in terms of ambition and attack even if one could not discount Chelsea until the very last moment.

Others might have crumbled. That Chelsea did not will give Xabi Alonso hope for a team that did not feature the injured Moisés Caicedo and is now without the departed Enzo Fernández. Yet he will also recognise that his childhood friend from San Sebastián in the other dugout has created a side that treated the game, and their place in it, with an urgency that looks different. The first two minutes might have been ragged for Arsenal but after that they did not let the game happen to them.

News.title: Antonelli walks on water while Hamilton rages from mountaintop
News.content:
The 20-year-old also benefited from a perfectly-timed (from his perspective at least) mid-race virtual safety car when Lance Stroll retired his Aston Martin, which allowed Antonelli a cheap stop to switch to fresh mediums while Russell stayed out on used hards. But at some point you just have to take your hat off to the youngster.

Antonelli was irresistible. He had already surged from 19th on the grid to 12th by the time the red flag came out at the end of lap 2. He was up to sixth a couple of laps after the race resumed. And by lap 18 of a 53-lap race, he had passed Russell for the lead for the first time. That is some going.

Having caught up to Russell, the two Mercedes drivers engaged in an entertaining battle for a few laps, the pair of them yo-yoing in and out of the lead before Russell got past Antonelli on lap 23 and managed to make it stick.

But the key moment of the race came on lap 27 when Stroll stopped at the first chicane and the VSC came out. For Antonelli, the decision to switch to fresh mediums was clear. He was going to struggle to make it to the end of the race. Far better to drop a few positions and fight back on fresh rubber.

For Russell, it was far trickier. He was in the lead of the race. He was on hard tyres which he knew could get to the end of the race. And he also had the problem of Red Bull’s Max Verstappen, who at the time he was struggling to shake off.

Mercedes chose to keep Russell out there. In hindsight, it may have been the wrong decision. Had he stopped at that point, he would at least have stayed ahead of Antonelli, and on the same tyres. By staying out, he kept the lead but found himself relentlessly hunted down by the Italian.

By lap 49, the Italian had caught up to him. Antonelli botched his first attempt at reclaiming the lead, going wide onto the gravel at the first chicane. But he made no mistake one lap later as Russell was once again left licking his wounds.

News.title: VAR a scourge on the Premier League as Forest denied by off-field meddling
News.content:
“I don’t know if it’s streetwise but he knows how to win,” Maresca said, who is in line to hand Fernández his debut against Coventry on Saturday. “When you want to compete or win, it’s much more important to have players that already know how to do that than players who have never done it in the past.

“Enzo is not the only one. This squad has many players who know how to win titles and how to compete and this is what we are looking for.

“I know Enzo quite well and I know what he can bring to the team. He is a winner, [has] a winner’s mentality and knows how to win [after] the World Cup, Club World Cup [success].

“I just said he is a winner and when you belong to the squad and another winning player arrives, they are always happy.

“I can promise you that in the last four or five days, four or five players from the squad were asking if was coming or not because they wanted him to be with us. It’s very important that he is with us.”

Maresca said he planned to use Fernandez predominantly as a No 6 or No 8 depending on the game. “I see Enzo as a six, a little bit more deep, or [an eight] a little higher arriving in the box,” he said.

News.title: Newcastle’s limitations exposed by Bournemouth before hosts fight back for draw
News.content:
A reality check is not necessarily a bad thing. There has been a lot of hype and excitement on Tyneside and a self-congratulating tone to their own end of summer appraisals.

But this was a reminder of the team’s limitations and the fact that only three of their eight summer signings started the game, with two more coming off the bench, underlined they are a work in progress.

In truth, that is fine. It is the start of September and the Premier League campaign is only three games old. They have a new manager and a new-look team. There has been a significant amount of change in a very short period of time.

It was not the easiest summer, and despite the insistence from senior figures at the club that they had always remained calm and methodical during their summer reset, there was a whiff of crisis only a few weeks ago.

When Eddie Howe quit as manager and Bruno Guimarães, the captain, forced his move to Arsenal at the start of August, Newcastle looked in disarray. So, to have started the season unbeaten from three games against Liverpool, Tottenham Hotspur and Bournemouth is encouraging.

It is also worth highlighting just how good the visitors were. In the first half Bournemouth were superb, rushing Newcastle, forcing mistakes and pouring forward in numbers. In Alex Scott, just as he was in their victory here last season, Bournemouth had the best player on the pitch.

That opens up another conversation. Newcastle played like this a lot at home in Howe’s final season in charge, especially in the second-half of the campaign, but tended to lose not draw the game.

On this occasion, they secured a decent point with a late equaliser thanks to substitute Ramsey, who looked good when he replaced the off-colour Lewis Miley.

Bournemouth will feel they should have held on. They had taken a deserved lead through Marcus Tavernier, who took advantage of a static and ball-watching Amar Dedić to bundle home from close range.

News.title: Relentless Springboks give All Blacks 15 minutes of hell to lead series
News.content:
There will be no repeat of the All Blacks historic Test series victory in South Africa 30 years ago, after the home side ruthlessly ensured they will lead 2-1 going into the concluding weekend.

And the manner in which the Springboks blew away their fierce rivals in the last 15 minutes made Rassie Eramus’s men overwhelming favourites to finish the job in America next Saturday.

However, there were passages of this brutal battle that suggested that Rugby’s Greatest Rivalry could still produce a finale worthy of the billing if New Zealand can learn the lessons from this brutal encounter at the FNB Stadium in Johannesburg.

There was a late Kiwi try to give the scoreboard a humdinger hue but Erasmus’s side were well deserving of their second victory in as many Saturdays over their fierce rivals, and credit to the South Africa coach for outwitting counterpart Dave Rennie without needing to change his starting XV just before the kick-off, like he did seven days before.

Amazing what one can do with a simple but chilling game plan. The old scoundrel knew that if he slowed it down and let his scrum walk round the All Blacks scrum that his backs would have the precious space.

Yet, however it might feel away from Springbok turf, New Zealand will still fancy their chances of levelling it, especially after matching their opponents’ haul of four tries. Their fly-half, Ruben Love, missed five simple-enough points and until that last quarter it was an even contest. Yet, as it tends to, South Africa’s physical intensity and their almighty scrum eventually prevailed.

News.title: Gasly takes shock Italian GP pole and denies Russell
News.content:
Welcome to Telegraph Sport’s live coverage of and qualifying for the Monza Grand Prix.

Before the weekend’s racing, George Russell was, at least publicly, less than bullish about his chances in Italy.

He did, though, believe he would deliver a better showing than he had in recent weeks.

“I don’t know if we can say we’re favourites this weekend, but we probably have a greater opportunity than we’ve had in the last two races where it’s been less about the power unit and more about the chassis,” he said.

“It’s so close right now, that last tenth in qualifying can be the difference of a couple of positions, which can change the podium. Right now, I don’t know who is going to be the team to beat.”

Russell was almost a minute off winner Lando Norris of McLaren in Hungary, finishing seventh in his Mercedes. Two weeks ago, in the Netherlands, he took the last spot on the podium, with Norris winning again.

However, in the second practice session on Friday and FP3 today, Russell was quickest. He led his former colleague, Ferrari’s Lewis Hamilton, who was second fastest.

Red Bull’s Max Verstappen hinted at a rare good weekend as he was third fastest, about a third of a second behind Russell.

Russell, of course, needs a win soon, or he is in danger of seeing the championship run away from him entirely, as Kimi Antonelli already leads him by 59 points in the world title chase.

Perhaps psychologically just as pressing is that erstwhile teammate Hamilton is tied with Russell on 183 points, in third because he has one victory compared to Russell’s two. Slipping down the rankings could knock his confidence.

Russell has not secured pole for the last four races, so a strong showing in qualifying might be the boost he needs ahead of Sunday’s race, while Norris is looking for a pole position hat-trick.

Sports.title: Jose Mourinho can seal Champions League history with Real Madrid but must answer burning question
Sports.content:
THERE are managers who crave recognition, attention, the spotlight.

And then there is Jose Mourinho.

A man who believes the football world — maybe even the whole globe — revolves around him.



But if the Portuguese is going to become the first boss to lift the Champions League with three different clubs, it is surely now.

Or, perhaps, continue the journey towards the obscurity which would leave even Mourinho, for all his ego, destitute.



His return to Real Madrid seems to have been scripted as the ultimate redemption story.

The self-styled Special One was hounded out of the Bernabeu 13 years ago, jettisoned as the victim of player power from a dressing room that refused to be told what to do.



Then this summer, recruited once more by Florentino Perez and hailed as the antidote to fix a different Madrid squad that spent last term bickering with the coaching staff and physically taking actual lumps out of each other on the training ground.

We all know the Mourinho story. A force of nature at Porto, Chelsea and Inter Milan — winning the Champions League with the Portuguese and Italian clubs — conquering unlikely peaks while fighting with every fibre of his body.

Yet equally, the fall-out at Madrid, the return to Chelsea that brought a third Premier League crown but internal war, including a fatal public spat with the team doctor and an ignominious exit.

And the short-lived spells at Manchester United, Tottenham, Roma, Fenerbahce and Benfica, a gradual fading of the light that once burned so bright.



SUN VEGAS WELCOME OFFER: GET UP TO £100 BONUS

Fixtures Results Table AEK Athens 17:45 League Stage LASK Club Brugge 17:45 League Stage Villa Real Madrid 20:00 League Stage Inter Lille 20:00 League Stage Betis Dortmund 20:00 League Stage Villarreal Porto 20:00 League Stage Man City Lyon 1 – 2 AGG 2 – 3 Fenerbahçe Celje 1 – 2 AGG 2 – 3 Slovan Viking 3 – 1 AGG 5 – 3 Dinamo Zagreb AEK Athens 4 – 0 AGG 4 – 0 Levski Bodø/Glimt 3 – 0 AGG 6 – 1 NEC LASK 5 – 1 AGG 5 – 4 Celtic Pld Pts GD W D L 1 AEK Athens 0 0 0 0 0 0 2 Arsenal 0 0 0 0 0 0 3 Villa 0 0 0 0 0 0 4 Atlético 0 0 0 0 0 0 5 Barcelona 0 0 0 0 0 0 6 FC Bayern 0 0 0 0 0 0 7 Bodø/Glimt 0 0 0 0 0 0 8 Dortmund 0 0 0 0 0 0

It means this second Madrid incarnation is make or break. While regaining LaLiga supremacy is important to the club, triumphing in Europe is Mourinho’s driving ambition.

The recent three-part Netflix documentary gives an insight into his soul.

Long-held suspicions that he considers himself the inheritor of the navigators, who discovered uncharted lands for colonisation, were confirmed.

But unlike Christopher Columbus, Vasco da Gama and Ferdinand Magellan, Mourinho wanted to dominate old worlds, not conquer new ones. As he admitted: “I wanted to make history — and nothing was going to stop me.”

That has not changed. But neither has time stood still.

Mourinho, 63, is more than two decades older than he was when he ran down the touchline as Porto boss at Old Trafford in 2004, his grey coat flapping.

The chiselled features are no longer quite so sharp, even if the acid tongue remains. But going one beyond the two-club European title feats of old foes Pep Guardiola and Carlo Ancelotti, as well as reigning champion Luis Enrique, would cement Mourinho’s status.



In his own words: “Greatness is to be in history.”

Kicking off against former club Inter, in a match which could feature five English players, Mourinho knows all too well the expectations . . . and the opportunity.

While Arsenal have laid down their domestic marker already, the other four Prem clubs are all under new management, while Paris Saint-Germain have two last-gasp draws and a defeat from their opening three Ligue 1 games.

The big question, as ever with Jose, is how he copes when things do not go right.

Mourinh) joined Madrid first time round believing every player was a potential ally but left convinced each of them was the enemy.



Burning question

The tall poppy theory became a self-fulfilling and damaging prophecy. So far, he has been on his best behaviour.

After the surprise 1-0 defeat at Real Betis on Friday, when a dreadful VAR call meant Kylian Mbappe was denied the chance to rectify his spot-kick miss, Mourinho avoided the blame game.

Yet the suspicion is that, if things go wrong, he will target one of his stars, Mbappe, Vinicius Jr — who will harbour doubts after Mourinho’s defence of Benfica winger Gianluca Prestianni’s abusive comments last term — or Jude Bellingham.

In the documentary, Mourinho insists: “I wanted to be loved.”



He does. But he also loves to be hated. The danger is that he finds it increasingly easier to attract the latter than the former. This feels like the final chapter.

No time to hand in chips

JUST three weekends in and the folly of Premier League chiefs refusing to use the World Cup-style connected ball has been exposed.

Spain’s LaLiga, which also uses a Puma ball, has introduced the chip technology this season but bosses decided it was not necessary here. Cue the furore over Neco Williams’ “handball goal” against Tottenham.

The chip would have helped detect any contact with a “non-goalscoring” part of Williams’ body — his arm — allowing VAR Peter Bankes to make an informed decision, rather than taking a punt.

Bankes probably made the right call to disallow the goal — photo stills seem to show Forest’s Williams accidentally handled.



But under the protocols, it’s hard to figure out how he could see it sufficiently to overturn the on-field decision from the camera angles at his disposal.

Using the latest modern technology — good enough for the second-best domestic league in the world — would have shut down the controversy.

Purrfect for Mikel

MIKEL ARTETA was the cat that got the cream on Sunday night. You couldn’t blame him, either, for his purrs of contentment.

The Basque tactician deployed his lexicon of positive adjectives at his team’s outstanding performance.

Arsenal were “exceptional”, “spectacular” and “beautiful”, Ezri Konsa “phenomenal”, Kai Havertz “amazing”, Martin Odegaard “perfect”.



Arteta had two audiences. The one in the Emirates press conference room was secondary.

After Chelsea’s pretensions were put into context, he wanted his words to reverberate around the Etihad — to get Enzo Maresca and his Manchester City team talking.

What a Fox up

A DECADE ago, Leicester were preparing for their first Champions League campaign as Premier League winners.

And five years later, it was Napoli in the Europa League as FA Cup holders. Today, Foxes fans are licking their wounds following the humiliating 4-0 League One home drubbing by Oxford.

Boss Russell Martin looks like a one-trick pony that hasn’t actually got a trick, with the club’s very future unclear and League Two football next term more than possible. Never forget, nothing in football is permanent.

Sports.title: New footage emerges of Nottingham Forest’s controversial disallowed goal vs Spurs – but it wasn’t available to VAR
Sports.content:
A NEW camera angle has surfaced of Nottingham Forest’s controversially disallowed goal against Tottenham — but it is still unlikely to end the VAR row.

Forest and Spurs played out a dramatic goalless draw at the City Ground on Saturday, which saw Roberto De Zerbi’s side pick up their first Premier League point of the season after losing their opening two matches.



However, Nottingham thought they scored the winner on 67 minutes when Neco Williams bravely lunged to the ball head first to meet captain Morgan Gibbs-White‘s lob.

Williams, 25, tried to protect his physical wellbeing by placing his arms on his face to protect himself from Tottenham star Sandro Tonali’s flying boot.



Referee Craig Pawson awarded the goal but VAR Peter Bankes stepped in to give a handball – leaving Forest and fans across the country incredulous.

Now, fresh footage appears to show the ball DID his Williams’ arm on its way into the back of the net.



But it is still not totally conclusive.

Incredibly, this angle wasn’t even shown to the VAR during the game.

The incident has been replayed over and over this weekend as fans search for conclusive proof of what happened.

Some have even claimed that even if the goal was ruled out, Forest should have been awarded a penalty for Tonali‘s kick at Williams’ head.



CASINO SPECIAL – BEST CASINO BONUSES FROM £10 DEPOSITS

PGMOL chief refereeing officer Howard Webb backed Bankes but plans to lobby for the law to be changed regarding accidental handballs.

The rule states that a goal must be axed if the ball goes into the net off a player’s hand or arm – even if completely accidental.

Webb said: “It is a law I would definitely look to change. So Pro Ref and the Premier League are going to try and lobby for that to be changed.

“At the moment, if the ball goes into the goal off your hand, accidentally or otherwise, you have to disallow that.

“And if it touches your hand accidentally or ­otherwise and then [you] score with your foot, you have to disallow the goal.



“The problem is that forces VARs on every goal to look at what body part the ball went in off.

“Most times it’s dead obvious it has come off the head or the foot. But there’s a fair number of situations where it is close to hitting the arm. The VAR has to look at it from different angles.

“There might be six angles focusing in on the player and the first three might not be conclusive.

Sports.title: Three ways Arsenal baffled Chelsea with ‘Mr Freeze’ Kai Havertz single-handedly dismantling his old side’s defence
Sports.content:
ARSENAL proved why they are the reigning Premier League champions by producing a tactical masterclass in their win over Chelsea.

Kai Havertz and Martin Odegaard sealed a crucial comeback victory after Morgan Rogers had given the West Londoners an early lead.



Mikel Arteta’s side looked completely reborn, playing with renewed freedom and swagger that suggested the crushing weight of last season’s title race has finally lifted off their shoulders.

Gone was the defensive attitude that Arsenal have been slammed for in massive fixtures in the past.



Instead, the Gunners went straight for Chelsea’s throat and they kept them penned back inside their own half even after going in front.

I predicted before the London derby that Havertz would have a big role to play against his former club.

And the German striker single-handedly dismantled Chelsea’s defensive shape.

A whopping 47 per cent of Arsenal’s attacks came down the right-hand side.

With Christos Tzolis putting in a massive shift on the left flank, Bukayo Saka, Ben White and Odegaard were reunited on the opposite side and the Gunners strategically targeted the Blues’ weakest defensive spots.

KAI SPY

The absolute key to Arsenal’s right-sided dominance was Havertz, playing right where he belongs as a roaming centre forward.

The Emirates favourite completely ruined Chelsea’s back three system by repeatedly drifting over to the right-hand channel to create an overload triangle with Saka and White.

I highlighted this exact movement in our Tactics Exposed Team Talk episode last week, calling it the “Mr Freeze” trick – and Havertz executed it to absolute perfection.

By dragging Chelsea defender Maxence Lacroix over into wide areas he desperately hated, Havertz left Wesley Fofana completely frozen in no man’s land.

That created a massive 19-metre canyon between Chelsea’s centre-backs, allowing the likes of Riccardo Calafiori and Saka to drive straight through the heart of their backline early on.



Arteta deliberately targeted this side because Blues winger Rogers pushes extremely high up the pitch on the left flank, leaving acres of space behind him for Arsenal to exploit.

With Chelsea’s best natural defenders – like Reece James – operating on the opposite side, their left flank was completely exposed.

Time and time again, Havertz unlocked Chelsea’s shape – including a brilliant nutmeg flick through Fofana’s legs for Saka and a clever dummy that set up Odegaard’s winner.



S-MARTIN ODEGAARD

Point number two belongs to skipper Odegaard, who delivered one of his bravest, most aggressive, and most dominant midfield performances in an Arsenal shirt.

Odegaard’s touch map was heavily stacked inside the opposition half, proving he was operating as a genuine, magic-making No10 rather than picking up touches on the halfway line.

When Chelsea attempted to execute a high press, Odegaard solved the problem single-handedly.

The ex-Real Madrid man dropped deep into a tight pocket between four rivals and turned sharply to instantly launch an attack.

But his biggest impact was higher up the pitch, where he spearheaded Arsenal’s brave six-man box-crashing unit.



Instead of sitting back and inviting pressure at 2-1 up, Arsenal pushed Odegaard, Gabriel, and White high into Chelsea’s penalty area, completely overwhelming their low block and keeping possession.

Odegaard’s goal was a carbon copy of his strike in the Community Shield, arriving late into the box to round off a slick team move through the heart of Chelsea’s defence.

He even took on Havertz’s “frozen man” role for Arsenal’s opener. The Norwegian talisman dragged a defender away to give his team-mate enough space to send a clinical finish past Emiliano Martinez.

Operating alongside Myles Lewis-Skelly in a balanced double pivot, the England man acted as the Gunners’ ultimate insurance policy against Chelsea’s rapid counter-attacks.

With Odegaard given total freedom to operate high up the pitch, Rice was tasked with covering an incredible amount of ground – sprinting forward to press man-for-man before rapidly tracking back.

He even showed a nasty, pragmatic side by committing a cynical Bernardo Silva-style tactical foul on his international team-mate Rogers to break up a dangerous Chelsea break.

The two of them were then involved in a bust-up, with the Arsenal man avoiding a booking.



When Joao Pedro bypassed Arsenal’s centre-backs to send Cole Palmer through, it was Rice who produced a miraculous recovery sprint to poke the ball back to safety.

By holding down the fort with Lewis-Skelly, Rice provided the rock-solid foundation for Arteta’s front line to destroy Chelsea.
