Sports.title: Crystal Palace under investigation over use of ILLEGAL sub during win at the weekend with refs also in firing line
Sports.content:
CRYSTAL PALACE have landed themselves in hot water after breaking Women’s Super League rules in their season-opening win.

The newly-promoted Eagles sealed a 1-0 victory over Everton thanks to Lexi Lloyd-Smith’s first half strike on Sunday.



But WSL chiefs have launched an investigation after Palace used four substitution windows during the showdown.

Competition rules state clubs can only make changes in a maximum of three stoppages in play.



And Palace are now at the centre of a probe which could result in being slapped with a severe punishment.

A WSL statement read: “We can confirm there was a breach of competition rules in the Crystal Palace versus Everton match.



“Crystal Palace used a fourth substitution opportunity during a fourth stoppage in play, when the rules permit a maximum of three substitution opportunities per match.

“We will now conduct an investigation alongside both clubs and Pro Ref and update in due course.”

The WSL does not have an automatic penalty for substitution rule breaches.

But Palace may be referred to an independent tribunal, which would have the power to impose a warning, fine, points deduction or other sporting sanctions including replaying the clash.

The Eagles breached WSL rules in the seventh minute of stoppage time, when Kirsty Howat replaced Shannon O’Brien.

Palace boss Jo Potter had already used three separate substitution windows to send on Abbie Larkin, Ashleigh Weerden and Allyson Swaby.

It has been confirmed the investigation will involve both clubs and referee body Pro Ref.

And the match officials for Palace’s win over Everton, including whistleblower Megan Wilson, have been stood down from the next round of fixtures after failing to comply with regulations.



Palace were promoted to the WSL last season after grabbing the runners-up spot in the second-tier.

"Oleksandr is always open to big challenges. But serious intentions are backed by a concrete offer, not statements in the press."

Usyk announced in June that he was vacating the three heavyweight belts he still held at the time, but the 39-year-old said he was not yet retiring, and has recently been linked with a fight against Deontay Wilder.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Mayor of London Sadiq Khan has called for Anthony Joshua and Tyson Fury to fight in London

Usyk, who holds a perfect 25-0 professional record, claimed successive wins over Joshua in 2021 and 2022, but has become part of the Brit's training team over the last year.

Both Joshua and Fury have signed individual contracts for what was slated to be a November contest, but have yet to agree on where the fight will take place, with speculation suggesting it could be held in New York City.

Joshua's promoter Eddie Hearn says he and his fighter want the contest to take place in London, while Fury says his rival is trying to avoid a bout that has been more than a decade in the making.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Eddie Hearn claimed that Anthony Joshua feels a responsibility to UK fight fans that AJ vs Fury should happen in the UK

"This will only lead me to a fight with Oleksandr Usyk," Fury said in a video posted on Instagram.

"Oleksandr you're his [Joshua's] trainer and his sensei and you know he is weak minded... and that he would never fight the Gypsy King which you have had the guts to do twice.

"You got the decisions last time, fair play to you. Good luck to you, let's do it again. Let's run it back in November. The ball is now in your court... do you want to fight me this year, 2026, or are you calling it quits?

"Let me know because I am now looking for a new opponent."

Sports.title: Zheng stages epic comeback to reach US Open quarters after Swiatek implodes
Sports.content:
Qinwen Zheng staged a second epic comeback at the US Open in as many days to stun former champion Iga Swiatek and book her place in the quarter-finals for the third time.

Two days on from saving match point while trailing 5-0 in the third set to Madison Keys, Zheng mounted another remarkable fightback on Arthur Ashe.

Swiatek won the first five games but Zheng simply refused to roll over, winning the next seven games to clinch the first set before overpowering her shellshocked opponent to complete an astonishing 7-5 6-3 victory.

A stunned Swiatek never recovered, and the 2022 champion succumbed in straight sets, 7-5 6-3, leaving the court in tears after her campaign unravelled in unthinkable fashion.

The former world No 4 from China, who had come through qualifying after being sidelined by a long-term elbow injury, became the first qualifier to reach the quarter-finals since Emma Raducanu won the tournament in 2021.

Zheng's reward is a last-eight tie against either Naomi Osaka or Elena Rybakina.

Image: Qinwen Zheng has matched her best ever performance at the US Open by reaching the quarter-finals

Zheng revels in being back on big stage

"I started the match not so well but I found my rhythm," Zheng said.

"It has been a long, long time since I played on a centre court and I really appreciate being here on Arthur Ashe Stadium.

"I took it point by point and little by little I started to play better and find my game.

"I even forgot the score at 4-5 in the first set, which showed I was focused. To come back from 0-5 is not lucky, that's all I can say."

Image: Qinwen Zheng, US Open (Associated Press)

'One of the great comebacks'

Sky Sports Tennis' Jonathan Overend:

"It's a straight-set win but it's one of the great comebacks. Go figure. How's that possible? Zheng made it happen.

"Two games in a row, 5-0 down in sets. She got the win against Madison Keys to get the first set today, before completing victory against Swiatek for only the second time in her career."

"The Chinese dream lives on as the qualifier makes it into the final eight."

Potapova in tears after late injury in Andreeva defeat

Anastasia Potapova was in floods of tears as her stay in New York came to an end.

The 25-year-old Austrian won the first set against fifth seed Mirra Andreeva, but, at 5-3 down in the third she badly twisted her knee chasing a forehand down.

Potapova had the knee heavily strapped up and bravely finished the match, but did not win another point as French Open champion Andreeva triumphed 5-7 6-4 6-3.

"Anastasia is a good friend, and seeing what a battle we have and then seeing her fall is not easy," said Russian teenager Andreeva.

"It's not the way you want to finish the match. I just told her she is playing amazing and I'm sure she'll come back even stronger, she's a warrior."

Sports.title: Red Bull's Hadjar to miss Spanish GP as injury absence continue
Sports.content:
Isack Hadjar will miss this weekend's Spanish Grand Prix in Madrid as he continues to recover from a fractured wrist.

Liam Lawson will replace Hadjar for a third successive race as Max Verstappen's team-mate at Red Bull, while Yuki Tsunoda continues at Racing Bulls.

Hadjar suffered a hairline fracture in a bone in his wrist during the summer break in a routine workout that involved boxing which forced him to miss the Dutch, Italian and now Spanish Grands Prix.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Isack Hadjar was reinstated to the Monaco podium last week after a Red Bull appeal.

A Red Bull statement said: "After racing for the team in Zandvoort and Monza, Liam will continue to drive alongside Max at this weekend's Spanish Grand Prix in Madrid.

"The decision has been taken as Isack's recovery continues to progress positively. While he is not yet ready to return to the cockpit, he will be in Madrid supporting the team.

"Everyone at Red Bull Racing looks forward to welcoming Isack back behind the wheel very soon."

Sports.title: Pakistan investigating 'discipline and conduct' in latest twist on crisis tour
Sports.content:
The Pakistan Cricket Board has launched an investigation into "media reports concerning discipline and conduct" amid the team's crisis tour of England.

Pakistan last week took the unprecedented step of sending seven players home and calling up seven after losing heavily at Headingley and Lord's to fall 2-0 down in the three-match series.

Head coach Sarfaraz Ahmed and assistant Umar Gul have also been replaced, with Mike Hesson, in charge of Pakistan's white-ball sides, and former Australia seamer Ashley Noffke overseeing the third Test at Edgbaston, which begins on Wednesday.

A statement read: "The Pakistan Cricket Board has initiated an internal disciplinary inquiry following media reports concerning discipline and conduct, which are currently being reviewed internally.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Watch the best of day four at Lord's as England thumped Pakistan by 194 runs to take an unassailable 2-0 lead in the three-match Test series

"The PCB handles such matters in accordance with its standard procedures. The process is being conducted under PCB regulations, ensuring that all concerned individuals are given due consideration.

"At this stage, any speculative reports or unverified claims circulating on certain platforms, particularly those originating from hostile external sources, should not be regarded as credible."

The banished senior players included Salman Ali Agha - who captained Pakistan in the first Test before being dropped for the second - wicketkeeper Mohammad Rizwan and Imam-ul-Haq, who did not bat in either innings after suffering a low-grade calf strain in the field.

Former captain Shahid Afridi described the PCB's decision to make sweeping alterations to the travelling party as the "most shocking decision ever by a selection committee".

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Pakistan's Saud Shakeel missed out on a Lord's century, holing out off Josh Tongue to fall for 97 against England in the second Test

Of the seven replacements who have been called up, only batters Saim Ayub and Abdullah Fazal have Test experience.

The PCB's statement on Monday added: "The PCB will not comment further at this time. The board advises stakeholders and the public to rely on official PCB communications."

New Pakistan coaches in the dark over investigation

Noffke addressed the media in Birmingham on Monday, admitting he was unaware of the specifics of the probe.

"I can be really honest in that I don't know too much," he said. "I sit outside of that decision-making model, (which is) above us as coaches. We try and keep the players focused on what they need to worry about.

"One thing that I've learned about being in Pakistan and coaching for a period of time, nearly 15 months now with the white-ball team, is there's always something going on in the background.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Take a look at some funny moments from the England vs Pakistan Test series!

"I think most of the time it's out of the players' control. They need to focus on the cricket that they have in front of them and the opportunity they have in front of them.

"We're not really in the position to even know the outer workings of what's happening at PCB in that context."

Noffke also admitted that taking over mid-series as part of head coach Hesson's staff was "unusual".

He added: "It doesn't happen very often and I guess from Mike and my perspective is all we can do is come in and add positivity.

"We want to listen to the players as much as we can, so there's obviously a feeling of uncertainty but also they've just got back on the job."

Sports.title: Leicester have sunk to new low under Martin but can he turn it around?
Sports.content:
A decade ago in September 2016, Leicester City were getting ready to play in the Champions League.

Now? They sit 17th in League One, the lowest position in the club's history since they entered the Football League in 1894.

Russell Martin has led the Foxes to just one win in their first five games, and on Saturday they were battered 4-0 at home by Oxford United.

Leicester fans were chanting 'you're getting sacked in the morning' at Martin at the King Power Stadium, who would have been desperate for a good start to turn his reputation around after a dismal end to his time at Southampton, and then a gruelling spell at Rangers.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Highlights of the Sky Bet League One match between Leicester City and Oxford United.

But can he turn it around? Former Leicester City assistant manager Michael Appleton believes he can.

"It's a difficult moment, there's no doubt about it," Appleton told The EFL Show on Sky Sports News.

"Russell Martin is a very experienced guy now. It was always going to be a difficult job, with big expectations from a club that not too long ago was playing in the Premier League and winning the Premier League.

Martin's miserable record Russell Martin has managed just three league wins since the start of the 2024/25 season, with Southampton, Rangers and Leicester, in 28 attempts.

"With those expectations, you've got to deliver. It's still very early, but losing 4-0 at home, along with the results against Plymouth and Burton, makes it a very difficult start. They've got to start winning games very quickly to address it.

"What I would say is that he's got experience. He's been here before, at a big club with expectations in the league they were in, and he didn't get off to the start he wanted.

"He'll draw on those experiences and maybe use them behind the scenes with the players and staff, speaking about how they dealt with those situations and trying to keep everyone calm.

"It's still very early and there are some good games coming up for them. I always say that when you're in a difficult moment and you're losing games, it feels much worse when you're at home. I'm not saying losing 4-0 at Oxford would have been a good result in any stretch of the imagination, but when it happens at home, it feels so much worse.

"There's a big expectation to deal with, but I think he's more than comfortable doing it."

Meanwhile, Reading co-CEO Joe Jacobson believes the inexperience in the squad is hurting their progress this season.

"They've got a really young team at the minute," he said. "You look at the players they're bringing off the bench and they're taking off experienced players and bringing on younger ones.

"It's difficult for those young players, who will feel the pressure and feel the atmosphere in the stadium. The fans are waiting to turn because of what's happened over the last couple of years. It takes a long time for a fan base to turn and get right behind their team again.

"They have a really tough job on their hands and Russell Martin will know that. He knows exactly what he wants to do and how he wants his team to play. Sometimes that causes division within the fan base, but I'm sure he'll be knuckling down on exactly what he wants to do with his team.

"It reminds me of when he was at Southampton. They lost four games in a row in September and then didn't lose a league match until February. If he can turn the ship, he might start to get a tune out of some of those players."

Jacobson also feels that the disconnect between the club and the fans is also causing an issue, especially since the owners announced Leicester was up for sale, having had a similar recent experience at Reading.

"It's been difficult at Reading because of what happened previously with the ownership there. We've felt it as well. It has taken a long time to get the fans to buy into what you want to do, and the ownership have done amazing things there over the years," he added.

"But when they recently came out and talked about wanting to sell the club and actively looking for a buyer, straight away the fans almost say, 'Well, you don't care now. You just want out. That's your main focus.'

"If the ownership are openly saying they want to sell, it's really difficult for the fans to buy into that. But I still think they're going to have a really successful season.

"Once these players get time on the training field with the manager, I'm sure they'll come good. At the minute, there's that anxiousness and a divided fan base. They want to support their club, but they also want to feel that everyone is pulling in the right direction."

Next up for Martin and Leicester is a trip to Stockport County on Saturday, who are currently sat third in League One.

A decade ago, the Hatters were in National League North. Now they welcome the Foxes to Edgeley Park as favourites for victory.

Sports.title: ‘Safety, security and service’: behind the scenes with police at Arsenal v Chelsea
Sports.content:
The concourses are silent when, deep in the Emirates Stadium’s bowels, Chief Inspector Pete Dearden’s briefing begins. Arsenal’s 4.30pm kick-off against Chelsea is still hours away but the fixture carries significance as a London derby and because the Premier League champions are hosting a realistic challenger.

Dearden is a senior officer in the Metropolitan police’s public order command and Sunday’s matchday commander. He is, to borrow football jargon, giving the pre-match team talk, running through intelligence and in-game tactics. “Set the right style and tone,” he says. After Dearden has finished, the police room becomes a pseudo-station for the afternoon, with all incidents triaged by the same crime officer. Football offences can be found in niche legislation, and the Met wants London’s matchdays to be, so far as possible, policed uniformly.

Matchday is the iceberg’s tip. The Met’s 17 dedicated football officers (DFOs) each work full-time on one club, planning each fixture with the matchday commander. All 500-plus games the Met covers per season are risk-graded using factors such as risk level of supporters, proximity, recent history and kick‑off time. Dearden labels Sunday’s game “medium medium”.

“Our mantra is safety, security and service,” Dearden says. “We appreciate that with 60,000 people in the stadium not everybody is going to behave, but we want to reduce the overall risk of the likelihood of disorder.”

View image in fullscreen Chief inspector Pete Dearden gives a briefing in the police room inside the stadium three hours before kick-off in the match between Arsenal and Chelsea. Photograph: Tom Jenkins/The Guardian

View image in fullscreen Pete Dearden: ‘We appreciate that with 60,000 people in the stadium not everybody is going to behave, but we want to reduce the overall risk of the likelihood of disorder.’ Photograph: Tom Jenkins/The Guardian

Three police support units (PSUs), each containing an inspector, three sergeants and about 21 constables, have been assigned to the match. In addition, there are the senior team and 20 operational football officers, or “spotters”, on duty.

Clubs also have their own in-house safety teams, with, in effect, both parties doing their homework before collaborating. Arsenal’s operation involves about 1,000 stewards and response team members. They are the first responders to any incidents within Arsenal’s footprint. When a Chelsea fan overzealously reacts to his team’s early lead, the response team remove him.

Stadiums are not policed as standard, but clubs can request (and, if the request is accepted, pay for) special police services (SPS). Arsenal asked for one PSU to work within the Emirates for Chelsea’s visit but even then, police intervene only when required. Dearden estimates policing football costs the Met £23m a season, with approximately 10% recovered from clubs for SPS.

The Met is looking to close that gap, with aspects such as road closures and hostile vehicle mitigation now managed, and financed, by clubs. Dearden says his department is looking at “mitigation measures to reduce risk, which means that we don’t have to have as many police resources and we don’t compromise safety and security”.

Using spotters is one such measure. They work under the DFOs, are usually locally based for their day-to-day duties and operate consistently with one club. Dearden estimates that their expertise allows them to do the work of double the number of public order officers that would otherwise be needed. “They will go to pubs in the wider footprint where these people gather and try to identify what their plans are, get a good feeling for their mood and the numbers,” Dearden says.

Some Chelsea spotters are in Holborn and will follow when supporters journey to Arsenal by tube. Fans being unwilling to engage with spotters may indicate they are planning something. “You can get a good idea of whether they are potentially going to cause problems at a game because of that lack of engagement,” Dearden says. “It’s that communication approach again – even with some of the supporters that cause us problems, albeit a minority, there’s still engagement to be had. There are still opportunities to say: ‘Don’t do that.’”

Immediately before the match one spotter performed CPR on a supporter. The intervention was life-saving.

View image in fullscreen Arsenal fans walk past live facial recognition cameras on their way to the ground. Photograph: Tom Jenkins/The Guardian

View image in fullscreen The Premier League has invested millions of pounds into the intelligence-led live facial recognition pilot. Photograph: Tom Jenkins/The Guardian

Outside the Emirates, two blue vans contain officers monitoring the data from cameras scanning passersby as part of an intelligence‑led live facial recognition pilot. The trials were funded thanks to a multimillion-pound Premier League investment.

Passing the cameras is voluntary, with signs alerting pedestrians to their presence. Faces are biometrically scanned and compared with a watchlist containing the several thousand people subject to football banning orders (FBOs) and individuals wanted for more serious crimes.

“We are targeting high-harm offenders, sex offenders, those with FBOs, who, if they came to an event, could spoil it for others, commit crimes, or exploit opportunities such as crowded spaces,” Dearden says.

The two-hour pilot yields six interventions, one while Guardian Sport is present. Officers intervene to speak to the individual, who is with their family. They have an FBO, although are not restricted from being around the Emirates. They have also recently been released from prison for human trafficking and are wearing a tag.

Dearden feels half a dozen hits is proportional to what would be expected. “What we can’t measure is the deterrent effect,” he says.

Noticeable is the relative lack of police visibility compared with recent years. That is by design, not accident. A heavy police presence does not necessarily make an event feel safe. “We don’t work on a ‘just in case’ basis these days,” Dearden says. “We deal with known knowns.” Arsenal fans in Naples on Wednesday are likely to meet a vastly different approach.

Immediately before the match, the Guardian laps the ground with the day’s three-person violence against women and girls (VAWG) team. “We want to change the culture of what perhaps in the past was tolerated,” Dearden says, giving the example of staff being targeted with misogynistic abuse.

“We’ve had people at football matches come forward and say: ‘I’ve heard you talk three or four times now and I’m now confident enough to report that I think I’m a victim of domestic abuse and controlling behaviour.’”

The VAWG team are also watching for those who may target vulnerable individuals.

View image in fullscreen A constable high-fives a young Arsenal fan as he patrols the podium level at the Emirates. Photograph: Tom Jenkins/The Guardian

View image in fullscreen An officer acts as a spotter at the Emirates before kick-off. Photograph: Tom Jenkins/The Guardian

For the match, Dearden heads to the command room with Arsenal’s safety team and the other emergency services. Proximity and open dialogue are vital. Because of the game’s risk level, there is a bronze commander, Inspector Rachel Duckett, at ground level. A half-time briefing allows all parties – including medical, the London fire brigade, the local authority, the Premier League, and British transport police – to compare notes and address issues. Dearden and Duckett then discuss the strategy for the game’s end.

For all the planning, much of what happens at football is result-driven. With Arsenal 2-1 up and time running out, a late Chelsea equaliser might have changed the mood. Home and away fans cross paths after, outside the 3,000-strong Chelsea end, where there is no cordon. Arsenal supporters gloat; some Chelsea fans react. A pair of Chelsea content creators try to record in the middle of the departing crowd and receive an expletive-laden reaction from passing Arsenal fans. They are advised to move on for their own safety.

Striking is the speed at which potential flashpoints are spotted and then defused. Officers are calm, not confrontational, and act as an external subconscious: “‘C’mon, think – do you really want to do that?’”

View image in fullscreen A Chelsea supporter is escorted out of the ground by Arsenal stewards. Photograph: Tom Jenkins/The Guardian

View image in fullscreen Officers support a Chelsea content creator as he tries to record a piece after Arsenal’s 2-1 victory. Photograph: Tom Jenkins/The Guardian

An hour after the final whistle, the stadium is silent again, and Dearden and his senior team debrief pitchside. A dozen incidents occurred around the game, with two arrests made – one for assaulting a steward and another for racial abuse and assault. A further 10 people were reported for offences including drinking in view of the pitch, missile throwing, low-level assault of a steward, homophobic chanting and possession of drugs.

Dearden says the number is “slightly higher than we’d like” but points out that it demonstrates proactivity. For example, stewards are told not to tolerate pushes as simply part of the job. Outcomes will be proportionate and consistency is key. In the days and weeks ahead, everything will be analysed, assessed, fed into data. Incremental improvement will be sought and further action may be required for the reported incidents.

But, for a few hours at least, all involved can reflect on a matchday’s work completed well.

Sports.title: Fitter, happier, more productive: Arsenal could hardly have started better | Jonathan Wilson
Sports.content:
Three league games played, three games won. For Arsenal this season could only have started better if Manchester City, who look like being one of their two most serious challengers, had dropped points. But it’s not just about results: Arsenal have been comfortably the better side in each of those three games, approaching each of them in very different ways.

After the controlled victory over Coventry City and the tight game against Aston Villa that was won thanks to ratcheting up the pressure in the 15 minutes after half-time, came success in a far more open game in which they conceded for the first time this season. Chelsea tested Arsenal on Sunday, went ahead, and yet Mikel Arteta’s side still always looked like they would win – even if it did take a superb late save from David Raya to keep out an Estevão shot. But the goalkeeper too is part of their strength; even if an opposing team can work a shooting opportunity, Raya has the capacity for spectacular saves that can dispirit opponents.

Arsenal threatened from set-pieces but also from open play; they can beat opponents in multiple different ways, even when Declan Rice, probably their player of the season last year, has an off day (his unpunished late trip on Morgan Rogers was cynical and nasty, one of those deliberate offences miles from the ball that the game would benefit from treating as a red card offence).

The uplift may simply be confidence, the pressure of not having won the title, of those three successive second-place finishes, now lifted. But there are also individuals who look sharper, livelier, fresher than they did at any point last season. Martin Ødegaard is perhaps the most obvious. He struggled with injuries last season and scored only one goal; already this season he has two in the league and one in the Community Shield. Some players return from the World Cup and look exhausted or find the readaptation to the grind of the domestic game difficult; Ødegaard seems reinvigorated.

There is an imagination to his play, a lightness, and he took his goal against Chelsea superbly. His link-ups with Kai Havertz, another at times mercurial presence, were often delightful, conjuring space and angles where none seemed to exist and bringing the winner. In a team that last season developed a reputation for uncompromising physicality, there is something almost otherworldly about seeing two such ephemeral talents combining, sprites glimmering on a castle wall.

But it’s not just Ødegaard. For Bukayo Saka, last season felt like chickens coming home to roost. He is only 25 but Sunday brought what was already his 205th league start, while playing regularly for England as well. Fatigue had been stored up, which is always a worry for players who emerge as early as he did. Thomas Tuchel didn’t use him in the World Cup semi-final for reasons of tiredness or injury that remain opaque (the situation was promptly confused when he scored a hat-trick in the third-place game). But he seems back to something like his best in the early weeks of this season, fizzing in from the right-hand side and delivering dangerous corners on demand.

The other standout in the early weeks of the season is Riccardo Calafiori, who has already developed a very promising relationship going forward with Christos Tzolis, even if a few issues remain to be resolved defensively on that flank. The Italian, who scored Arsenal’s opener in the Community Shield, is not only a threat from set-plays but is very good at breaking through the lines, making him a real weapon against low blocks.

Chelsea are improving. Xabi Alonso’s side were far less open through midfield than they had been against Fulham and Brighton – easier as that can sometimes be to manage against sides who don’t instinctively cede possession. It may be, especially as the attrition of European fixtures strikes others later in the season, that they emerge as a very serious force. Arsenal, though, are very, very good now, and that means they could be several points clear by the time that putative Chelsea challenge emerges.

skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Twice weekly Sign up to Soccer Desk Jonathan Wilson and Guardian journalists bring expert analysis and reporting on the biggest stories in soccer. Enter your email Sign up after newsletter promotion

Arteta’s side are not merely playing with great authority; the fixtures have also fallen well for them, getting Villa away and Chelsea at home while both sides are still finding their patterns of play. It’s still very early. We haven’t even got to the first international break yet. Pitfalls are always waiting, and football is not a sport that reacts well to being taken for granted. But for Arsenal, their title defence could hardly have started better. Things could change but, at this moment, it seems more likely that they’ll have it won with several games still to play than that their grasp on the title will have slipped.

Sports.title: Emery ready to ignite Aston Villa’s season at Club Brugge after familiar slow start
Sports.content:
Unai Emery is not panicking. He may kick every ball on the touchline but, behind closed doors, Aston Villa’s players are used to him being the calmest person in the room, routinely more demanding after victory than defeat. John McGinn tells a story in which the Villa manager, early in his now almost four-year tenure, broke character and lost his cool during a half-time interval not owing to a lukewarm performance but because he witnessed his captain tearing into teammates. In Emery’s eyes, it was McGinn expending unnecessary energy rather than seeking solutions.

Emery, McGinn and Villa have been here before. Just last season, in fact; at this point, they were pointless in the Premier League and still another 157 minutes from registering their first goal. So in one sense Villa, who shook off a slow start to qualify for the Champions League for the second time in three seasons, are ahead of schedule. Villa’s goalless draw at Hull on Saturday was not the most absorbing display but there were enough green shoots to trust Emery when he says he is confident they can again exceed expectations.

It is hard to disbelieve a man with Emery’s record, having overseen the most successful era in the club’s recent history. “When we started the project here, the ambition we had, it was [not even] in our highest expectations to be in Europe four years in a row,” the Villa manager says. “It was very difficult when we started working together but it was the ambition of the owner. We set our standards high with the players to be there and we are. Now is the moment to remember how we got here and the way we did. Now it is a different moment and chapter.”

In these moments, Emery tends to double down on his methods. Last season they did not taste victory until their seventh game of the season in all competitions, McGinn scoring the only goal in a Europa League win against Bologna. Before that game, players assembled around 11.30am for the kind of opposition analysis meeting to which they have grown accustomed, so much so McGinn says they now walk in like robots.

Emery lasers in on players’ positioning and tactical details. Jhon Durán, now on loan at Benfica from Al-Nassr after spells at Fenerbahce and Zenit St Petersburg, is famously the only player to have requested to leave mid-meeting.

Villa face Club Brugge on Tuesday for the fourth time in the past two years, hoping Europe will again ignite their season.

After that victory against Bologna last September, Villa embarked on an extraordinary run of 17 wins in 19 matches. Half of the 14 players involved in that game have departed but one of those who did feature, Emiliano Buendía, is hopeful that Emery’s new-look squad can put together a similar run. “It has not been the start we wanted, but we are trying to take the positive things from every match,” said the Argentinian, who has started all four Villa games this season. “We will try to change this momentum in terms of results and try to get our confidence back to perform well and [achieve] the results we want.”

View image in fullscreen Unai Emery is remaining calm despite Aston Villa’s slow start to the season. Photograph: Allstar Picture Library Ltd/Stewart Kendall/Apl/Sportsphoto

Another Champions League campaign should not be taken for granted and returning to this stage, after winning the Europa League last season, is arguably Emery’s greatest feat. The strides made under Emery will surely occupy the minds of supporters as they wander the cobbled streets of Bruges and when they explore Barcelona in November, too.

Crucially, Emery is energised by the challenge, helped by the odd siesta at Villa’s Bodymoor Heath base. “Sometimes I need a good nap, after intensive work in the morning,” he said with a smile last week.

skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Every weekday Sign up to Football Daily Kick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of football Enter your email Sign up after newsletter promotion

For now, George Hemmings’s 13th‑minute shot against Hull represents Villa’s sole effort on target this campaign. In the same game it was the 19-year-old, who joined from Nottingham Forest aged 16, who supplied Buendía for a golden chance. It is easy to focus on the shortcomings but it would also be remiss to overlook Villa’s encouraging performance in the Super Cup against, in Emery’s view, the best team on the planet; defeat against Paris Saint-Germain was less than a month ago and Villa have only strengthened since.

One of the most exciting of their 11 summer arrivals, the 18-year-old Ibrahim Mbaye, was an unused substitute for PSG in Salzburg. Another talent signed this summer, Johan Manzambi, continues to step up his fitness after a knee injury and could feature as early as Saturday against Nottingham Forest.

Only two of Villa’s new arrivals – Zion Suzuki and Nicolas Jackson – started at Hull last time out. Matteo Ruggeri, Aaron Wan-Bissaka and Alejandro Garnacho arrived from the bench. Taylor Harwood-Bellis, a £25m buy omitted from Villa’s Champions League squad, had a watching brief in Yorkshire. João Gomes was sent off on debut. Leon Goretzka, who joined on a free after leaving Bayern Munich, will not feature until at least October after a knee injury setback.

Emery often takes time to integrate signings. Youri Tielemans had to wait four months for his first Villa start before embedding himself as one of Emery’s undroppables. He demands a lot of his players and even more of himself. “In football, if you are expecting transition, maybe you are not in the right way,” he said last month. “We have to rebuild the team as fast as possible. I don’t know if we need time or not. We are progressing – still not enough because we are not getting good results – but tomorrow is a new test in Europe.”

Sports.title: Chelsea’s midfield a headache for Alonso after Arsenal press advantage | Jacob Steinberg
Sports.content:
There have been seasons when Chelsea have turned up at the Emirates Stadium and parked the bus. “You know, I think 10 years without a title is boring,” José Mourinho said in response to criticism from Arsenal fans after a stultifying 0-0 draw in April 2015. On Sunday, though, there was no holding back from Chelsea. “I want to compete in the best possible way to win,” Xabi Alonso said after seeing his new side edged out by Arsenal in a breathless encounter. “Today we didn’t want to sit deep from the first minute. We wanted to be active.”

The plan worked at times. Chelsea maintained their habit of scoring early goals, going ahead through Morgan Rogers, and created further openings. But they were facing the champions and do not have Arsenal’s completeness. Shortcomings were exploited, particularly in midfield. Declan Rice romped through the middle at one point and the winning goal owed much to Reece James losing track of Martin Ødegaard as Arsenal’s captain strode through to fire past Emiliano Martínez.

It was expected to be a key battleground, and the way Arsenal went 2-1 up was felt keenly by Chelsea given their difficulties on deadline day, when Enzo Fernández got his £125m move to Manchester City and no one was signed to replace the Argentinian. However, it is worth remembering Chelsea were short not only of Fernández’s offensive skills as they fell to their first defeat under Alonso. It was also significant that Moisés Caicedo was out again, an unspecified issue proving a nuisance, and it is a concern that Alonso lacks a suitable stand‑in for the Ecuador international whose ability to cover ground, snap into challenges and shield his defence would have come in handy against a midfield as powerful as Arsenal’s.

There is much to like about Alonso’s vision. Chelsea are not obsessed with possession and are speeding forward on the counterattack. Yet while they look menacing with every attack there is a cost to the chaos. Alonso has found balance elusive. Chelsea have conceded seven goals in three games, are without a clean sheet in the league since January and need the oomph provided by Caicedo if they are to make this full-throttle style work.

Caicedo, such an important presence since joining for £115m in 2023, is yet to start this season. He missed the 3-2 win against Fulham and was replaced 14 minutes after coming on during the 4-3 victory against Brighton. Alonso is erring on the side of caution. He stressed there was no long-term problem after the Arsenal game and admitted Caicedo was rushed back against Brighton. “I don’t want to make the same mistake again,” Alonso said, keeping the wider picture in mind. It is a long season, even with no European football, and the physical demands of the league means there is no point Caicedo playing through pain when doing so would surely cause more problems down the line.

View image in fullscreen Romeo Lavia and Cole Palmer (right) of Chelsea try to dispossess Myles Lewis-Skelly of Arsenal. Photograph: Tom Jenkins/The Guardian

As it stands, though, Chelsea are too open and cannot strengthen until January. Compromises are necessary but the jury is out on some fixes.Alonso is a believer in James, whose shift from right‑back to central midfielder started under Enzo Maresca, but the captain is learning the role and his lack of feel for the position was exposed by Ødegaard.

Arsenal found the gaps. Roméo Lavia started alongside James but is yet to complete 90 minutes since joining Chelsea three years ago. The Belgian has struggled with injuries and ran out of steam against Arsenal after an hour, at which point Alonso looked to his bench and replaced Lavia with Malo Gusto, leaving his expensively assembled side to play out the closing stages with two repurposed right-backs in the middle.

This was never the plan. Chelsea looked at replacements for Fernández. They wanted Alex Scott but Bournemouth would not sell. Crystal Palace’s Adam Wharton has admirers, there was interest in Roma’s Manu Koné, whilea move for Monaco’s Lamine Camara, which collapsed as the summer window closed, left Chelsea fuming.

In January Chelsea will hope to find a player more suited to Alonso’s system than Fernández, who is not the most mobile. They are not missing him in an attacking sense. Chelsea are scoring and the bigger headache is what to do out of possession. They do not have another player with Caicedo’s skillset.

skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Every weekday Sign up to Football Daily Kick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of football Enter your email Sign up after newsletter promotion

Dário Essugo was billed as Caicedo’s deputy when he joined last year but does not have Alonso’s trust and has been loaned to Strasbourg. Jordan Henderson is recovering from a broken wrist and is 36, and sending on Gusto over Valentín Barco was an early pointer. Barco, signed from Strasbourg this summer, is promising but the 22-year-old is inexperienced and, in any case, is more passer than destroyer.

Quick Guide Play our football trivia game, On the ball Show The Guardian's daily football game, On the ball, is now live in the app for both iOS and Android. Can you identify the Premier League star from the clues? Was this helpful? Thank you for your feedback.

Arsenal started with Rice, Ødegaard and Myles Lewis‑Skelly in midfield. They kept the £75m Bruno Guimarães in reserve and brought on two Spanish World Cup winners in Mikel Merino and Martín Zubimendi, another player wanted by Chelsea.

The gulf in midfield resources told and it was the absence of Caicedo that mattered most for Chelsea. Perhaps Alonso could have adjusted and fallen back. If Chelsea continue to look so vulnerable at the back in the big games the tactics will be called naive. Yet Alonso will trust that sticking to his ideals will be rewarded in the long run. This is the start of a process. He is introducing a new system and accepts it comes with risks. The problem is that he does not have a midfielder to put out fires if Caicedo is out.

Sports.title: Joey Barton to remain in custody until trial after bail application turned down
Sports.content:
The former footballer Joey Barton will remain in custody until his trial next year after a bail application was refused.

The 44-year-old had been due to stand trial at Liverpool crown court last week accused of causing grievous bodily harm with intent to Kevin Lynch, 51, at Fairway, Huyton, on 8 March. But on Wednesday the case was adjourned and put back to March next year.

Barton, wearing a grey zip-up fleece, appeared over video link from HMP Liverpool at a hearing on Monday, when the judge David Potter refused a renewed bail application. Barton nodded as the judge remanded him in custody in advance of a pre-trial hearing on 11 December.

His trial will take place exactly a year after the alleged assault, meaning the defendant, who was arrested shortly after the incident, will have spent 12 months on remand.

Barton is accused of carrying out the attack on Lynch after they had been drinking together at Huyton and Prescot golf club. Lynch, a former non-league football manager and founder of the special education school NexGen Academy, was said to have sustained serious injuries to an eye.

Barton, the former Manchester City and QPR midfielder, of Widnes, Cheshire, won one England cap and also played for Newcastle, Rangers, Burnley and Marseille. After stopping playing he moved into coaching and had managerial spells at Fleetwood and Bristol Rovers.

Sports.title: Football Daily | Big day for Ødegaard with balaclavas, Basques and a boot to the head
Sports.content:
PERFECT START CONTINUES

Perusing assorted Social Media Disgrace for some Monday inspiration, Football Daily was struck by the amount of scorn and ridicule heaped upon a large group of men dressed in black, many of them wearing balaclavas to hide their identities. Formed with the intention of creating something resembling a matchday atmosphere in and around the Emirates Stadium, the Ashburton Army is a group of wannabe ultras who would almost certainly retreat at the speed of light if confronted by one of the more hardcore continental firms they style themselves after. While many fellow fans view them with utter disdain for their “try-hard” aesthetic, on the same day a large group of identically attired and significantly older men were marching on Portsmouth to intimidate a boat-load of asylum seekers, the feeling persists that on this occasion, those pouring derision on this gang of overenthusiastic Ruperts might have set their sights elsewhere.

Widely billed as The Basque 44-Year-Olds Who Grew Up Together In The Antiguo Locale of San Sebastián and Remain Close Friends To This Day derby, there was atmos aplenty at the Emirates Stadium as Arsenal hosted one of very few teams given a snowball’s chance in hell of challenging them for the title this season. And while Xabi Alonso’s Chelsea took a very early lead courtesy of some uncharacteristically shonky Arsenal defending at a set-piece, the champions ultimately prevailed. Their victory was due in no small part to Martin Ødegaard, who put in the kind of purring performance we simply did not often see from the frequently absent or knack-plagued Norwegian as his teammates ground out victory after victory en route to last season’s title. “I think he is enjoying his football,” whooped Mikel Arteta as he praised his captain after the game. “His personal life is settled. He is available. He is training. He has his routine and if he is intelligent, he can take a lot of benefits from the players around him. I think he was outstanding today.”

Having watched Arsenal play three, win three and score all six of their goals from open play in the Premier League so far, cynics who spent large tracts of last season criticising Arteta’s side’s over-reliance on set-piece goals have had to find new nits to pick. No stranger to controversy last season, on Sunday Gabriel Magalhães prompted a nationwide chorus of grumbles for escaping a red card despite kicking the Chelsea goalkeeper in the head. “Martínez has got the ball in his hands and he boots him in the head,” observed Wayne Rooney with a chuckle on Match of the Day. “I think he’s extremely lucky to stay on the pitch.” And while Football Daily is largely against heads being kicked on the football pitch or elsewhere, the decision not to dismiss Arsenal’s defender was correct because there was no malice aforethought as the Brazilian scrapped for the ball and he did not throw his boot with excessive force. In so many ways this is an Arsenal we are not used to seeing, but one that already looks far better than the one that won the league.

QUOTE OF THE DAY

“Two months after the events, we note that our questions remain unanswered to date. Given the importance of transparency and clarity for all parties involved, we request the necessary explanations and, at the same time, wish to explore where improvements to the current processes are possible, so that similar cases can be handled in a clear, consistent and efficient manner in the future”​ – Pascale Van Damme, president of the Royal Belgian Football Association. Belgium are currently a “nah” to supporting Gianni Infantino’s run for another go at being Fifa president after an unsatisfactory conclusion to inquiries about how USA USA USA’s Folarin Balogun was suddenly available for selection to face them at the World Cup despite a red card.

double quotation mark Re: Kieron Dyer and his MJ press conference (Friday’s Football Daily, full email edition). I wish he’d just beat it” – Marc Meldrum.

double quotation mark ‘Mike’ Hackett? Let’s start a new trend and give every referee the moniker ‘Mike’, going back as far as 1891. Mike Langenus. Mike Horn. Mike Ellis. Mike Taylor. Mike Partridge. Mike Courtney. Mike Collina. Mike Clattenburg. Heck, even Mike ‘Mike’ Dean. Why not, since they’re all miked up theses days anyway” – Ben van Maaren.

double quotation mark I was wondering if the World Cup had taken some players over that threshold between good and great. Thinking about players who had a brilliant competition and have come back men, not boys. No more nerves or inconsistency. Eg Haaland, post-haircut … maybe Ødegaard? Can you think of anyone else transformed? And, conversely, how would a bad WC affect someone? Or, again, what about Cole Palmer? Four years of hurt or dodged a bullet?” – Russell Richardson.

double quotation mark A promoted team like Hull may be in the top four. Chelsea may sell/loan 40 players and still carry a bench worth half a billion GBP. Manchester United may suddenly look like a team that can play 90 minutes without imploding. Nothing is certain, except Spurs staying in the relegation zone until MD 36. Thank you Spurs, for such stability” – Krishna Moorthy.

If you have any, please send letters to the.boss@theguardian.com. Today’s letter o’ the day winner is … Krishna Moorthy, who gets a copy of The Mbappé Project by Philippe Auclair. Copies are available in the Guardian Bookshop if you are not the lucky scribe. Terms and conditions for our competitions, when we run them, are here.

Sports.title: Karius keeps Kane at bay as Schalke nullify Bayern on Neuer’s return | Andy Brassell
Sports.content:
If one goalkeeper was going to dominate the discussion in this game, it actually felt as if it would be the less busy one. Schalke fans do not take kindly to being dumped and even if Manuel Neuer left the club behind 15 years ago – and even if most of the world associates him with Bayern Munich rather than his home town club – he is still given a rough ride when he returns.

Opposing sporting directors Max Eberl and Frank Baumann had words to say about that after Saturday evening’s latest visit, but it wasn’t Germany’s legendary goalkeeper who took the headlines – or not he alone, at least. It was always going to be a landmark afternoon with Schalke playing a first home game in the top flight since May 2023, but this was way beyond what anyone could have expected. The numbers said it all – with Bayern failing to score for the first time domestically since a goalless draw at Leverkusen more than 18 months ago, meaning they finished the weekend not on top of the table for the first time in almost two years – but told nothing of the story.

For at the end of this goalless draw, the story was Loris Karius. A goalkeeper who, once upon a time, might have hoped to back up Neuer in the national team on the rare occasions that the totem was indisposed, but whose career has become about attrition rather than aspiration. At 33, this was a day in the sun that seemed like it would never come. Little was expected of Miron Muslic’s team here, with damage limitation and a swift moving on to more winnable battles perhaps the realistic aim, with last week’s 3-0 loss at Augsburg (a bright start followed by a frank reality check) indicative of the task facing them back at the top table.

View image in fullscreen Schalke manager Miron Muslic congratulates Loris Karius after his clean sheet.

Photograph: Martin Meissner/AP

Little has been expected of Karius for a long time, going all the way back to what turned out to be his final Liverpool appearance, the error-strewn Champions League final against Real Madrid in Kyiv in 2018. By the time we learned that Karius’s mistakes were likely conditioned by a concussion suffered earlier in the game, the die had been cast and the damage to his reputation done.

You may know some of the tale since. A move to Besiktas which ran aground when he was forced to take action against the club (twice) for unpaid wages. Another loan to Union Berlin which led to just four Bundesliga appearances – the only league games, mind you, that he would play between leaving Istanbul in May 2020 and being drafted in late to Newcastle’s lineup against Arsenal in February 2024 after Martin Dubravka fell ill on the day of the game. A year before he had been brought in to cover for the suspended Nick Pope in the Carabao Cup final, his first first-team game in two years, and performed creditably.

If the journey has been confusing to us, imagine what it was like for Karius. “Even today,” he told Welt this summer, “I don’t know what I should have done differently. I just felt empty. I even considered ending my career, but I was only 25 years old and couldn’t just stay home.” When he joined Schalke in January 2025 it was six months after his Newcastle deal ended, and then-coach Kees van Wonderen made it clear Karius was signing as second choice. Yet by February he had made the starting spot his own – before picking up a calf injury four games in that forced him to miss the rest of the season.

Last season the worm began to turn. Muslic put his faith in him – as the club already had by extending his contract – and Karius started 30 of the 34 games as the coach’s belt-and-braces side conceded a league-low 31 goals and won the 2.Bundesliga. This summer, his deal was extended again, to 2028.

All of these landmarks in Gelsenkirchen have been victories, but it felt like there were limits for Karius, just like there are for this Schalke, the original giants of German football, the Bayern-before-Bayern, who have been living on reduced means for a number of years now. If they had been the high rollers of just a few years ago, there would have been little need or inclination to give Karius his chance.

But he had his chance here, and he took it. There was command, confidence and a string of fine saves, capped by a stunning, flying one-hander to prevent Harry Kane smashing a late winner. It may be pointed out that neither Kane nor Michael Olise started in a game that also saw Jamal Musiala make a comeback from the bench; it should also be noted that when Vincent Kompany rotated his star pair in the latter stages of last season to keep them fresh around Champions League games, it was a cheat code, unleashing the league’s two best players on tiring defences.

Karius had all the answers, and was warmly greeted by Kompany at full-time, who had been a senior when he was a young player at Manchester City about 15 years ago. That amount of time seemed like nothing on an evening when the past loomed large.

View image in fullscreen Manuel Neuer was given his usual rough ride by the Schalke supporters. Photograph: Christopher Neundorf/EPA

For this, “very likely my last game” in Gelsenkirchen before an eventual retirement, every boo, catcall and chant directed at Neuer felt pertinent. He started training at Schalke when he was five, used to watch matches from the same Nordkurve that rained their displeasure down on him and made over 200 appearances for the first team. The reception was not unexpected but, perhaps accentuated by the sense that this season might be Neuer’s victory lap, there were plenty who felt the need to fight his corner. Eberl called the treatment of his goalkeeper “inappropriate”, and Baumann, his opposite number at Schalke, had disapproving words for his own fans. Neuer’s fellow Gelsenkirchner Olaf Thon wrote in his column in Kicker that “Gelsenkirchen should be proud of him”, rather than booing him.

The man himself was a little more sanguine, having invited a cluster of family members. “That’s love,” he said. “Every whistle is a compliment.” Both Neuer and Karius could tell you that the life of a goalkeeper is thus; setbacks inevitable, but comebacks somewhat less so.
