World.title: Speaker of Azerbaijani Parliament addresses 4th International Workshop of Academics and Parliamentarians (PHOTO)
World.content:
BAKU, Azerbaijan, September 7. Speaker of the Milli Majlis Sahiba Gafarova delivered an online address as a special gust of the 4th International Workshop of Academics and Parliamentarians, themed ‘The role of parliaments in the face of technological transformation, political fragmentation and the crisis of democratic confidence’ and organised by the Group of Latin American and Caribbean Countries (GRULAC) in Buenos Aires, Argentina.

This was reflected in the statement of the Parliament’s Press and Public Relations Department.

The Speaker observed that digital technologies are transforming the work of state institutions and their interaction with citizens fundamentally in the modern era. She stated that, whilst opening up great opportunities for parliaments, this process gives rise to serious responsibilities at the same time. Emphasising that digitalisation enhances the transparency and accessibility of parliaments, the Speaker drew attention to the fact that technology can in no way replace accountability, political dialogue and strong institutional structures.

As she was talking about the rich experience of Azerbaijan in this field, the Speaker of Parliament remarked that policy of digitalisation, e-government, artificial intelligence and innovations is being co-ordinated successfully in the country by the Digital Development Council under the leadership of First Vice President Mehriban Aliyeva. As Sahiba Gafarova pointed out, the Milli Majlis is strengthening the legal frameworks consistently and is using the e-documentation, e-vote and legislative monitoring systems actively. She remarked that the new legislative acts being passed provide a complete legal basis for holding public discussions and parliamentary hearings also in the electronic format.

Technologies are but means whereas the level of democratic confidence in a society depends directly on how those means are employed, the Speaker said.

According to the Speaker of the Milli Majlis, the challenges that technological transformation poses affect every region and every parliament; still, not all the parliaments possess the same research and digital resources.

She proceeded to say that not one parliament could withstand alone such global challenges immune to borders as artificial intelligence, cybersecurity and protection of data, and the Inter-Parliamentary Union (IPU) being the international parliamentary organisation with the broadest representation coverage in the world plays an important role of a platform in this regard.

The Speaker emphasised that the IPU ought to ensure co-operation amongst parliament in spite of differences and promote the achievement of consensus at earlier stages. The question of how artificial intelligence can make democratic institutions stronger without steepening equality and weakening human responsibility must land amongst the topmost topics for discussion in the regular dialogues organised under the aegis of the IPU.

The Speaker of Parliament also drew attention to that even though all the Member Parliaments enjoy equal rights, their researching capacities and access to technologies are not equal. Therefore, the IPU should bridge that gap by way of exchange of knowledge, connecting parliaments to universities and experts.

Speaker of the Milli Majlis Sahiba Gafarova concluded her address by emphasising that the main force of international parliamentary platforms lies in their diversity and that this diversity must be employed to restore global trust.

World.title: Growers forced to find off-farm incomes after fruit fly financial hit
World.content:
On a building site hundreds of kilometres away from his home, Jody Miltenoff works to make an income to offset the financial losses of Queensland fruit fly.

He has taken on a contract as project manager on a new hotel development in Port Adelaide, leaving his son to run his nursery business in Cambrai and orchards in Sunlands.

Mr Miltenoff said managing his jujube business from afar was challenging.

Jody Miltenoff says while he enjoys project management, he prefers farm life. (ABC News: Guido Salazar)

But between extreme heatwaves last summer damaging most of his crop and the ongoing cost of fruit fly management, he was glad to have a safety net.

"I'm lucky that I've got the construction industry to fall back on and supplement our income," Mr Miltenoff said.

" I've heard of some apricot growers that are getting close to retirement and just walking away, just saying that it's too hard. "

Mr Miltenoff said sending some of his dried jujubes to Tokyo had been a boon but the loss of his fresh fruit market access had been tough.

Jujubes are a small, sweet fruit sometimes called a Chinese date or red date. (ABC Landline: Kerry Staight)

Sending fruit to his main market of Adelaide requires costly cold treatment or fumigation, while shipping to the east coast means poor returns.

"Growers in the Riverland that have been affected by fruit fly have been sending to the eastern states, so they flood that market and … the prices dropped quite severely," he said.

Funding unused

The Riverland is one of two internationally recognised Pest Free Areas (PFA) in Australia, which provides growers with a trade advantage when exporting produce.

But since a Queensland fruit fly outbreak was declared in Renmark West in late December 2020, the region has been subject to rules which restrict produce movement and require approved treatments before it can be sold.

Queensland fruit fly is endemic to Australia. (Supplied: PIRSA)

State department of primary industries (PIRSA) budget data shows of the $43 million allocated for fruit fly management in the last financial year, $10 million was unspent due to fewer detections of the pest.

According to a department spokesperson, in 2024-25 there were 7,794 Queensland fruit fly detections in South Australia, while there were 4,030 detections in 2025-26.

With fruit fly deductions almost halved, Citrus SA chair Mark Doecke said it was a step in the right direction.

"Any money saving is good money saving, that's for sure," he said.

But Mr Miltenoff said it would have been worthwhile to use the funds to adopt new technology to boost eradication efforts.

A PIRSA spokesperson said in a statement that allocation of funds was subject to approval through normal state budget processes.

Pathway to pest-free

Grower industry bodies Citrus SA and Summerfruit SA organised meetings in Renmark and Waikerie last week for growers and packers to hear about a pathway to release towns in Riverland west from the fruit fly exclusion zone.

Some growers want to see more advanced fruit fly traps. (ABC Riverland: Anita Ward)

The area known as Zone Two includes the towns of Waikerie, Cadell, Holder, Sunlands and Taylorville, which have all had consistently low detections of the pest in the past 12 months.

It follows the release of Swan Reach, known as Zone One, which was officially declared fruit fly free by PIRSA last November.

Mr Doecke said PIRSA had "taken too long" to lift restrictions.

"We started talking about getting some of these areas out three years ago," he said.

Mark Doecke says fruit fly restrictions are costing the citrus industry about $20 million a year. (ABC News: Jackson Byrne)

" If we can get some of these areas out that will instil confidence back in the public and we can ask them to get behind us and keep that fight going. "

But the process to reinstate Pest Free Area status is complicated, and dependent on variables, such as the time of year because of the fruit fly life cycle.

A PIRSA spokesperson said it required "no further fruit fly detections for an agreed period of time and all protocol requirements are met".

World.title: Live: Building company collapse exposes private credit issues
World.content:
The collapse of the Bathla Group puts in peril 2,000 homes under construction or almost completed, and a pipeline of more than 13,000 in various stages of development.

One of the big issues is private credit.

Banks are loath to lend to developers because of the high risk and because of the substantial length of time between the outlay (buying land, securing staff and materials, construction) and the pay-off (completing the project and selling the homes).

That's pushed the construction sector into the realm of private credit, non-bank lenders willing to extend credit that is secured against the assets the developer has (usually the land and the value of the deposits future buyers have made).

As ever, more risk more (potential) reward.

Private credit charges higher rates on the money they lend, making it more expensive.

But there are issues.

In recent weeks, the corporate regulator ASIC warned of "significant cracks" in the system, warning it is facing its "first real test" amid the collapse of several large borrowers and the limiting of redemptions at several major funds.

But hey, not me, right?

Even if the issue is new to you, you are almost certainly invested in private credit through investments made by your superannuation fund.

Here's Australian Securities and Investments Commission (ASIC) chair Sarah Court:

"We've called out before that private credit is important for all Australians because of the involvement of people's superannuation funds. "This is not some peripheral issue over to one side. "This really matters, and that is why we've been talking about it for such a long time."

Here's more on the issue, from colleague David Taylor.

World.title: Australia's oldest coalmine plans to expand under Sydney's water catchment
World.content:
Peabody's plan to extend its Metropolitan coalmine at Helensburgh, south of Sydney, until 2044 has drawn warnings about the drinking water catchment while winning strong union support.

The US-based company has submitted a scoping report to the NSW government, formally beginning the State Significant Development process for 22 additional underground longwall tunnels west of the mine's existing operations.

The Metropolitan Mine near Helensburgh, south of Sydney and north of Wollongong. (Supplied: Peabody.)

The project would extract about 31 million tonnes of run-of-mine coal over 12 years, at a rate of up to 2.7 million tonnes annually.

Peabody said it would preserve about 400 existing jobs, support 450 suppliers and continue providing coal to BlueScope's Port Kembla steelworks and overseas customers.

More than 40 per cent of Metropolitan's current product supplies Australian steelmaking, according to the company.

Above the Helensburgh mine. (Supplied: Peabody )

Union backs expansion

Mining and Energy Union district secretary Andy Davey said the union supported the extension "100 per cent".

"This would be huge, not only for the workers, but the community," he said.

" Helensburgh is the oldest continuous mine being worked. The quality of coking coal that comes out of there is the best in Australia. "

Mr Davey said the project would provide significant employment certainty for Metropolitan's approximately 400 workers.

He acknowledged the proposed expansion was within the catchment but disputed claims it would drain water into the mine.

"What people have to understand is that there's a massive sandstone conglomerate in the roof support," he said.

" While people believe we're fracturing creeks and the water runs into the mine, that is far from the truth. "

A new map of the Helensburgh mine plan. (Supplied: Peabody)

Peabody explains new design

Peabody said the proposed expansion would be west of existing operations and away from Woronora Reservoir.

Its scoping report confirms the project would remain within the Woronora Special Area, which forms part of Sydney's drinking water catchment.

The company proposes using 163-metre-wide extraction panels separated by 55-metre pillars to reduce subsidence effects.

A Peabody spokesperson said Metropolitan had consistently complied with consent conditions requiring "negligible impacts" to upland swamps and water quality and quantity since its current project approval was granted in 2009.

The spokesperson cited a 2018 NSW expert panel finding "no evidence" of fractures connecting the underground workings to the surface.

"Metropolitan will keep operating its proven, conservative mining design in order to comply with its consent conditions," the spokesperson said.

Peabody said the proposed continuation area would add about 1,300 hectares, compared with 6,200 hectares covered by its existing mining leases.

The company also proposes a methane-abatement plant, which it said would begin operating in 2032.

Separately, Peabody is also seeking approval to extend Longwall 317 and add Longwall 318 which remains under assessment and has received critical advice from the federal Independent Expert Scientific Committee (IESC).

It found Peabody's modelling did not provide an adequate or defensible basis for predicting impacts on protected upland swamps, groundwater-dependent ecosystems and waterways flowing into Woronora Reservoir.

"The IESC cannot envisage any feasible mitigation measures, including offsets, that could safeguard these irreplaceable water resources and water-dependent [matters of national environmental significance]," it said.

Metropolitan Mine has operated at Helensburgh since 1888. (Supplied: Peabody)

Greens raise catchment concerns

NSW Greens Environment spokesperson Sue Higginson said mining had already damaged parts of the Woronora catchment.

"It's a legacy mine situated where no mine should be," she said.

" It's past time to shut it down, not extend its life. "

Wollongong Greens councillor Deidre Stuart described the scale of the new project as "massive".

Last year, she unsuccessfully moved for Wollongong City Council to oppose the Longwalls 317 and 318 modification and request an Independent Planning Commission determination.

Cr Stuart said the smaller proposal had indicated Peabody intended to pursue a larger western expansion.

"I just feel a bit sickened and disgusted, to be honest," she said.

" There's no job of any kind, let alone a coalmining job, that's worth having if you haven't got water to drink and to live with. "

"I want to see our water catchment protected because that supplies the water and it holds the water."

The Metropolitan Mine at Helensburgh has been operating for about 138 years. (Supplied: Peabody )

Proposal at an early stage

Planning Minister Paul Scully said the department was awaiting further information from Peabody about the smaller proposal's potential impacts on waterways and nearby swamps.

It has also requested technical advice from the NSW Independent Expert Advisory Panel for Mining.

The separate 22-longwall project remains at the earliest planning stage, with no full development application lodged.

If an application is lodged, it will undergo an environmental assessment and a public exhibition.

It will be referred to the Independent Planning Commission if it receives more than 100 eligible objections.

World.title: Barambah Organics founder and daughter die in plane crash
World.content:
The founder of a popular dairy company and his daughter have been revealed as the victims of a light plane crash south of Brisbane on Monday.

Father and daughter Ian Campbell and Hannah Campbell died when a plane they were travelling in crashed shortly after 11am in a field in Stockleigh, in Logan, causing a grass fire.

Emergency services located two occupants of the aircraft, a 56-year-old man and a 23-year-old woman, both from Ascot. They were declared dead at the scene.

Ian Campbell's family has been farming for generations. (Supplied)

The fourth-generation dairy farmer founded Barambah Organics, a family-owned dairy farming company in Queensland, alongside his wife, Jane.

The family still part-owns the company.

The Campbell family have been farmers for many generations and were based in the South Burnett region for more than 100 years.

More recently, the Campbell family founded Mañana Pastoral in the Goondiwindi region. The farm produces extra virgin olive oil, as well as grass-fed lamb and beef.

Investigation into crash

Initial investigations indicated the plane left Archerfield Airport at about 10:57am before crashing at approximately 11:10am, police said.

Eight Queensland Fire Department crews were on the scene to extinguish a fire caused by the crash.

Detailed circumstances of the crash are still being investigated by Queensland Police Service and the Australian Transport Safety Bureau (ATSB).

The plane crashed in the Stockleigh area shortly after 11am yesterday. (ABC News)

The ATSB "deployed a team of three transport safety investigators from its Brisbane offices" to the accident site.

Those teams specialise in aircraft operations, maintenance and engineering.

Yesterday afternoon they began gathering evidence and examining the wreckage.

Aircraft components will be sent for further examination at the ATSB's technical facilities in Canberra.

World.title: Mixed emotions as Andreeva embraces injured idol after US Open win
World.content:
US Open fans have witnessed a display of sportsmanship as Mirra Andreeva tended to and consoled an injured Anastasia Potapova as the fifth seed won their fourth-round match.

Potapova jarred her knee as she lost the first point of what turned out to be their final game on Louis Armstrong Stadium, prompting Andreeva to rush to the other end of the court to check on her.

She helped the 24th seed up and Potapova was able to limp to her bench, where Andreeva asked if someone could bring her ice.

The French Open champion finished off the next three points for a 5-7, 6-4, 6-3 victory that sent her to the quarterfinals in Flushing Meadows for the first time, jogging around the net again for a warm embrace.

"It's not the perfect end to the match," 19-year-old Andreeva said.

Potapova appeared to be tearing up as Andreeva came around the net for a long embrace after the final point.

Potapova represents Austria but was born in Russia and still played under that flag when she won the junior Wimbledon championship in 2016.

"For me, Nastya, she was always like a prodigy," Andreeva said of her 25-year-old opponent.

"She came on tour early. She also had a lot of wins. I also remember we were all watching and cheering for her when she won juniors Wimbledon title. I remember watching that match.

"For me, she was always, like, a little star that I was kind of always looking at."

Potapova (right) appeared to be tearing up as the pair embraced after match point. (Getty Images: Pete Staples/USTA)

Potapova won their first meeting on tour in 2022 but Andreeva has won the last four, preventing Potapova from reaching her first grand slam quarterfinal.

"First, she just beat me. So after, I just kind of knew that she's a tough player to play, but at the same time, she was so nice," Andreeva said.

"Then since then we would practice together, and just like that, the more you see each other, the more you spend time together, then you just talk about everything, discuss everything. Then, just like that, I feel like we have a good connection off the court."

Elsewhere, Qinwen Zheng mounted another extraordinary fight back to upset six-time major winner Iga Świątek and reach the quarterfinals.

Qinwen Zheng is the first qualifier since 2021 to make it this far in the women's draw. (Getty Images: Al Bello)

Zheng has become Flushing ‌Meadows' most entertaining escape artist this year, coming back from a 0-5 deficit in the deciding set against third-round foe Madison Keys.

She let the first five games slip through her fingers in 20 minutes against the ‌2022 champion Świątek before digging in, and she collapsed to the court with her hands ⁠in her face after sealing the win on the fourth match ‌point.

China's Olympic champion is the first qualifier ​since Emma Raducanu in 2021 ‌to reach the quarterfinals of the women's draw, as she battles back from a chronic elbow injury that had stunted her career.

Two-time winner Naomi Osaka was summarily swept aside by second seed Elena Rybakina, who won 6-1, 6-4 in just over an hour.

2023 champion Coco Gauff plays Iva Jovic in an ​all-American clash to decide the final women's quarterfinalist.

The ABC of SPORT Sports content to make you think... or allow you not to. A newsletter delivered each Saturday.

Reuters

World.title: French wine output predicted to be lowest in 30 years
World.content:
French wine output is likely to be at one of its lowest levels in three decades, with champagne output set to halve this year after severe heat and drought damaged vines and grapes.

The world's second-largest wine producer recorded its hottest summer in 2026 amid increasingly frequent extreme weather events in Europe, which scientists say is experiencing the fastest climate change-driven warming of any continent.

Following on from low output in 2024 and 2025, France was projected to produce 33.9 million hectolitres of wine — equivalent to about 4.5 billion standard bottles — in 2026.

That would be 6 per cent below last year and 17 per cent down on the 2021–2025 average.

Drought conditions and heatwaves affected grapes in Saint-Fiacre-sur-Maine near Nantes. (Reuters: Stephane Mahe)

The farm ministry said conditions early in the year had been favourable, but then the summer drought and heatwaves damaged vines and reduced yields.

Most wine producers in France tarted harvesting grapes unusually early this year, the ministry said.

France is traditionally the world's second-largest wine producer, behind Italy, and the largest exporter in value.

In addition to the challenge from the weather the industry was also hit by US tariffs last year and consumption is at its lowest in more than 60 years as economic pressures, changing tastes and health concerns deter drinkers.

French agriculture hit hard

France is the world's second-largest wine producer. (Reuters: Yves Herman)

Wine output in Champagne is expected to be 49 per cent down on 2025, and 47 per cent below the five-year average.

Bourgogne-Beaujolais is forecast to be down by a third and Val de Loire and Charentes by 12 per cent and 6 per cent, respectively.

Production in Languedoc-Roussillon, which makes the most wine in France, should rise 5 per cent from last year's weak harvest due to improved yields, though output has remained below average.

Bordeaux is expected to rebound 10 per cent from 2025 after late-August rain helped offset drought stress, but production remains well below its five-year average.

The production area was 2.5 per cent smaller this year compared with last as oversupply in the face of falling consumption has led winemakers to uproot a portion of their vineyards.

More broadly, French agriculture has been hit by this summer's record heatwaves and lack of rain.

France on Friday announced an emergency aid package for farmers of more than €1 billion ($1.6 billion).

Baranby Joyce doesn't think One Nation should have to model the impact of its plan to allow people to divert a portion of their super contribution to boost their income.

Fresh offa heated interview with ABC's 7.30 last night, the One Nation treasury spokesperson is back for another round: this time with ABC's Radio National Breakfast's Sally Sara.

Joyce is asked if One Nation modelled the inflationary impact of the policy, after economists suggested it would only put further pressure on the cost of living.

World.title: Toowoomba Hospital maternity review fails to answer mother's concerns
World.content:
For Ashleigh Hills, the joy of the first few weeks with her newborn baby boy were diminished by a traumatic birth.

"It's something I'm still dealing with every day," she said.

"I feel like it really probably took away a lot of the joy of having a newborn and those first early weeks and what that should be like."

Maternity Unit problems persist, review finds Longstanding issues at Toowoomba Hospital's troubled maternity unit are yet to be resolved, according to an independent review of the ward.

Ms Hills is one of the mothers who participated in an assurance review of the Toowoomba Hospital's maternity unit, following years of complaints about its services.

A five-page summary of the report was released yesterday, indicating that while progress was underway, several longstanding issues had not been resolved.

Queensland Health commissioned the review in February, with a focus on addressing how complaints were handled in the maternity unit.

A traumatic birth

Last year, Ms Hills said she was sent home from the Toowoomba Hospital after doctors told her she was not in labour yet.

She said she spent the next 24 hours at home in labour, before going back to the hospital.

Baby Austin was later born via an emergency caesarean section, and the doctors discovered Ms Hills had developed a rare condition called Bandl's ring.

"So basically, my uterus had formed a constriction ring around Austin," she said.

"Everyone was yelling. It was just really scary, and there's no chance for anyone to explain if I'm OK, if baby's OK."

Ashleigh Hills's son had a fractured skull, which was not picked up by several medical professionals. (ABC Southern Qld: Elly Bradfield)

Ms Hills believed she developed the condition due to prolonged obstructed labour.

"They tried to get Austin out multiple times and they couldn't … ended up having to pull him out by his feet," she said.

After the birth, the first-time mother noticed a lump on her baby's head, which was assessed several times by hospital staff.

When Austin was two weeks old, their GP confirmed he had a fractured skull.

"He could have suffered brain damage … he could have needed surgery," Ms Hills said.

In the days after her birth, her GP also discovered Ms Hills had pre-eclampsia, which she said had been missed by the emergency department.

Ms Hills said Austin was seven months old when she finally got a meeting with the hospital, after several failed attempts.

"I think it just would have been nice to have felt listened to in some of those situations," she said.

Review into maternity unit

The recent report was prepared by independent experts who examined the hospital's response to five previous reviews since 2018.

Darling Downs Health Service chief executive Annette Scott said the hospital was acting on 117 recommendations, but it was a continual process.

Annette Scott says she is committed to improving the maternity service. (ABC Southern Qld: Brandon Long)

She said the report found deficits in the complaints process and it was "unacceptable" for complaints not to be followed up with.

"I don't want that on my watch at all," she said.

"If things are getting lost then we need to learn from that because that is not fair on them and it's not fair on the staff here."

Ms Scott said the hospital has appointed a new director of obstetrics, improved the hospital's midwife vacancy rate, and improved training and education.

In a statement, Health Minister Tim Nicholls said the review found there were recommendations from reviews dating back to 2018 that were incomplete.

"The Darling Downs Health Service must now focus on delivering the recommendations made, ensuring women and families can have confidence in the maternity care they receive at Toowoomba Hospital," he said.

Calls for a 'Part 9 Investigation'

Shadow Health Minister Mark Bailey said it was an insult to the parents involved, that only a five-page report was released.

"The full report should absolutely be released and made public," he said.

"There is so much important material to cover and there is so much that needs to be done to overcome what has been an appalling situation."

A Queensland Health spokesperson said its reports were not routinely published in full because of "legal, privacy, ethical, and confidentiality obligations".

Mark Bailey says the five-page report summary "raises more questions than it answers". (ABC News: Lucas Hill)

Mr Bailey said the opposition was calling for a Part 9 Investigation, a high-level inquiry commissioned under the Hospital and Health Boards Act.

"[It] is a much more comprehensive root and branch investigation with some independence," he said.

" We stand with the mothers who have been affected in this regard, because all they want is firstly the truth to be acknowledged and they want it never to happen again to any other parents on the Darling Downs. "

Going into the review, Ms Hills said she did not realise it was mainly focused on the complaints process.

"I do think it needs to be looked at, but I think there are bigger issues," she said.

"It would be great if that Part 9 Investigation was able to happen so that we could get to the bottom of what was really going on."

World.title: ‘No one is prepared’: ChatGPT maker’s top scientist sends an AI warning
World.content:
OpenAI’s top scientist has warned that artificial intelligence is evolving so rapidly that it is becoming increasingly difficult for humans to understand and control, and said he expects AI labs to voluntarily slow development for safety reasons.

In a relatively short space of time, AI models can operate computers, collaborate with humans and other AI systems and carry out research projects, wrote chief scientist Jakub Pachocki in a post titled “An Alien Mind” on Sunday. It won’t be long until they can also improve themselves without human intervention, a process known as recursive self-improvement, he said.

“I expect and hope for voluntary slowdowns to become commonplace until shared safety bars are established.“: OpenAI chief scientist Jakub Pachocki.

“This is a time that calls for extreme caution,” Pachocki wrote in the post. “I am concerned no one is prepared for the consequences of a continued rapid rise in machine intelligence.”

Developers can either try and steer AI more closely to align with human interests or “slow down future development as needed,” he wrote.

World.title: ‘A very costly lemon’: Business groups prepare for working-from-home challenge
World.content:
NationalVictoriaVictorian Parliament ‘A very costly lemon’: Business groups prepare for working-from-home challenge Angus Delaney September 8, 2026 — 5:30am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Blistering legal advice from two barristers will underpin a High Court challenge to Victoria’s working-from-home laws from state business groups, as several of the country’s largest property companies are highly critical of Labor’s plan. Premier Ben Carroll is looking to pass the bill – which will permit most employees the right to work from home two days a week – in parliament this week with some pro-business amendments. However, business groups have again said they are prepared to launch a legal challenge if the bill passes before the state election in November. Employer groups are threatening to launch a High Court challenge against Labor’s working-from-home bill. Eddie Jim “There’s no doubt that there will be a constitutional challenge by employer groups to this legislation if it goes ahead, and we fully expect that it will be a very strong and likely successful challenge,” said Tim Piper, chair of the Victorian Congress of Employer Associations and Victorian head of the Australian Industry group. Piper said he had been approached by “many companies” inquiring and offering to resource a constitutional challenge.



“We have a duty to our members to make sure that legislation passed in Victoria is constitutionally valid and economically reasonable. This one is neither.” Carroll said that flexible work “attracts the best talent in Victoria, and it gets women back in the workforce”. The premier also said that while the government had heard the message that “work from home works” loud and clear, he acknowledged that “laws need to work for business, too, because the reality is if it’s not practical for employers, the law won’t last”. The High Court threat comes as independent legal advice given to the Property Council of Victoria suggests the bill is probably unconstitutional and would be ineffective if it passed parliament.



Lawyers Nick Wood, SC, and Leigh Howard on Monday said Labor’s plan to amend Victoria’s anti-discrimination laws to enshrine working from home as a protected attribute alongside race, sexuality and gender clashed with the federal Fair Work Act. The Constitution states that when a state law is inconsistent with a federal law, it becomes invalid. “In our view, the WFH Bill is inconsistent with the Fair Work Act, and will therefore be inoperative if it is enacted,” the lawyers advised the Property Council. “There would be no question of whether or not part of the WFH Bill is able to be preserved; the entire scheme that is established by the WFH Bill would be inoperative.” They also said there were multiple red flags in the bill, including that it would create a potentially unfair, two-tiered system for workers. Their full legal advice was not provided to The Age and is commercial in confidence pending a High Court challenge. Property Council Victoria executive director Cath Evans said Wood and Howard’s findings should prompt the government to re-think its policy.



Editor's pick Analysis

Victorian election On working from home, Carroll has retreated from a fight about nothing “On the basis of the legal advice we have received, the Victorian public is being sold a very costly lemon,” Evans said. “The government has a choice: listen to the legal concerns, withdraw the bill and give businesses certainty, or push ahead with legislation that could create prolonged costly legal challenges.” Legal experts have previously cast doubt over whether the proposed working-from-home law would interfere with federal industrial relations powers and leave it vulnerable to a High Court challenge. Businesses have also repeatedly challenged Carroll’s assertion that the bill would attract talent into the state, and instead say it would push jobs and investment out.



Peter Menegazzo, chief executive of real estate investment manager Investa, said on Monday that the legislation was already deterring investors. “The state government’s working-from-home legislation is not going away ... so, Melbourne is just not a buy for us at the moment,” he told The Australian Financial Review Property Summit. If the bill passes parliament, it would apply to full-time employees, as well as part-time and regularly employed casuals on a pro rata basis. Employers would also be compelled to pay “reasonable costs” to enable their staff to work remotely. Business groups have discussed a number of amendments with the government, but remain overall opposed to the legislation. Possible amendments include broadening the grounds on which businesses can refuse a working-from-home arrangement, strengthen employers’ ability to manage OH&S obligations, tighten the definition of reasonable employer costs, and give the Victorian Equal Opportunity and Human Rights Commission powers to dismiss frivolous complaints from employees.

World.title: Minor change to title costs worker her job
World.content:
BusinessWorkplaceUnfair dismissal Minor change to title costs worker her job Millie Muroi September 8, 2026 — 5:17am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Employees have been delivered a warning from Australia’s workplace umpire, which has ruled that an insurance broker’s decision to change her title in a legal document justified her dismissal. On Friday, the Fair Work Commission ruled that broker Foula Dendroulakis, who had been employed at Victoria-based insurance company CCIB Services since 2021, was properly dismissed after she dropped the word “senior” from her role as an account manager in formal correspondence. The senior account manager said she was remorseful and apologetic about her conduct. Dendroulakis was at odds with the company over seating arrangements, productivity and working from home when she wrote to the Fair Work Commission alleging she had been forced to take on a more senior job without more pay. But in her correspondence with the commission, she did not include the word “senior” in her title, which CCIB Services viewed as an act of dishonesty and used to dismiss her.



The commission upheld that move, though in part because the insurance broker was a small business, it did not look at whether the employers’ beliefs were ultimately correct or whether the dismissal was harsh on Dendroulakis. When Dendroulakis started at CCIB, her employment contract labelled her only as an “account manager”. But the company said she was recruited to a “senior account manager” position and paid accordingly, and that her business cards and email signature also reflected this. Dendroulakis also referred to herself as a “senior account manager”, including on her LinkedIn profile. Related Article Privacy Canva account at centre of legal fight over employee privacy In 2022, Dendroulakis sought a pay rise in which she referred to herself as a “senior account manager” and was given a pay increase alongside a copy of her position description labelling her as such. In 2025, one of CCIB’s directors, Kurt Alder, decided Dendroulakis was not being productive while working from home. When she was in the office, she was spending “lots of time on personal calls in the boardroom during the work day”, he concluded.



On one occasion, Alder said Dendroulakis had left the office early and did not return. When another co-director, Ryan Fisher, raised the issue with her, he said Dendroulakis “kept changing her story”, initially claiming she had left early to take a lunch break, then saying she was too busy and worked from her phone in her car. In a later email, Dendroulakis said she had left early to allow extra time to arrive at a client’s premises due to poor weather conditions. Later that year, when the company altered seating arrangements in the office, Dendroulakis raised concern about the temperature of the location allocated to her and its impact on her ability to focus and work efficiently. She said that, as a senior team member, she would appreciate an opportunity to “discuss an alternative seat, a private office arrangement, or a work from home agreement for two days a week”. The company said it would not be revisiting the desk issue and that Dendroulakis’ “productivity metrics did not support working two days from home”.



In what the commission termed a “lengthy response”, Dendroulakis then expressed concern about the job title in her employment contract. Related Article Unfair dismissal ‘Classic pub punch’ costs man his job after trading slurs with colleague The company acknowledged the word “senior” had accidentally been omitted from the employment contract and that it had “no concerns” about formally changing her job title. The same month, Dendroulakis was issued a first and final warning about her “inability to perform effectively while working from home”. In December 2025, Dendroulakis made a legal claim with the commission. She alleged that the firm had changed her role without a lawful basis or more pay.



Dendroulakis claimed she had been underpaid and that she was required to perform duties of a “senior account manager” when her title was “account manager”. She also attached a copy of a letter she had previously sent to the company around the time of her pay rise, but removed the word “senior” from her job title in the document. CCIB also got a copy of Dendroulakis’ claim and noticed the omission. Dendroulakis said she had removed the word as a “reflexive correction” in line with her employment agreement, but that it was not deliberate and that she had not intended to mislead the commission. Her lawyers said she was “sincerely remorseful and apologetic” for the oversight, and that “significant work-related stress and anxiety” had affected her attention to detail. Fisher said in evidence that Dendroulakis had become a “liability” to the business and its workplace and had been “blatantly dishonest on more than one occasion”.



Alder claimed Dendroulakis’ conduct was “effectively fraud” designed to bolster her claims against the company in an attempt to mislead the commission and falsely support her general protections claim. Dendroulakis’ conduct was “sufficiently serious,” the commission said – with the employer holding a genuine belief on reasonable grounds about the gravity of the conduct – for immediate dismissal to be justified. This masthead attempted to contact Dendroulakis for comment. CCIB declined to comment. The Business Briefing newsletter delivers major stories, exclusive coverage and expert opinion. World.title: ASX set to slide as oil prices rise; Copper prices soar
World.content:
BusinessMarketsWorld markets ASX set to slide as oil prices rise; Copper prices soar Levin Stamm and Will Standring September 8, 2026 — 5:12am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

European stocks were weighed down by higher oil prices and a drop in Novartis following the failure of a heart drug, while Wall Street was closed for the Labor Day holiday. The Australian sharemarket is set to retreat, with futures at 4.51am AEST pointing to a fall of 7 points, or 0.1 per cent, at the open. The ASX edged 0.1 per cent higher on Monday. The Australian dollar was trading higher at US72.18¢. The ASX is set for a muted open this morning. Oscar Colman Mining stocks are set to jump as copper surged to its highest-ever price on the London Metal Exchange after a weeks-long rally fuelled by anticipation that President Donald Trump will expand US tariffs to imports of refined metal. Benchmark three-month futures on the LME gained as much as 0.8 per cent to reach $US14,533 a tonne, beating the previous record set in January, before paring some of those advances.



Overnight, the Stoxx Europe 600 Index was little changed at the close in London. Energy stocks outperformed, buoyed by higher commodity prices after the US and Iran traded strikes on tankers, while the media and insurance sectors were among the biggest laggards. US stock futures fell in cautious trading. S&P 500 futures dropped 0.2 per cent while Nasdaq 100 contracts gained. Related Article Opinion

Trade wars Trump would plunge the US into crisis if he carried out his latest bizarre threat Stephen Bartholomeusz Senior business columnist Novartis shares fell 3.2 per cent, the most they have retreated, since April on news that pelacarsen, a potential blockbuster cholesterol drug, failed in a final-stage study. Semiconductor supplier SOITEC rose 12 per cent, outperforming peers in a strong day of trading for AI-adjacent names including Infineon Technologies, which gained 6.9 per cent after an upgrade at MP Capital Markets. Brent crude traded near $US98 per barrel, its highest level since July, after US attacks on Iranian tankers and Tehran’s threat of a new restricted zone outside the Strait of Hormuz raised concerns about prolonged disruptions to energy flows through the waterway. Iran also said a deal with Oman to manage shipping through the strait is imminent. “It appears that everyone has digested a world with slightly higher baseline oil,” said Andrea Gabellone, head of global equities at KBC Securities.



Europe’s sensitivity to energy prices hasn’t stood in the way of a strong second-quarter earnings season and an overall constructive mood among investors that’s rooted in upbeat macroeconomic data. The benchmark Stoxx 600 is less than 2 per cent away from its all-time closing record, though it has edged lower in three out of the past four weeks. “There is a clear cyclical recovery in manufacturing, the PMIs provide clear evidence of this,” said Geoff Yu, a senior macro strategist at Bank of New York Mellon. “Valuations and positioning also help, but it feels like the market is tactical, and of course energy costs this winter will be problematic.” In other single stocks, Nordex SE shares rose as much 12 per cent after the wind turbine maker was upgraded at Bank of America. World.title: Is this the most expensive subject your child could pick?
World.content:
NationalQueenslandSchools Is this the most expensive subject your child could pick? Catherine Strohfeldt September 8, 2026 — 5:00am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Experts fear changes to the Queensland curriculum are turning families away from music studies, as the number of teachers falls, schools reduce the courses on offer, and those that remain have high out-of-pocket costs. Metropolitan schools retain music students through to high school more successfully than other creative arts subjects, partly because of extracurricular offerings such as school bands. However, not all families are prepared to pay. Kelvin Grove State College’s instrumental music program requires families to pay $175 each year to cover uniform costs, with additional instrument hire fees. Kelvin Grove State College / Instagram Instrumental music programs at some of Brisbane’s largest state high schools can cost families $175 each year, and more than $130 in instrument hiring costs, without factoring in private tuition.





For instrumental music, Jenkins said, the state ran a program for selected students from year 3 onwards. “Selection for the music program is up to each school’s individual policy, with consideration given to the ensemble’s make-up, time available and whether the program is a good fit for the student.” The updated Queensland primary curriculum includes one semester of assessable learning every two years as the minimum requirement for creative arts subjects from years 1 to 6. Kathleen Jenkins on a music and education panel at Bigsound in Brisbane. Simon Gorman Clark The curriculum required students to have participated in all five arts subjects – dance, drama, media, music and visual arts – at least once by the end of year 6.



If schools could employ a classroom music teacher, that teacher would teach each year level for between 30 and 40 minutes each week. Queensland Teachers’ Union vice-president Leah Olsson. Catherine Strohfeldt Queensland Teachers’ Union vice-president Leah Olsson said there were about 500 full-time equivalent classroom music teachers across more than 900 primary schools in the state. “Schools are now employing people as art specialists, where they deliver the whole spectrum of the arts,” Olsson said. “Previously, music was its own specialty area, and the classroom teacher would actually take on the responsibility to teaching [other creative arts].”



The union formed a focus group for primary music education 11 years ago, after teachers noticed fewer students choosing music, particularly in the regions where music teachers often covered multiple schools. Related Article University ‘ATARmaxxing’: The school trend experts say is quashing the creative sector Jenkins said industry and external providers could fill the gaps in the public system, but funding was an issue. “We’ve got all sorts of sports grants – we’ve got the Play On vouchers that parents can apply for,” she said. “It’s awesome ... my kids are playing sport because of them, and I bet my kids would probably be learning more about music if we had them [for the creative arts].”



When asked whether it had considered cost-of-living help for arts courses, an Education Department spokesperson said parents could speak to principals about fee waivers. The department’s Back to School Boost program – which will jump to $150 for each primary school child next year – can be applied to music-related costs if they are invoiced directly by the school. A department spokesperson said remote and regional schools could access travel grants and funding for creative arts incursions. World.title: Japan is overrun with tourists, but this city wants more visitors
World.content:
InspirationJapan Japan is overrun with tourists, but this city wants more visitors Ben Groundwater September 8, 2026 — 5:00am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

It’s ironic, that for hundreds of years the only place you would find a foreigner in all of Japan was Nagasaki. This city was once the gateway to the outside world, the lifeline, the only port where non-Japanese ships were allowed to make contact and trade with locals. During the isolationist Edo era, from 1600 to 1868, Japan’s independence was fiercely guarded, and Dejima, an island connected by footbridge to the Nagasaki mainland, was the only spot Portuguese and then Dutch traders were permitted to land. The port city of Nagasaki. iStock Step across the bridge, and you would be captured and executed. Stay on the island, however, and you could meet with Japanese officials and trade goods.



But modern-day Nagasaki is no longer Japan’s only contact point with the outside world – the city now has among the fewest foreign visitors of any Japanese hub. Just 1 per cent of the annual 42 million tourists who visit Japan make their way to this southern prefecture; by comparison, almost 50 per cent of Japan’s tourists visit Tokyo, 43 per cent visit Osaka, and 32 per cent go to Kyoto. 



Nagasaki is in Kyushu, the island at the south of Japan. Cruise ships call in here occasionally, pouring forth a stream of tourists who whip through the key attractions, but for the most part this is a city that feels like the old Japan, the Japan of 20 years ago, when there were few foreign visitors and little dedicated infrastructure to cater for them. If Nagasaki is known for anything on the world stage these days, it is probably the events of August 9, 1945, when US forces dropped a nuclear bomb on the city, killing 35,000 people, making it one of only two cities in the world to suffer such a horrific fate. The Nagasaki Atomic Bomb Museum is therefore the first port of call for many visitors, a moving and often disturbing demonstration of the day and the fallout that the city’s residents will never forget. Read the stories, look at the twisted shards of metal that were once factories and bridges, and marvel at the idea that Nagasaki can even still exist. flowers divide the staircases of the Nagasaki Peace Park. iStock Not all the history here, however, is so confronting. Walk the quiet, tidy streets of Nagasaki and you notice temples and cafes, gardens and shopping malls, a harmonious blend of cultures known locally as “wakaran”, “wa” meaning Japan, “ka”, meaning China, and “ran” referring to the Netherlands. This place has long welcomed visitors, has taken influence from them and moulded them into its own identity.



Consider the local cuisine. This city was the birthplace of yoshoku cuisine, or Western food made in Japanese style, and perhaps the signature dish in Nagasaki is toruko rice, a frankly bonkers plate of food that translates to “Turkey rice”, Turkey being the country that’s half in Asia and half in Europe, as this dish is. Toruko rice has a rice pilaf on the bottom of the plate, topped with a pork katsu, which itself is topped with a mild curry sauce, and then on the side there’s a giant pile of spaghetti with a Neapolitan sauce that’s made up in large part of tomato ketchup. The Peace Statue, Nagasaki. iStock I meet an Italian tourist, Giovanni, while I’m at a bar in Nagasaki, and he offers this opinion on the pasta: “You know, it’s not as bad as I thought.” High praise. Nagasaki is also the home of champon, a vegetable-heavy noodle soup that has been heavily influenced by Chinese cuisine. I sample it at Kanro, a no-frills diner on a quiet backstreet, and enjoy the absolute charm of a true throwback, with its high-backed wooden chairs, its doily-style tablecloths and the TV softly playing Japanese soap operas in the corner.



Tokyo has many things, but it doesn’t have Kanro. That famous island in Nagasaki, Dejima, the lifeline to the world, still exists, though it has since been surrounded by reclaimed land. The site has been preserved in its historic state, a collection of small warehouses and living quarters that once served as the claustrophobic home for the few Portuguese and Dutch traders who were allowed to live there. Unlike those traders, I’m not staying. Instead, I’m heading north to another Kyushu prefecture that remains underappreciated by the tourist masses: Fukuoka, another port city with a long history of welcoming visitors. Fukuoka’s famous dish of tonkotsu ramen. iStock This is an area known for its relaxed, friendly style, a city with plenty going for it, even if the bulk of visitors to Japan still haven’t wised up to it. Again, here it feels different to the “golden triangle” cities, with fewer signs in English, fewer foreign faces in the crowds.



They like their food big and bold in Fukuoka with a preference for punchy flavours and unusual ingredients. I realise this on my first night, as a local guide takes me to a few izakaya, or sake bars, and orders the local specialties. We start with gomasaba, a dish of raw mackerel fillets that are slathered with a thick, soy-and-sesame sauce. We move on to motsunabe, a hotpot with beef intestines. My guide decides against yobuko ikizukuri, a famous local dish of raw squid served so fresh it should still be twitching. Fukuoka’s other famous dish, and the one that it’s well worth travelling here just to experience, is tonkotsu ramen. This is probably the best known, globally, of all Japan’s ramen styles, with a rich, emulsified broth made with pork bones, mixed with thin noodles and draped with slices of pork chashu. Street side eateries are packed in Fukuoka. iStock My idea is to visit the most famous shop in Fukuoka, Hakata Issou, but I find a queue there that must be at least 50 metres long, stretching two city blocks, so I detour to the main train station, which has a huge ramen alley that includes the city’s second-most famous shop, Shin Shin.



The line here is only about 30 metres long. Score. Related Article Japan The delightful region of Japan tourists haven’t discovered yet There’s a good reason, however, that all these people are lining up for so long: the ramen is incredibly tasty, hearty and filling and packed with umami goodness, and it costs the equivalent of about $11. From there, Fukuoka is a place to stroll, to enjoy quiet streets and shop unhassled by the hordes. Here you can pick up a few local delicacies and plan your next Japanese adventure, somewhere that’s not already popular. Five more underappreciated prefectures



Ehime

On the western end of the island of Shikoku, Ehime is a quiet, historic prefecture with plenty to offer. Matsuyama, the capital, has a 17th-century hilltop castle, as well as one of Japan’s most famous hot springs, Dogo Onsen. It’s also known for its cycling routes. Niigata

Want to go skiing, but without Australians? Niigata is your prefecture, with plenty of mountains, lightning-fast shinkansen access from Tokyo, and yet barely any foreigners. This prefecture is also known for the quality of its sake, and the eponymous capital is a buzzing city with an excellent dining scene. Aomori

There’s a vast swathe of land to the north of Tokyo, known as the Tohoku region, that goes largely untouched by foreign tourists. Wakayama

Given the quality of its experiences, it’s a wonder Wakayama prefecture, near Nara and Kyoto, isn’t more popular. This is where you will find the Kumano Kodo, a series of pilgrimage trails through old-growth forest. There’s also Koyasan, a mountaintop village known for being the centre of Shingon Buddhism, and Nachi Falls, Japan’s highest waterfall. Toyama

You get the best of both worlds in Toyama: soaring mountains – a section of the Japanese alps with undulating scenery ripe for exploration – and coastline, which means excellent seafood, and yet more chance for active adventure. Toyama city has parks, markets and a well-known glass art museum.

World.title: Australia news LIVE: Labor’s social media changes to go before the Senate; Joyce flounders under pressure to clarify One Nation’s superannuation proposal
World.content:
Barnaby Joyce has fronted up to the ABC again this morning, just 12 hours after he told the 7.30 program that he was One Nation’s treasury spokesman, “not Jesus Christ”, when he was pushed to explain his party’s superannuation policy.

The policy proposes to allow renters and mortgage holders access to a quarter of their future superannuation contributions over the next three years.

It still appears as though One Nation has not modelled its own proposal, as Joyce was unable to answer questions about the impacts the policy would have on individual households or the wider economy.

Barnaby Joyce and One Nation leader Senator Pauline Hanson during a press conference at Parliament House on Monday. Alex Ellinghausen

He said the suggestion One Nation were expected to model its policy was “perverse”.

“The implications, the implications that I have to model you getting your own money, I find a little bit perverse. It is actually your money,” he told ABC’s Radio National moments ago.

Joyce maintained that the policy would have no inflationary impact, despite critics noting the idea was inherently inflationary.

World.title: ‘No one is prepared’: ChatGPT maker’s top scientist sends an AI warning
World.content:
OpenAI’s top scientist has warned that artificial intelligence is evolving so rapidly that it is becoming increasingly difficult for humans to understand and control, and said he expects AI labs to voluntarily slow development for safety reasons.

In a relatively short space of time, AI models can operate computers, collaborate with humans and other AI systems and carry out research projects, wrote chief scientist Jakub Pachocki in a post titled “An Alien Mind” on Sunday. It won’t be long until they can also improve themselves without human intervention, a process known as recursive self-improvement, he said.

“I expect and hope for voluntary slowdowns to become commonplace until shared safety bars are established.“: OpenAI chief scientist Jakub Pachocki.

“This is a time that calls for extreme caution,” Pachocki wrote in the post. “I am concerned no one is prepared for the consequences of a continued rapid rise in machine intelligence.”

Developers can either try and steer AI more closely to align with human interests or “slow down future development as needed,” he wrote.

World.title: ‘A very costly lemon’: Business groups prepare for working-from-home challenge
World.content:
NationalVictoriaVictorian Parliament ‘A very costly lemon’: Business groups prepare for working-from-home challenge Angus Delaney September 8, 2026 — 5:30am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Blistering legal advice from two barristers will underpin a High Court challenge to Victoria’s working-from-home laws from state business groups, as several of the country’s largest property companies are highly critical of Labor’s plan. Premier Ben Carroll is looking to pass the bill – which will permit most employees the right to work from home two days a week – in parliament this week with some pro-business amendments. However, business groups have again said they are prepared to launch a legal challenge if the bill passes before the state election in November. Employer groups are threatening to launch a High Court challenge against Labor’s working-from-home bill. Eddie Jim “There’s no doubt that there will be a constitutional challenge by employer groups to this legislation if it goes ahead, and we fully expect that it will be a very strong and likely successful challenge,” said Tim Piper, chair of the Victorian Congress of Employer Associations and Victorian head of the Australian Industry group. Piper said he had been approached by “many companies” inquiring and offering to resource a constitutional challenge.



“We have a duty to our members to make sure that legislation passed in Victoria is constitutionally valid and economically reasonable. This one is neither.” Carroll said that flexible work “attracts the best talent in Victoria, and it gets women back in the workforce”. The premier also said that while the government had heard the message that “work from home works” loud and clear, he acknowledged that “laws need to work for business, too, because the reality is if it’s not practical for employers, the law won’t last”. The High Court threat comes as independent legal advice given to the Property Council of Victoria suggests the bill is probably unconstitutional and would be ineffective if it passed parliament.



Lawyers Nick Wood, SC, and Leigh Howard on Monday said Labor’s plan to amend Victoria’s anti-discrimination laws to enshrine working from home as a protected attribute alongside race, sexuality and gender clashed with the federal Fair Work Act. The Constitution states that when a state law is inconsistent with a federal law, it becomes invalid. “In our view, the WFH Bill is inconsistent with the Fair Work Act, and will therefore be inoperative if it is enacted,” the lawyers advised the Property Council. “There would be no question of whether or not part of the WFH Bill is able to be preserved; the entire scheme that is established by the WFH Bill would be inoperative.” They also said there were multiple red flags in the bill, including that it would create a potentially unfair, two-tiered system for workers. Their full legal advice was not provided to The Age and is commercial in confidence pending a High Court challenge. Property Council Victoria executive director Cath Evans said Wood and Howard’s findings should prompt the government to re-think its policy.



Editor's pick Analysis

Victorian election On working from home, Carroll has retreated from a fight about nothing “On the basis of the legal advice we have received, the Victorian public is being sold a very costly lemon,” Evans said. “The government has a choice: listen to the legal concerns, withdraw the bill and give businesses certainty, or push ahead with legislation that could create prolonged costly legal challenges.” Legal experts have previously cast doubt over whether the proposed working-from-home law would interfere with federal industrial relations powers and leave it vulnerable to a High Court challenge. Businesses have also repeatedly challenged Carroll’s assertion that the bill would attract talent into the state, and instead say it would push jobs and investment out.



Peter Menegazzo, chief executive of real estate investment manager Investa, said on Monday that the legislation was already deterring investors. “The state government’s working-from-home legislation is not going away ... so, Melbourne is just not a buy for us at the moment,” he told The Australian Financial Review Property Summit. If the bill passes parliament, it would apply to full-time employees, as well as part-time and regularly employed casuals on a pro rata basis. Employers would also be compelled to pay “reasonable costs” to enable their staff to work remotely. Business groups have discussed a number of amendments with the government, but remain overall opposed to the legislation. Possible amendments include broadening the grounds on which businesses can refuse a working-from-home arrangement, strengthen employers’ ability to manage OH&S obligations, tighten the definition of reasonable employer costs, and give the Victorian Equal Opportunity and Human Rights Commission powers to dismiss frivolous complaints from employees.

World.title: Minor change to title costs worker her job
World.content:
BusinessWorkplaceUnfair dismissal Minor change to title costs worker her job Millie Muroi September 8, 2026 — 5:17am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Employees have been delivered a warning from Australia’s workplace umpire, which has ruled that an insurance broker’s decision to change her title in a legal document justified her dismissal. On Friday, the Fair Work Commission ruled that broker Foula Dendroulakis, who had been employed at Victoria-based insurance company CCIB Services since 2021, was properly dismissed after she dropped the word “senior” from her role as an account manager in formal correspondence. The senior account manager said she was remorseful and apologetic about her conduct. Dendroulakis was at odds with the company over seating arrangements, productivity and working from home when she wrote to the Fair Work Commission alleging she had been forced to take on a more senior job without more pay. But in her correspondence with the commission, she did not include the word “senior” in her title, which CCIB Services viewed as an act of dishonesty and used to dismiss her.



The commission upheld that move, though in part because the insurance broker was a small business, it did not look at whether the employers’ beliefs were ultimately correct or whether the dismissal was harsh on Dendroulakis. When Dendroulakis started at CCIB, her employment contract labelled her only as an “account manager”. But the company said she was recruited to a “senior account manager” position and paid accordingly, and that her business cards and email signature also reflected this. Dendroulakis also referred to herself as a “senior account manager”, including on her LinkedIn profile. Related Article Privacy Canva account at centre of legal fight over employee privacy In 2022, Dendroulakis sought a pay rise in which she referred to herself as a “senior account manager” and was given a pay increase alongside a copy of her position description labelling her as such. In 2025, one of CCIB’s directors, Kurt Alder, decided Dendroulakis was not being productive while working from home. When she was in the office, she was spending “lots of time on personal calls in the boardroom during the work day”, he concluded.



On one occasion, Alder said Dendroulakis had left the office early and did not return. When another co-director, Ryan Fisher, raised the issue with her, he said Dendroulakis “kept changing her story”, initially claiming she had left early to take a lunch break, then saying she was too busy and worked from her phone in her car. In a later email, Dendroulakis said she had left early to allow extra time to arrive at a client’s premises due to poor weather conditions. Later that year, when the company altered seating arrangements in the office, Dendroulakis raised concern about the temperature of the location allocated to her and its impact on her ability to focus and work efficiently. She said that, as a senior team member, she would appreciate an opportunity to “discuss an alternative seat, a private office arrangement, or a work from home agreement for two days a week”. The company said it would not be revisiting the desk issue and that Dendroulakis’ “productivity metrics did not support working two days from home”.



In what the commission termed a “lengthy response”, Dendroulakis then expressed concern about the job title in her employment contract. Related Article Unfair dismissal ‘Classic pub punch’ costs man his job after trading slurs with colleague The company acknowledged the word “senior” had accidentally been omitted from the employment contract and that it had “no concerns” about formally changing her job title. The same month, Dendroulakis was issued a first and final warning about her “inability to perform effectively while working from home”. In December 2025, Dendroulakis made a legal claim with the commission. She alleged that the firm had changed her role without a lawful basis or more pay.



Dendroulakis claimed she had been underpaid and that she was required to perform duties of a “senior account manager” when her title was “account manager”. She also attached a copy of a letter she had previously sent to the company around the time of her pay rise, but removed the word “senior” from her job title in the document. CCIB also got a copy of Dendroulakis’ claim and noticed the omission. Dendroulakis said she had removed the word as a “reflexive correction” in line with her employment agreement, but that it was not deliberate and that she had not intended to mislead the commission. Her lawyers said she was “sincerely remorseful and apologetic” for the oversight, and that “significant work-related stress and anxiety” had affected her attention to detail. Fisher said in evidence that Dendroulakis had become a “liability” to the business and its workplace and had been “blatantly dishonest on more than one occasion”.



Alder claimed Dendroulakis’ conduct was “effectively fraud” designed to bolster her claims against the company in an attempt to mislead the commission and falsely support her general protections claim. Dendroulakis’ conduct was “sufficiently serious,” the commission said – with the employer holding a genuine belief on reasonable grounds about the gravity of the conduct – for immediate dismissal to be justified. World.title: ASX set to slide as oil prices rise; Copper prices soar
World.content:
BusinessMarketsWorld markets ASX set to slide as oil prices rise; Copper prices soar Levin Stamm and Will Standring September 8, 2026 — 5:12am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

European stocks were weighed down by higher oil prices and a drop in Novartis following the failure of a heart drug, while Wall Street was closed for the Labor Day holiday. The Australian sharemarket is set to retreat, with futures at 4.51am AEST pointing to a fall of 7 points, or 0.1 per cent, at the open. The ASX edged 0.1 per cent higher on Monday. The Australian dollar was trading higher at US72.18¢. The ASX is set for a muted open this morning. Oscar Colman Mining stocks are set to jump as copper surged to its highest-ever price on the London Metal Exchange after a weeks-long rally fuelled by anticipation that President Donald Trump will expand US tariffs to imports of refined metal. Benchmark three-month futures on the LME gained as much as 0.8 per cent to reach $US14,533 a tonne, beating the previous record set in January, before paring some of those advances.



Overnight, the Stoxx Europe 600 Index was little changed at the close in London. Energy stocks outperformed, buoyed by higher commodity prices after the US and Iran traded strikes on tankers, while the media and insurance sectors were among the biggest laggards. US stock futures fell in cautious trading. S&P 500 futures dropped 0.2 per cent while Nasdaq 100 contracts gained. Related Article Opinion

Trade wars Trump would plunge the US into crisis if he carried out his latest bizarre threat Stephen Bartholomeusz Senior business columnist Novartis shares fell 3.2 per cent, the most they have retreated, since April on news that pelacarsen, a potential blockbuster cholesterol drug, failed in a final-stage study. Semiconductor supplier SOITEC rose 12 per cent, outperforming peers in a strong day of trading for AI-adjacent names including Infineon Technologies, which gained 6.9 per cent after an upgrade at MP Capital Markets. Brent crude traded near $US98 per barrel, its highest level since July, after US attacks on Iranian tankers and Tehran’s threat of a new restricted zone outside the Strait of Hormuz raised concerns about prolonged disruptions to energy flows through the waterway. Iran also said a deal with Oman to manage shipping through the strait is imminent. “It appears that everyone has digested a world with slightly higher baseline oil,” said Andrea Gabellone, head of global equities at KBC Securities.



Europe’s sensitivity to energy prices hasn’t stood in the way of a strong second-quarter earnings season and an overall constructive mood among investors that’s rooted in upbeat macroeconomic data. The benchmark Stoxx 600 is less than 2 per cent away from its all-time closing record, though it has edged lower in three out of the past four weeks. “There is a clear cyclical recovery in manufacturing, the PMIs provide clear evidence of this,” said Geoff Yu, a senior macro strategist at Bank of New York Mellon. “Valuations and positioning also help, but it feels like the market is tactical, and of course energy costs this winter will be problematic.” In other single stocks, Nordex SE shares rose as much 12 per cent after the wind turbine maker was upgraded at Bank of America. World.title: Is this the most expensive subject your child could pick?
World.content:
NationalQueenslandSchools Is this the most expensive subject your child could pick? Catherine Strohfeldt September 8, 2026 — 5:00am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Experts fear changes to the Queensland curriculum are turning families away from music studies, as the number of teachers falls, schools reduce the courses on offer, and those that remain have high out-of-pocket costs. Metropolitan schools retain music students through to high school more successfully than other creative arts subjects, partly because of extracurricular offerings such as school bands. However, not all families are prepared to pay. Kelvin Grove State College’s instrumental music program requires families to pay $175 each year to cover uniform costs, with additional instrument hire fees. Kelvin Grove State College / Instagram Instrumental music programs at some of Brisbane’s largest state high schools can cost families $175 each year, and more than $130 in instrument hiring costs, without factoring in private tuition.





For instrumental music, Jenkins said, the state ran a program for selected students from year 3 onwards. “Selection for the music program is up to each school’s individual policy, with consideration given to the ensemble’s make-up, time available and whether the program is a good fit for the student.” The updated Queensland primary curriculum includes one semester of assessable learning every two years as the minimum requirement for creative arts subjects from years 1 to 6. Kathleen Jenkins on a music and education panel at Bigsound in Brisbane. Simon Gorman Clark The curriculum required students to have participated in all five arts subjects – dance, drama, media, music and visual arts – at least once by the end of year 6.



If schools could employ a classroom music teacher, that teacher would teach each year level for between 30 and 40 minutes each week. Queensland Teachers’ Union vice-president Leah Olsson. Catherine Strohfeldt Queensland Teachers’ Union vice-president Leah Olsson said there were about 500 full-time equivalent classroom music teachers across more than 900 primary schools in the state. “Schools are now employing people as art specialists, where they deliver the whole spectrum of the arts,” Olsson said. “Previously, music was its own specialty area, and the classroom teacher would actually take on the responsibility to teaching [other creative arts].”



The union formed a focus group for primary music education 11 years ago, after teachers noticed fewer students choosing music, particularly in the regions where music teachers often covered multiple schools. Related Article University ‘ATARmaxxing’: The school trend experts say is quashing the creative sector Jenkins said industry and external providers could fill the gaps in the public system, but funding was an issue. “We’ve got all sorts of sports grants – we’ve got the Play On vouchers that parents can apply for,” she said. “It’s awesome ... my kids are playing sport because of them, and I bet my kids would probably be learning more about music if we had them [for the creative arts].”



When asked whether it had considered cost-of-living help for arts courses, an Education Department spokesperson said parents could speak to principals about fee waivers. The department’s Back to School Boost program – which will jump to $150 for each primary school child next year – can be applied to music-related costs if they are invoiced directly by the school. A department spokesperson said remote and regional schools could access travel grants and funding for creative arts incursions.
