World.title: Japan is overrun with tourists, but this city wants more visitors
World.content:
InspirationJapan Japan is overrun with tourists, but this city wants more visitors Ben Groundwater September 8, 2026 — 5:00am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

It’s ironic, that for hundreds of years the only place you would find a foreigner in all of Japan was Nagasaki. This city was once the gateway to the outside world, the lifeline, the only port where non-Japanese ships were allowed to make contact and trade with locals. During the isolationist Edo era, from 1600 to 1868, Japan’s independence was fiercely guarded, and Dejima, an island connected by footbridge to the Nagasaki mainland, was the only spot Portuguese and then Dutch traders were permitted to land. The port city of Nagasaki. iStock Step across the bridge, and you would be captured and executed. Stay on the island, however, and you could meet with Japanese officials and trade goods.



But modern-day Nagasaki is no longer Japan’s only contact point with the outside world – the city now has among the fewest foreign visitors of any Japanese hub. Just 1 per cent of the annual 42 million tourists who visit Japan make their way to this southern prefecture; by comparison, almost 50 per cent of Japan’s tourists visit Tokyo, 43 per cent visit Osaka, and 32 per cent go to Kyoto. 



Nagasaki is in Kyushu, the island at the south of Japan. Cruise ships call in here occasionally, pouring forth a stream of tourists who whip through the key attractions, but for the most part this is a city that feels like the old Japan, the Japan of 20 years ago, when there were few foreign visitors and little dedicated infrastructure to cater for them. If Nagasaki is known for anything on the world stage these days, it is probably the events of August 9, 1945, when US forces dropped a nuclear bomb on the city, killing 35,000 people, making it one of only two cities in the world to suffer such a horrific fate. The Nagasaki Atomic Bomb Museum is therefore the first port of call for many visitors, a moving and often disturbing demonstration of the day and the fallout that the city’s residents will never forget. Read the stories, look at the twisted shards of metal that were once factories and bridges, and marvel at the idea that Nagasaki can even still exist. flowers divide the staircases of the Nagasaki Peace Park. iStock Not all the history here, however, is so confronting. Walk the quiet, tidy streets of Nagasaki and you notice temples and cafes, gardens and shopping malls, a harmonious blend of cultures known locally as “wakaran”, “wa” meaning Japan, “ka”, meaning China, and “ran” referring to the Netherlands. This place has long welcomed visitors, has taken influence from them and moulded them into its own identity.



Consider the local cuisine. This city was the birthplace of yoshoku cuisine, or Western food made in Japanese style, and perhaps the signature dish in Nagasaki is toruko rice, a frankly bonkers plate of food that translates to “Turkey rice”, Turkey being the country that’s half in Asia and half in Europe, as this dish is. Toruko rice has a rice pilaf on the bottom of the plate, topped with a pork katsu, which itself is topped with a mild curry sauce, and then on the side there’s a giant pile of spaghetti with a Neapolitan sauce that’s made up in large part of tomato ketchup. The Peace Statue, Nagasaki. iStock I meet an Italian tourist, Giovanni, while I’m at a bar in Nagasaki, and he offers this opinion on the pasta: “You know, it’s not as bad as I thought.” High praise. Nagasaki is also the home of champon, a vegetable-heavy noodle soup that has been heavily influenced by Chinese cuisine. I sample it at Kanro, a no-frills diner on a quiet backstreet, and enjoy the absolute charm of a true throwback, with its high-backed wooden chairs, its doily-style tablecloths and the TV softly playing Japanese soap operas in the corner.



Tokyo has many things, but it doesn’t have Kanro. That famous island in Nagasaki, Dejima, the lifeline to the world, still exists, though it has since been surrounded by reclaimed land. The site has been preserved in its historic state, a collection of small warehouses and living quarters that once served as the claustrophobic home for the few Portuguese and Dutch traders who were allowed to live there. Unlike those traders, I’m not staying. Instead, I’m heading north to another Kyushu prefecture that remains underappreciated by the tourist masses: Fukuoka, another port city with a long history of welcoming visitors. Fukuoka’s famous dish of tonkotsu ramen. iStock This is an area known for its relaxed, friendly style, a city with plenty going for it, even if the bulk of visitors to Japan still haven’t wised up to it. Again, here it feels different to the “golden triangle” cities, with fewer signs in English, fewer foreign faces in the crowds.



They like their food big and bold in Fukuoka with a preference for punchy flavours and unusual ingredients. I realise this on my first night, as a local guide takes me to a few izakaya, or sake bars, and orders the local specialties. We start with gomasaba, a dish of raw mackerel fillets that are slathered with a thick, soy-and-sesame sauce. We move on to motsunabe, a hotpot with beef intestines. My guide decides against yobuko ikizukuri, a famous local dish of raw squid served so fresh it should still be twitching. Fukuoka’s other famous dish, and the one that it’s well worth travelling here just to experience, is tonkotsu ramen. This is probably the best known, globally, of all Japan’s ramen styles, with a rich, emulsified broth made with pork bones, mixed with thin noodles and draped with slices of pork chashu. Street side eateries are packed in Fukuoka. iStock My idea is to visit the most famous shop in Fukuoka, Hakata Issou, but I find a queue there that must be at least 50 metres long, stretching two city blocks, so I detour to the main train station, which has a huge ramen alley that includes the city’s second-most famous shop, Shin Shin.



The line here is only about 30 metres long. Score. Related Article Japan The delightful region of Japan tourists haven’t discovered yet There’s a good reason, however, that all these people are lining up for so long: the ramen is incredibly tasty, hearty and filling and packed with umami goodness, and it costs the equivalent of about $11. From there, Fukuoka is a place to stroll, to enjoy quiet streets and shop unhassled by the hordes. Here you can pick up a few local delicacies and plan your next Japanese adventure, somewhere that’s not already popular. Five more underappreciated prefectures



Ehime

On the western end of the island of Shikoku, Ehime is a quiet, historic prefecture with plenty to offer. Matsuyama, the capital, has a 17th-century hilltop castle, as well as one of Japan’s most famous hot springs, Dogo Onsen. It’s also known for its cycling routes. Niigata

Want to go skiing, but without Australians? Niigata is your prefecture, with plenty of mountains, lightning-fast shinkansen access from Tokyo, and yet barely any foreigners. This prefecture is also known for the quality of its sake, and the eponymous capital is a buzzing city with an excellent dining scene. Aomori

There’s a vast swathe of land to the north of Tokyo, known as the Tohoku region, that goes largely untouched by foreign tourists. One of the most interesting prefectures is Aomori, where you will find Hirosaki, with a samurai-era castle popular during cherry blossom season, while Aomori city is known for its huge annual festival. Wakayama

Given the quality of its experiences, it’s a wonder Wakayama prefecture, near Nara and Kyoto, isn’t more popular. This is where you will find the Kumano Kodo, a series of pilgrimage trails through old-growth forest. There’s also Koyasan, a mountaintop village known for being the centre of Shingon Buddhism, and Nachi Falls, Japan’s highest waterfall. Toyama

You get the best of both worlds in Toyama: soaring mountains – a section of the Japanese alps with undulating scenery ripe for exploration – and coastline, which means excellent seafood, and yet more chance for active adventure. Toyama city has parks, markets and a well-known glass art museum.

World.title: Hamilton pensioners going without food, charity says
World.content:
A charity says the high cost of living is forcing some older people to go with little food.

Hamilton's St Vincent De Paul have made pensioners the focus of their service after noticing the elderly have been falling through the cracks.

When Sandra saw Shonae George with a trolley full of food at the supermarket, she commented on how large her family must be.

But George was shopping for the St Vincent de Paul food bank.

And Sandra, with just cat food in her trolley, needed its help.

It still took her two weeks to pluck up the courage to call.

"Ever since then I look forward to Vinnie's coming because they've been so wonderful and kind, and I want to cry."

She and her husband are two of the 90 pensioners St Vincent de Paul delivered food parcels to every fortnight. They're delivered across four days in the week between fortnightly pension payments.

The couple had worked hard all their lives and owned their home, but with just the pension coming in now, things had got hard.

"We're so grateful because all we get is a bloody pension and everything is going up, the rates and everything."

Some of the food stocked up at St Vincent De Paul's food bank warehouse. RNZ/Rachel Moore

St Vincent de Paul's special projects manager Shonae George said while families were struggling, it could be harder for pensioners.

"Our hearts are quite sad for our pensioners because as much as times are hard for families, it's harder for them because their money doesn't get increased.

"They're real genuine, like they need it."

While the food parcel isn't heaps, it's stocked with the basics.

"We still try to give them toilet paper, stuff like that. Underneath's got milk, cereal, tea bags. We've got some butters, we've got cans of food, pasta and then a whole chicken for today.

"We've been told it's Christmas when they get one of these parcels. There'll be food in here like an orange that they haven't had for a long time, that just one little orange makes their year, you know?"

John was another food bank recipient. He said the food parcels take the pressure off.

"I do alright, but its a big struggle.

"It just touches my heart, mate."

St Vincent de Paul's general manager Mike Rolton said 80 percent of their food parcels would now go to pensioners and the criteria was simple - their only income had to be the pension.

"They get their pension by the time they pay their power, their rent. There's very little left for food, sometimes as much as about $20 is all that's left.

"We've had pensioners come in here looking for underwear because they can't afford to buy it.

"They're starving. The ones that we see are coming to our [community] lunch currently are very, very hungry and they've told me that's the only meal they get.

"They've done their time. Let's look after them for a bit better."

World.title: Human remains found at Northland property
World.content:
Police are investigating after human remains were found at a property in Waiomio, Northland.

Detective inspector Michele Gillespie said police were called to the property on Monday afternoon and a scene guard has been in place overnight.

Gillespie said police are working to recover the body and the death is currently being treated as unexplained.

World.title: What Methanex's departure will do to gas prices
World.content:
Methanex closure unlocks large gas supply Nine To Noon Download MP3 13m

With New Zealand's single biggest gas consumer Methanex announcing a decision to close from next year and sell off its gas contracts, what impact will it have on households and small businesses?

Methanex was at times using close to half of the country's total natural gas supply.

The Canadian multinational's departure releases a huge amount of gas supply into a market that has struggled in recent years.

Electricity generator-retailer Genesis Energy has announced it has picked up major gas contracts that run from March next year through to December 2029.

Ben Gerritsen is general manager of customer and regulation at Clarus - the company that runs the gas transmission network in the North Island. He told Nine to Noon on Tuesday it was a "big shift" and "big deal" for the local Taranaki economy, which Methanex was a part of for more than four decades - but not a surprise.

"Thinking about Methanex's decision in the context of the overall gas market, it's not surprising and it is part of a transition in the New Zealand gas industry that started a few years ago when supply constraints started to emerge and gas has kind of been redirected, if you like, to its highest value use.

"Methanex's business model globally is to operate in countries with plentiful gas and export that in the form of methanol. So with the decline in gas production in New Zealand, it's not surprising."

But will it translate into cheaper prices for other users, be they industrial or household? Gerritsen said he had to be "careful" predicting future prices, but expected an easing in the near-term for both.

And it might even help some companies stay afloat, rather than shut up shop due to high costs.

"Ultimately that is in the hands of the gas retailers in terms of competition between the likes of Genesis Energy, Contact, Nova, others. But certainly having availability of more gas, that's been the key constraint in recent years.

"So when you've heard industrial consumers being concerned that they can't get a contract on terms that they used to, I think this extra supply in the short term will help that challenge. "

But the challenge remained in the long-term, he said, because New Zealand's known gas fields were "in a pattern of decline" with some expected to close soon.

Big energy companies, such as Genesis, had limited capacity to store gas, Gerritsen said - and may use what it has to produce electricity when needed.

"I think what Genesis may well look to do is, the sort of flexibility that Methanex has provided in recent years where it will essentially turn off during winter and redirect the gas to electricity generation - we may see Genesis look to other industrial customers to operate in a similar mode.

"So the industrial consumer will get the gas on relatively favourable price terms. It can use it during summer, it can use it during wet years. But when the electricity generator is needed, the gas can be redirected to generate electricity."

Households should not expect a price drop, particularly in the North Island where there are fixed costs involved in the pipeline supply network.

"The costs of the pipeline network and delivering gas throughout the North Island are essentially fixed. They're the infrastructure costs. of transporting the gas."

Further into the future, Methanex's absence could drive up prices, Gerritsen said, as local sources become scarce.

World.title: Internal polling has Labour Party above 30 percent, Chris Hipkins says
World.content:
Weekly interview with opposition leader, Chris Hipkins Morning Report Download MP3 11m

Labour's internal polling has the party above 30 percent, compared to the latest Taxpayers' Union Curia poll which has the party at 25.9 percent, Chris Hipkins says.

It comes as the Labour leader hints at a climate change policy to be announced later on Tuesday.

Hipkins brushed off the latest TPU-Curia poll result released on Monday, saying the only poll that matters is the election result.

That's despite dismissing last month's result, which had slightly higher support for Labour, as "rogue".

Speaking to Morning Report on Tuesday, Hipkins said it was "the National Party's poll, and it is lower than we want to be".

He stopped short of calling the poll unreliable, saying all polls were a valid sample of the people who they poll, "but the reality is there's there's a whole variety of different poll results out there at the moment".

Hipkins also referred to the previous RNZ Reid-Research poll that had Labour on 32.2 percent.

"Your own polling indicated a significantly different result to the one that you're questioning me about now [TPU-Curia], which of course is the National Party's poll."

Asked multiple times what Labour's internal polling, done by Talbot Mills, had the party on, Hipkins refused to say - before admitting it was above 30 percent.

"It is significantly better than what the National Party's polls are saying."

Chris Hipkins announces Labour's campaign slogan. Rachel Graham / RNZ

It was put to Hipkins the trend in all polls was going downward, with Hipkins responding "our goal is to obviously turn that trend back around".

Asked about self-reflection on his own performance, and whether he'd been "phoning it in" and should have been trying harder, Hipkins said "we live in an age of anger".

"I'm not going to be an angry politician yelling at everybody and making them angry. I am optimistic about the future of New Zealand.

"We can provide New Zealanders with more opportunity. I'm not going to settle for a country in which your opportunities depend on how much money your parents have. I think we're a better country than that, and that is exactly what I'm going to be campaigning on."

Asked where he'd been - if not campaigning - for the earlier part of the political term, Hipkins said Labour had been holding the government accountable for its "misdeeds".

"That is the job of the opposition. When you get into the campaign, though, you get to talk more about what you're going to do, and we are doing that."

He also said Labour would be pushing back on the National Party during the campaign, "who are out there telling absolute lies about the Labour Party".

"They've got billboards up all over the country around tax that are just absolutely untruthful. There's nothing factual. There's nothing truthful about them."

National has been on the attack recently with billboards and social media ads claiming the opposition would "triple your taxes", with Labour's capital gains tax as well as multiple policies from other left-leaning parties that Hipkins has ruled out.

He described Labour setting out plans for fixing "the crisis in our health system" and around solar power, as well as foreshadowing an announcement on climate change later on Tuesday.

The Labour leader was also questioned about his policies and their costs, specifically the plan not to increase the fuel excise duty at all for an entire term if elected.

Hipkins said with the exception of that policy, every policy Labour had announced had come with an explanation of how it would be paid for.

Transport Minister Chris Bishop. RNZ / Mark Papalii

Transport Minister Chris Bishop has said Labour's policy on the fuel excise tax freeze would create a $4.6 billion shortfall.

Hipkins said Bishop was "absolutely wrong" because he hadn't included the government's own announcement "that they're doing half of what we have said".

"So they're going to freeze fuel taxes for the next 18 months, and they're putting extra money in to cover the cost of that.

"I'm saying that we would extend it for for the rest of the parliamentary term, beyond that, which by the way is hardly radical because it's what they've done this parliamentary term."

Asked multiple times for Labour's figure on how much it would cost, Hipkins refused to say.

Hipkins said he would release the costings once the government opens the books for the pre-election fiscal update (PREFU).

But it was put to him the PREFU outlined how much money there was to spend, rather than how much a party's policies cost, "that's for you to know, you don't have to wait for the PREFU", Morning Report co-host John Campbell said.

World.title: Fiji spearheads push to 'make rugby league great again' in the Pacific
World.content:
The Fiji National Rugby League (FNRL) is spearheading discussions for new regional tournaments aimed at creating playing opportunities for local players in the region.

FNRL chairman Rajesh Singh has confirmed that discussions are being held with New Zealand Rugby League (NZRL) and Asia Pacific Rugby League (APRL) to establish a Nines (9s) tournament series in the Pacific.

At the same time, there are also plans to have a 13-a-side tournament similar to rugby union's Pacific Nations Cup (PNC).

Singh told local media in Suva last week the new 9s tournament would feature Fiji, Samoa, Tonga, Cook Islands, New Zealand and Papua New Guinea.

"It will include all local players and it'll be a pathway for our local resident club players," Singh confirmed to local media.

"We need to give our local players in the islands the opportunity to have competitive matches so they can also develop their skills and knowledge of the game."

The 13-a-side tournament will follow the same format as the PNC, which had Fiji, Samoa and Tonga initially, but now includes Japan, Canada and the United States of America.

Singh said they also want test matches with the future Kiwis' teams and the Māori selections.

"We're going to have more discussions to make rugby league great again," he added.

NZRL chairman Justin Leydesdoff told local media in Suva that they are working with FNRL to grow the game in the country by providing opportunities for resident club teams.

"We're (NZ) in the same pool with Fiji in the World Cup and Fiji has done well against the Kiwis previously, so I can commit to supporting Fiji in every game, except against the Kiwis and Kiwi Ferns," he said.

"We have a long and strong relationship as a country and as a sport. It's about having close relations to ensure that we maximise the opportunities there."

APRL chairman Sandis Tsaka said they were assisting Pacific countries in developing the game.

"There's been a structured pathway and programs for elite players, but we feel we can do more within our region for our domestic competitions to support our young people," he said.

"The issues and challenges are the same across the region as discussed over the last 12 days."

India, China and stadium talks

Meanwhile, Singh said the FNRL is also in discussion with India and China on possible assistance for the construction of a stadium.

Fiji signed up to Australia's Pacific Rugby League Partnership last month, with that funding expected to boost the sport locally, especially in boosting youth and women's development.

Singh said as part of their focus on getting a NRL spot for a franchise club the FNRL would need to have a proper stadium to host NRL matches.

He confirmed discussions have started with both India, who have just been voted in as a member of the international federation, and China.

Singh said to be considered for NRL inclusion Fiji must have upgraded facilities, including a custom built stadium.

"That is important and we want to have that here," he said.

As far as the upcoming Rugby League World Cup (RLWC) is concerned, Singh said they have a 40-member squads registered with International Rugby League, for both the men and women's teams.

World.title: 'Ever evolving': PNG's unifying language celebrated in Tok Pisin Wik
World.content:
Members of Wellington's Papua New Guinea community say Tok Pisin is a versatile language that many people can use with relative ease.

Tok Pisin Wik is underway this week with a series of events around New Zealand celebrating Papua New Guinea's national language and traditional cultures.

The Ministry of Pacific Peoples has provided some useful resources for the week - Tenkyu tru!

Ancey Wamiri, a school teacher, told RNZ Pacific she uses Tok Pisin every day with family and friends, also teaches it during Tok Pisin Wik sessions.

Wellington's PNG community celebrate Tok Pisin language Pacific Waves Download MP3 4m

Describing Tok Pisin as being in her blood and bones, Wamiri explained that the language has been been an "essential unifying factor" for people in a country of many diverse cultures.

"The wonderful thing about Tok Pisin is it has united us as a country, to be able to connect amongst ourselves as a nation.

"If we didn't have Tok Pisin then we'd be a completely divided people. So it was essential to have Tok Pisin become a part of the unifying language for our people.

A traditional dance from Papua New Guinea's islands region performed at a cultural festival in the capital Port Moresby. RNZ / Johnny Blades

Wamiri said Tok Pisin is very much a living language that is never stagnant.

"It's ever developing and ever evolving and changing," she explained.

"The great thing is it is a recognised language and not just a creole or a slight version of the English language - because it does have quite a bit of English in it - but somehow along the way it's gone into waves, dips and highs to be a language that we can speak."

Living language

If you're nervous about giving it a go, don't be. As the Wellington community say, it's versatile, and there's often no one right way to say something.

A common exchange may go: "Yu olrait? (How are you?)" responded to with "Mi olrait, tenkyu (I am good, thank you)"

Tommy Poliap Posangat told RNZ Pacific that from its origin, Tok Pisin was created as a way to bridge diversity.

"I believe Tok Pisin was created during he plantation period, when they brought all the islanders, Melanesians, together to work the plantations," Posangat said.

"And because PNG's got a variation of languages, over 800 languages, they've had to come up with a language that they can all speak and understand each other - not just the Papua New Guineans but you have the Solomon Islanders, Fijians and the Vanuatuans coming together, so that's how Tok Pisin was formed backed then, and it's just been evolving ever since."

Synthetic wool and plastic have replaced plant fibre material in many Papua New Guinea cultures but the art of bilum making remains as vibrant as ever. RNZ Pacific/Scott Waide

Every day use

College student Naimah Leahy said the majority of her wider family still lives in PNG, so she makes an effort to stay in touch, which in turn helps keep her use of Tok Pisin alive.

"Apart from the time difference (two hours), I almost call them every day, message every day, make sure that I still am connected to those who are in Papua New Guinea because that's like my home," Leahy said.

Another college student from Wellington who is Papua New Guinean is Dziewanna Wamiri-Cokataki who said Tok Pisin is a beautiful language.

"It's like a wave, it's very up and down. You talk with a lot of emotion," she said, adding that using it with friends was a good way to keep growing the language.

"It's very cool to try and converse and learn, so that's what we try and do."

Em nau (that's right).

World.title: Christchurch man starts petition in hopes NZ Post will 'push pause' on service closures
World.content:
Fight to save postal services in Christchurch CBD Morning Report Download MP3 4m

A Christchurch man fighting to stop the closure of NZ Post's suburban postal services says the community should have been consulted.

NZ Post confirmed a total of 21 other services around Christchurch would close this year with a one-stop shop on Moorhouse Avenue to become the hub for the central city and surrounding areas.

Cashel St Pharmacy owner Annabel Turley wrapped up her postal services this month after NZ Post told her to cease services by November.

The move had been met with anger from some residents.

Planned closures of other Christchurch post shops - as part of NZ Post's rollback of countrywide counter services - had also been met with resistance.

Sockburn resident Luke Chandler has started a petition to prevent the closures.

Chandler told Morning Report he learned about the closure of the Sockburn shop when picking up his mail.

"I actually just walked past and noticed some signs in the window, went in to collect my mail that morning and it just had a couple of signs up saying that they're moving services to Moorhouse Avenue. No sort of consultation, nothing online, no flyers you can pick up to learn a little bit more [about it]," he said.

"I chatted with the staff and apparently it was some sort of an internal review that they did and some consultation with staff and that was the extent of it."

Sockburn would retain its PO Box service but would no longer have a staffed shop and parcel collection service, Chandler said.

"This is actually the pick-up hub for the southwest of the city. So this branch serves tens of thousands of people across western Christchurch, so it's a massive change."

Residents in southwestern parts of Christchurch would now be forced to travel into the central city.

"Sockburn specifically is well served by buses and is accessible on foot. Not everyone can simply jump in a car and drive to Moorhouse Ave," Chandler said.

"I think of residents that live out in Templeton and Halswell and even further beyond that that want to be able to pick up their parcels, they no longer will be able to do so from Sockburn.

"They will be forced to drive into the central city and to Moorhouse Ave to pick up parcels, which is quite the trek in itself."

Chandler had started a petition which he said had garnered more than 1500 signatures thus far.

"It's been a great response and shows that the community clearly wants to be listened to. NZ Post should push pause on what they're doing at the moment, consult with the community and listen to what they actually have to say."

There had been no community consultation over the planned closures of the Sockburn and Cashel Street branches, Chandler said.

"They were decided very last minute, and they conducted a review with their staff, but they didn't consult the public on these two particular branches."

He said people in his neighbourhood would be able to travel to other stores about three kilometres away, but this was limited to standard letter and parcel sending services.

Chandler said he had been inspired the efforts of National's Bay of Plenty MP Tom Rutherford who advocated for the retention of postal services in Pāpāmoa.

"I'm hopeful that NZ Post is going to come to the table and listen to us a little bit, push pause and just see what the community wants and just really understand the impacts of closing a branch that services tens of thousands of people across west Christchurch."

In a statement, NZ Post said after consultation with their people they had decided to close the Sockburn service.

World.title: Everything you need to know ahead of NFL Melbourne
World.content:
American Football will roll into the MCG for a regular-season NFL match for the first time on Friday.

The San Francisco 49ers will take on the Los Angeles Rams, who are the nominal home team for the game.

This will be the first regular-season NFL game ever hosted in Australia, although American Football matches have taken place in the country before.

Here's everything you need to know about the game.

When is the game?

Davante Adams (left) will look to continue his excellent form into the new year. (Getty Images: Brooke Sutton)

The game takes place on Friday morning AEST, with kick-off at 10:35am.

That is what time kick-off will be in Victoria, New South Wales, Queensland, Tasmania and the ACT.

In the Northern Territory and South Australia, that is a 10:05am kick-off. In Western Australia, kick-off will be 8:35am.

This is to cater for the Thursday night television audience in the United States, with a New York kick-off time of 8:35pm, while in LA the game will get underway at 5:35pm.

If you are going to the game, the gates open at 7am local time, with access to the Yarra Park precinct, which the NFL has dubbed the NFL Stadium Campus.

There will be food, entertainment, sponsor activations and fan activities to keep punters busy once they get inside.

Who is playing?

The 49ers and the Rams will meet in their season opener. (Getty Images: Brooke Sutton)

The Los Angeles Rams and San Francisco 49ers are the two teams who are set to play in this historic clash.

The Rams are the home team and come into the season as one of the favourites for this year's Super Bowl, with a stacked offence and miserly defence.

If you think the Rams sound familiar but the LA bit is confusing you, that's because the team has moved around a bit.

The team was formed in 1936 as the Cleveland Rams, moved to LA in 1946, but then shifted to St Louis in 1995, where they stayed for 20 years.

In 2015, the Rams moved back to Los Angeles.

You don't need a hat like this, but I'm sure it will help. (Getty Images: MediaNews Group/Pasadena Star-News/Keith Birmingham)

They are two-time Super Bowl Champions, winning their most recent in 2021. They play at SoFi Stadium in Inglewood.

The 49ers have always expected to reach the play-offs at an absolute minimum and will think they can do so again, despite a season beset by injuries last year.

Formed in 1944, the 49ers have always been based in the Bay area, although they currently play outside San Francisco at Levi's Stadium in Santa Clara.

They have won five Super Bowls, but have not won one since 1994, despite appearing in three Super Bowls since then, most recently in 2023.

How can I watch?

The game will be available to watch in Australia on Fox Sports/Kayo or on free-to-air on Channel Seven or 7Plus.

Coverage starts from 10am AEST.

Are tickets still available?

Want to join the Rams fans? There's still time. (Getty Images: Icon Sportswire/Greg Fiore)

If you'd rather watch the game live, as of Monday, there are still tickets available, both standing and seated, for the game at the MCG.

You can purchase the tickets via Ticketmaster.

Why is the NFL playing in Australia?

Heading into the 2026 season, there have been 62 regular-season NFL games played away from the USA.

Starting in 2005 with Mexico City, the NFL has gradually expanded its global reach, with games in nine different cities so far, with two more added in 2026.

Melbourne, Paris and Rio de Janeiro join London, Mexico City, Toronto, Berlin, Frankfurt, Munich, São Paulo and Madrid in hosting regular-season matches.

The idea is to spread the gospel and increase the global presence of a league that has no international competition outside of America.

MCG joins illustrious list

The MCG adds itself to an exclusive list of stadiums. (Getty Images: AFL Photos/Morgan Hancock)

Here's a pub quiz stat for you — the MCG will become the fifth stadium to host an NFL game and the opening/closing ceremony of an Olympic Games.

The Los Angeles Memorial Coliseum (1932, 1984), Berlin's Olympiastadion (1936), London's Wembley (1940) and the Estádio do Maracanã in Rio de Janeiro (2016) have all hosted an Olympic Games opening ceremony, as did the MCG in 1956.

The Stade de France (closing ceremony at Paris 2024) will join it on that list when it hosts its first game later in the season.

Given the Rams are the home team, they will now have hosted matches at two different Olympic stadiums, having played at the Coliseum between 1946-1979 and 2016-2019.

Perhaps less surprisingly, the MCG is the first stadium to have hosted a Cricket World Cup final and an NFL regular-season game, so there is that.

At 100,022, the stadium has the largest capacity of any that will be used by the league this season.

Players to watch: Rams

Matthew Stafford had a career-best year in 2025. (Getty Images: Kevin Sabitus)

Quarterback Matt Stafford led the league with 4,707 passing yards and 46 passing touchdowns last season, with just eight interceptions.

That was one reason why the Rams' offence was the best in the entire league, averaging 30.5 points per game last season.

He has two elite wide receivers in his armory in Davante Adams and Puka Nacua, who was rated as the fourth-best player in the entire league by the NFL cohort.

The potential issue is that Stafford is now 38 years old and has historically struggled to back up productive passing seasons in the past.

Defensively, Myles Garrett was recently polled as the number one player in the NFL by his peers, and it's easy to see why.

According to the NFL players, Myles Garrett is the best player around. (Getty Images: Ric Tapia)

The 30-year-old defensive end led the league in sacks (23) and tackles for loss (33) last season for the Browns and his acquisition fills a gaping hole that was ruthlessly exposed as the Rams struggled down the stretch in 2025.

It's not just Garrett who has come in, though. The Rams have recruited two elite cornerbacks in Trent McDuffie and Jaylen Watson.

They will also welcome back Super Bowl-winning defensive tackle Aaron Donald, who has come out of retirement to lead the defensive line one last time.

Players to watch: 49ers

Two of the 49ers best players either side of the ball; defensive end Nick Bosa and tight end George Kittle, are coming off serious injuries from last season, so all eyes will be on how they front up when they suit back up this year.

Brock Purdy will want to iron out his interceptions this season. (Getty Images: Luke Hales)

On the defensive side, the 49ers pass rush is a genuine concern, especially if Bosa can't return from the ACL injury that ended his season, which means former Dallas Cowboy Osa Odighizuwa may need to really up his game from defensive tackle

Offensively, Brock Purdy will be desperate to stay fit for long enough to really get into a rhythm this season.

Last year the young quarterback started just nine games and managed a TD/INT ratio of 20/10. That's too many interceptions for an elite quarterback and, given the addition of quality wide receivers Mike Evans and rookie De'Zhaun Stribling, the Niners fans will hope he can find his accuracy.

Given all those new toys for Purdy to play with, running back Christian McCaffrey shouldn't need to be thrown to as many times as he was last year.

Christian McCaffrey got through a mountain of work in 2025. (Getty Images: Ezra Shaw)

The running back had an astonishing 102 receptions — the sixth most of any player in the league — for 924 yards and seven touchdowns last season.

That's in addition to his day job of running with the ball, where he had 1,202 yards from 311 rushes for 10 touchdowns, the eighth most rushing yards of anyone in the league.

His backup is likely to be Kaelon Black, so keep an eye on him as to whether he can carry some of that running load this season.

World.title: Cricket Australia green lights BBL privatisation, defying power states
World.content:
The Big Bash League will be partially privatised, in what looms as one of the most significant shake-ups of Australian cricket in decades.

Cricket Australia will defy heavyweight states New South Wales and Queensland to forge ahead with plans to allow states to explore sell-offs of 49 per cent stakes in their BBL franchises.

The decision to proceed was effectively made at a Cricket Australia board meeting last week, and will be officially green lit on Monday night.

BBL privatisation 'inevitable': CA Cricket Australia chief executive Todd Greenberg says private investment in the Big Bash League is "inevitable" and waiting for too long could mean "we've missed the boat" as more competitions pop up around the world.

It is understood a formal announcement will be made by Cricket Australia on Tuesday, in concert with several superstars of Australian cricket — a coup, given some initial pushback from the Australian Cricketers' Association.

However, there remains several details to be ironed out between the ACA and the CA, which has argued, amongst other things, for a greater share of revenue for its players.

The ACA insists it's supportive of privatisation as long as the long-term interests of the game are protected.

The players' union will continue to negotiate with Cricket Australia over, among other things, just how big a slice of the pie the players will receive.

This will form part of a new memorandum of understanding between the two parties.

Tasmania, Victoria and Western Australia are in support of the decision, that will allow states to undertake a market sounding process for the sale of 49 per cent stakes in their teams.

BBL privatisation became more of a reality when Cricket Victoria made plans to sell the Melbourne Renegades franchise earlier this year. (AAP Image: James Ross)

But power states New South Wales and Queensland remain opposed to the plan and will undoubtedly be rankled by Cricket Australia's decision to press ahead without them fully on board.

South Australia remains lukewarm on the concept but is more open to the idea than New South Wales or Queensland.

New South Wales has long believed an injection of private equity would largely amount to a sugar hit, and broader structural reform is needed to ensure Cricket Australia's financial viability into the future.

Cricket New South Wales has been contacted for comment.

Cricket Australia believes the privatisation will allow the BBL to keep up with other domestic T20 competitions around the world, such as India's IPL. (AP)

In contrast, Cricket Australia believe that privatisation of the BBL will allow the league to keep pace with rival competitions around the world, with proceeds to be spread throughout the broader Australian cricket ecosystem.

Transactions could be complete before the start of next season.

It is likely that prospective international team owners will be courted across the upcoming summer, with potential buyers expected to be in Australia to cast their eye over this year's BBL tournament.

In June, the privatisation process was accelerated when Cricket Victoria pre-emptively made plans to sell the Melbourne Renegades, while retaining the Melbourne Stars licence.

Several state CEOs recently travelled to India and the UK to connect with prospective buyers, ahead of being given formal approval to commence a sell-off process by Cricket Australia.

World.title: V'landys accuses NRL players of 'not telling truth' on rule confusion
World.content:
Peter V'landys has accused players of "not telling the truth" about set-restart confusion, as a survey of finals captains revealed ongoing uncertainty around the ruck.

The topic of set restarts is set to dominate the NRL finals, after Melbourne star Harry Grant claimed widespread frustration from players at the weekend.

The Melbourne captain declared most no longer knew what constituted a fast or slow play-the-ball, and the NRL needed to decide between being rugby league or touch football.

An AAP survey of captains and representatives at Monday's finals launch backed up Grant's claims, with six of the sides indicating they were still not entirely clear on what ruck speed referees wanted.

According to V'landys, Storm skipper Harry Grant (pictured) has 'got it wrong' when it comes to set-restarts. (Getty Images: Brendon Thorne )

Also raised by players was the fact there is no chance to ask for clarification, given the game rolls on quickly with a set restart.

But V'landys disagreed, pointing to the fact there are only two reasons for set restarts and players had become more compliant for offside ones.

"I don't buy that," ARL Commission chairman V'landys said.

"The wrestling's got to go. The fans did not like the wrestling, they didn't like people slowing down the ruck speed. And we've accommodated that.

"The players know when they're trying to control the ruck speed.

" I think that they're not telling the truth if they believe when they're giving a six again, they didn't know what it was for. I mean, I think it's pretty obvious. "

Set restarts increased dramatically over the first half of the season, before dropping off through the State of Origin period and rising again in recent weeks.

The rise at the start of the year coincided with the NRL expanding the area in which they can be awarded to from 60 metres of the field to 80.

V'landys indicated they would not be repealed next season, rejecting Grant's claims there was confusion this year.

"I have the ultimate respect for Harry, and Harry's an absolute ornament of the game, but he's got this one wrong," V'landys said.

"When you look at the facts, the ruck speed is still the same as it was last year. It's around 3.5 seconds, and it remains that way.

Sharks co-captain Cameron McInnes (pictured) backed up Grant's viewpoint over the players' confusion. (Getty Images: Darrian Traynor)

"Some teams try to take advantage of the ruck and slow the ruck down … we make no apology that we're going to keep the ruck speed the same for both teams.

"The raw numbers don't back up what Harry is saying."

The majority of club representatives surveyed on Monday did not blame referees, but suggested there was still some grey area around ruck interpretation.

"With some of the six agains, who knows what they are for," Cronulla co-captain Cameron McInnes said.

"I just think about a fan watching at home … you just see them and think 'what was that for? It was like the tackle before'.

"That's a problem."

Warriors captain Roger Tuivasa-Sheck (pictured) is concerned that a faster game will lead to more injuries for the players. (AAP: Dan Himbrechts)

Asked if he shared the same confusion, McInnes suggested he did.

"I get the clear as day ones where guys are taking the piss … but then there are flops and re-grips that don't get called as well," he said.

"I don't know what their mindset is, but there will be some at the start of the game that is given a six again, and others that are not."

Some players at the NRL finals launch also raised concerns around whether a faster game had prompted an increased injury toll.

"I feel like it's not a clear understanding [of the interpretation]," injured Warriors veteran Roger Tuivasa-Sheck said.

"As players we understand they want a faster and more entertaining game, but they're risking that with the number of injuries every team has.

"That's what they have to weigh up.

"Yes we're building a very entertaining game and people love the product. But at the same time you lose all these big players out."

AAP

World.title: Knee scans reveal heartbreaking verdict for luckless Swans captain
World.content:
Callum Mills has suffered more September heartbreak, with scans confirming the Sydney captain has torn his anterior cruciate ligament (ACL) in his right knee.

The defender could also potentially miss the entire 2027 season after he went down with a serious knee injury during Sydney's 53-point upset of the Brisbane Lions.

Mills's knee gave way as he attempted to corral Brisbane's Will Ashcroft near the boundary, late in the first quarter after an understrength Swans outfit burst to a 40-8 lead.

Swans coach Dean Cox was already expecting the worst in the aftermath, with scans on Monday confirming the injury.

Mills will meet with a specialist to determine a date for surgery.

It is the latest setback for the luckless 29-year-old, who missed the Swans' 2024 grand final loss with a hamstring strain he picked up before the preliminary final.

Mills had played just seven games in 2024 after hurting a shoulder in a "Mad Monday" wrestling contest with a teammate.

This year was the first time the defender had played more than 20 games since Sydney's 2022 grand final run.

The upset victory against Brisbane followed a tumultuous few weeks in the fallout from the Pullman Hotel scandal.

Mills was seen on crutches as his Swans teammates celebrated their win over the Lions on Saturday. (Getty Images: Matt King)

Mills has earned significant praise for leading the Swans through the turmoil, which past players have admitted shattered the club's famed "Bloods culture''.

Star players Isaac Heeney, Chad Warner and Nick Blakey — All-Australian contenders before they were banned from being selected — are among the five serving club-imposed bans.

Important tagger James Jordon and defender Riley Bice are the other Swans who won't play again this season.

Cox's selection conundrum is further complicated with key forward Joel Amartey (Achilles) and winger Justin McInerney (hamstring) nearing full fitness.

Hayden McLean — playing as cover for Amartey — slotted three majors against the Lions, with fellow talls Charlie Curnow (five goals) and Logan McDonald (six) also busy.

AAP

World.title: AFL acts to reduce head trauma at training for men and women
World.content:
The AFL will introduce limits on contact training for the 2027 men's and women's season in a bid to reduce concussion and head trauma.

All 18 clubs will be required to audit contact training and provide training vision to the AFL on request as part of regulations announced on Monday.

The measures dictate limits for the upcoming men's pre-season, with in-season training and an AFLW framework to be later introduced.

Set by week, measures start from a total limit of 120 minutes, which includes 60 minutes of high-intensity contact training.

AFL hits Geelong with monster fine over concussion waiver scandal The AFL hands down its penalty after a meeting between the commission and Geelong regarding Jake Kolodjashnij's now-controversial contract.

From week five of pre-season, the standard limit will be a total of 160 minutes and 120 minutes of high-intensity training.

Clubs will not be allowed to put players through high-intensity contact training on consecutive days, with teams recommended to use these high-intensity drills sparingly across all contact levels.

Consulting across disciplines from coaches to club doctors and data analysts, the contact training limits follow the 2023 recommendations from the Victorian coroner's investigation into the death of former Richmond player Shane Tuck.

Tuck died by suicide in July 2020 and was subsequently diagnosed with the degenerative brain condition chronic traumatic encephalopathy (CTE).

A separate consultation process will commence in September to develop similar limits with adjustments for the AFLW.

Shane Tuck died in 2020 and was subsequently diagnosed with CTE. (AAP: Mal Fairclough)

These measures are not mandated for community football, with the league preparing the next release of its local football concussion guidelines.

Concussion and head trauma is one of the most pressing issues facing the AFL.

The training framework comes after the AFL last month fined Geelong $140,000 over Jake Kolodjashnij's concussion waiver.

In 2024, Geelong struck a secret agreement with Kolodjashnij whereby he took on legal responsibility for future brain trauma in a bid to exonerate the club and its medical staff from court action in the future.

Multiple players, including former Melbourne star Angus Brayshaw, champion West Coast defender Jeremy McGovern and premiership Magpie Nathan Murphy, were forced into retirement due to repeated concussions.

There is also a multi-million-dollar concussion class action case against the AFL, led by former Geelong defender Max Rooke, in the Supreme Court of Victoria that is set to go to trial next year.

AAP

World.title: 'Not value for money': Plans for Tuggeranong ice sports facility scrapped
World.content:
The ACT government has announced a proposed ice sports facility intended for Tuggeranong will not go ahead.

Plans for the facility featured two international-standard ice sheets for figure skating, ice hockey, broom-ball and speed skating.

But the government said today that despite extensive discussions with advocates of the project, it has been unable to reach an agreement on a way forward at the Tuggeranong site.

Sports Minister Chris Steel said an evaluation of an updated proposal to build and manage the facility found the project "did not represent value for money for the territory".

Canberra Brave players have been calling for an upgraded training facility. (ABC News, Monte Bovill)

Updated proposal presented 'unacceptable risks'

The multi-purpose ice sports facility, dubbed Canberra Arena, was promised by ACT Labor during its 2016 election campaign, and at one stage of the project's planning, the completion date was even listed as 2025.

In addition to the government investment of $16.265 million, the remaining funds needed to build the estimated arena — estimated at $70 million at one stage — were to come from developers Cruachan Investments and Pelligra Holdings, who would "build, own, operate and maintain it".

"Unfortunately, we haven't been able to find a way forward with the partners Cruachan and Pelligra to build, maintain and operate this facility in Tuggeranong," Mr Steel said.

"The tender evaluation found that unfortunately there were a range of unacceptable risks and the updated proposal that was provided to the ACT government in January did not represent value for money for the ACT government."

Chris Steel says he's disappointed the project will not progress. (ABC News: Callum Flinn)

Mr Steel said the proponents "were asking for more than double the territory's contribution to the project" in their latest updated proposal.

"That was one of the factors that led to the proposal being deemed not to be value for money," he said.

Cruachan chief executive Stephen Campbell said he supported the government's decision as additional costs associated with developing the site had become "prohibitive".

"We look forward to presenting a new proposal to the government in the coming months that will be more cost-effective, better meet community needs, and create improved access opportunities for all Canberrans," he said.

He said the Tuggeranong site was "too challenging" and the new proposal would include options for different locations.

Money to be spent on other sports facilities

Mr Steel said the $16.265 million that was committed to the facility would instead be spent "dollar for dollar" on upgrades to other sporting infrastructure projects in Tuggeranong.

Sporting clubs in the ACT have been invited to share their sporting and recreation infrastructure needs via a survey, which will inform how the money is spent.

"This investment will not be lost for Tuggeranong. The investment will go back into Tuggeranong to improve sporting infrastructure," he said.

Debate about the future site of a dedicated ice sports facility continues. (ABC News, Monte Bovill)

The proposed dedicated arena was to be a new training and competition facility for a variety of ice sports teams who currently use the aging Philip Swimming and Ice Skating Centre.

At one stage it was also to be a new home for the Canberra Brave ice hockey team which has been using a temporary ice rink set up at the Australian Institute of Sport in recent years.

Mr Steel acknowledged that the outcome would be "deeply disappointing" for the ice sports community.

"Now we will need to continue to work with our ice sports community on what the next steps are and what other opportunities there are to improve ice sport facilities in the ACT," he said.

"It's important to note that on the current Phillip site, the requirement for an ice skating facility that meets national competition standards still remains."

'Not the end game'

ACT Ice Sport Federation spokesperson Sandi Logan said they were "profoundly disappointed" but that it was "not unexpected".

"We've not had a great deal of confidence in recent times in the proponents' ideas and the proposals that they put up to amend the original concept of a community facility for the ACT ice sports community," he said.

"The second thing I'd say is that we've moved into overtime, this is not the end of the game.

"There's still a lot of work ahead of us, and we're grateful that Sports Minister Chris Steel and the ACT government continues to support us.

"And we're in a way grateful that we'll have another chance to come up with a better arrangement, a better partnership, and a better opportunity for the community to pursue ice sports in Canberra and the ACT."

The Phillip Swimming and Ice Skating Centre is now being run by Geocon. (ABC News: Joel Wilson)

He praised Geocon for how they had been managing the Phillip ice skating facility since taking over as lessees at the site.

"And maybe, just maybe, Geocon is looking at the Philip ice rink with a possibility for something into the future. I have no idea," he said.

"But we know that they have backed the Philip ice rink, maintained it, in fact, improved it to a state where we can now go with regular certainty that there'll be ice, there'll be a game, there'll be a sport to play."

Mr Logan said the foundation was in it "for the long run" until a solution was found.

"The ice may be thin under us, we may be skating on the proverbial thin ice, but we're here for the long haul, and we need to get a new ice rink built for the community."

World.title: Swans AFLW star says club's men's and women's players closer than ever
World.content:
Believing Sydney's men's and women's teams are closer than before, AFLW star Cynthia Hamilton has described the embattled club's resilience amid turmoil as "actually beautiful".

Hamilton is urging fans to continue their support, vowing the Swans won't disappoint on the field in Sunday's Sydney derby against rivals GWS at Henson Park.

The Swans women play in the Harbour City for the first time since the SCG double-header in round two, having played a home game in Coffs Harbour in round three.

Swans offer timely reminder of what 'Bloods' culture is meant to look like Many questions were asked about Sydney's famed culture in the wake of the Pullman Hotel scandal. As the finals got underway, the players showed exactly what it is supposed to look like on the field.

Fans came out in force at the SCG in the immediate aftermath of the men's Pullman Hotel scandal, with a crowd of 16,672 turning up for the victory over Essendon.

The attendance more than doubled Sydney's previous highest crowd for a home AFLW game.

In contrast, the men's team recorded its lowest SCG crowd of the season, just 30,058 fans watched them beat North Melbourne.

Star players Isaac Heeney, Chad Warner and Nick Blakey — All-Australian contenders before they were banned from being selected — are among the five serving club-imposed bans.

Important tagger James Jordon and defender Riley Bice are the other Swans who won't play again this season.

Errol Gulden (right) has been getting Sydney's men's and women's players together for breathwork sessions. (Getty Images: Cameron Spencer)

As the men's team aims to rebuild respect for the famed "Bloods" culture, Hamilton says the club have come together even over the smallest of details.

"This has honestly brought us closer. We're doing breathwork in the morning together, we're doing little things," Hamilton said.

"Errol Gulden's been flicking the message [about breathwork] across to join both teams together as an opportunity to come closer.

"The boys have been bloody awesome. They've really brought the two groups together.

" In light of what's happened, it's actually kind of beautiful how the club has reacted. I would say we're closer than what we were before. "

As a healthy contingent followed the women's to Whitten Oval last week, the men's team enjoyed renewed support for their 53-point qualifying final upset of reigning premiers Brisbane and played in front of 37,261 fans at the SCG.

"When you look on the weekend, and you see the support the boys are getting, and then vice versa when we were at the SCG as well, it just shows how special the Bloods bond is and that the culture is there," Hamilton said.

"Keep getting around us, keep showing up, and we won't disappoint, hopefully."

GWS forward Tarni Evans also threw her weight behind the Swans, after urging fans to support the AFLW fixture at the SCG last month.

Sydney's AFLW side has received a mountain of support from both inside and outside the club. (Getty Images: Kelly Defina)

The 14th-placed Giants are looking to retain derby bragging rights and bounce back from a dour 31-point away loss to the Lions, taking a three-game losing streak to Henson Park.

Sydney is also licking its wounds after a 27-point defeat to the Western Bulldogs, leaving the Swans fifth after a first loss of the season.

Both sides have claimed two wins from four previous derbies in the women's league.

"This weekend, this is such a great opportunity in women's sport, to get out and support it," Evans said.

"Getting people to the game is unreal and that's what we want.

"This weekend will be another testament to that, a great game of footy to watch."

AAP

World.title: Opals remain perfect at World Cup despite 2am fire alarm wake-up call
World.content:
Australia has made it two from two at the FIBA Women's Basketball World Cup with an 87-71 win over Türkiye in Berlin.

It was an improved performance by the Opals after their opening 70-54 victory over Puerto Rico, leaving Sandy Brondello's side set to progress to the knockout stages.

New captain Ezi Magbegor was instrumental in the second straight victory with 21 points on 10/14 shooting, leading the way with able support from Steph Talbot's 17 points.

It was an impressive performance considering the unceremonious 2am wake-up call the teams received when a fire alarm went off at the team hotel.

Ezi Magbegor led the way with 21 points. (Supplied: FIBA)

The players and coaches all had to evacuate the hotel before going back inside the building about an hour later.

There was no fire, someone had pushed the emergency alarm button in the elevator, according to Brondello.

"That's a what-if situation, isn't it?" Brondello said.

"Now we have that in our toolbox. Never done that before."

The interrupted sleep did not seem to hurt the Opals in the first game of the day that tipped at 11:30am local time.

"It was kind of crazy. Just kind of happened," Australia forward Ezi Magbegor said.

"Knowing that it's out of our control, so just getting back to sleep and waking up. No-one was going to feel sorry for us."

Turkish coach Andrea Masson said he and his players got about three hours of sleep because of the alarm.

"They had a really bad night last night," Masson said.

"That's not an excuse, but that's the reality."

The ABC of SPORT Sports content to make you think... or allow you not to. A newsletter delivered each Saturday.

ABC/AP

Tech.title: Audi’s new A2 E-tron is its most affordable and efficient EV yet
Tech.content:
is transportation editor with 10+ years of experience who covers EVs, public transportation, and aviation. His work has appeared in The New York Daily News and City & State.

Posts from this author will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

When shopping for an electric vehicle, affordability is becoming a more common trait. But affordable and energy efficient is truly a rare breed. Often you have to sacrifice one for the other. Want something affordable? Great, here’s a range loser. Want something that goes the distance? Be ready to pay the price.

Surprisingly, here comes Audi to split the difference. The German automaker’s new A2 E-tron compact crossover is inexpensive, starting at just £32,200 (about $45,000). And it absolutely impresses with an ultra low drag coefficient and a range of battery and drivetrain options that, when configured correctly, can produce a range of up to 401 miles.

Unfortunately for us Yanks, this rear-wheel drive compact car is just for the European market for now. But perhaps Audi will eventually see the error of its ways, or Americans will get their heads out of their tailpipes long enough to see the real advantages of a highly efficient, compact EV with an Audi badge.

Previous Next









1 / 6

Efficient is often synonymous with aerodynamic, and the A2 E-tron certainly confirms that. Flush door handles, cool air intakes, a fully enclosed underbody, and gap reducers around the wheel arches help reduce the drag coefficient down to 0.24, a first for Audi. Another first is bidirectional charging, which will help support vehicle-t0-load via an outlet in the trunk, or vehicle-to-home with the right compatible DC wall box.

With the right motor and battery setup, the A2 E-tron consumes just 12.8 kWh per 62 miles (100 km), while the real mile-eater of the lineup manages up to 401 miles (645 km) on the European WLTP cycle. Inside, the A2 E-tron features a standard curved MMI panoramic display that combines an 11.9 inch digital gauge cluster with a 12.8 inch center touch screen.

Previous Next











1 / 7

There’s also plenty of clever storage thanks to a Fidlock magnetic fastening system that allows owners to click things like cupholders and charging cable bags into dedicated points around the cabin and trunk. Cyclists may be familiar with the tech that can keep their water bottles attached to their bike without a cage, but Audi says this is the first time it’s making an appearance in a production car.

While Audi gave up on its EVs-or-bust pledge last year, the automaker is leaving the door open for a mix of gas, hybrid, and electrification. The A2 may not be appearing alongside its brethren like the impressive S6 Sportback E-tron at the dealership anytime soon, but nothing is set in stone.

Images by Audi

Tech.title: Six years later, Sony revisits its legendary XM4 headphones
Tech.content:
is a senior reviewer covering TVs and audio. He has over 20 years experience in AV, and has previously been on staff at Digital Trends and Reviewed.

Posts from this author will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

Six years ago Sony and Bose were in the middle of a noise-canceling battle, with each new model of headphones better than the last. In the fall of 2020, Sony released the WH-1000XM4 headphones to wide acclaim. They sat atop best headphones lists for years, thanks to their great sound, competitive ANC, and compact size, until they went out of stock. Now Sony has brought them back, with minor improvements, as the WH-1000XM4C.

The XM4C look identical to the original XM4 (although they now have a lavender option), with the same hinge design and ability to fold up. It’s a compact design that Sony moved away from when it released the XM5 in 2022, and then returned to (although not quite as compact) with the XM6. But it’s not just the look that’s returned. The XM4C still use the same QN1 processing chip and four microphones for ANC. That design is showing its age: The XM5 still used the QN1, but had eight mics. Last year’s XM6 have 12, plus the new QN3 chip.

In addition to the standard white and black, the XM4C will be available in lavender. Image: Sony

Sony did update the XM4C’s sound profile to bring it in line with current models, and the headphones have a 10-band EQ in the Headphones app, instead of the 5-band on the XM4, plus a gaming preset. The XM4C also support Bluetooth 6 instead of 5. Surprisingly, the battery performance on the new headphones is slightly worse. Sony claims the XM4C get up to 27 hours of use with ANC on as opposed to 30 hours previously. Not a huge difference, and still more than enough for a cross-country trip.

The XM4C will be available later this fall for $300, which is $50 cheaper than the XM4 when they first came out (and $100 cheaper than the XM6 are now), but more than they could be found for before being discontinued.

I have loved the Sony XM4 since they came out, and still have my pair hanging on the side of my desk. Beyond nostalgia, though, I’m confused why they’re coming back. A review sample of the XM4C arrived at my door while I was writing this, so some deeper investigation will be coming soon. But the headphones industry has moved forward in the past six years, and I’m not sure there’s a need to go back. And the XM5, while they don’t fold up as nicely as the XM4C, are excellent headphones and currently available for $200 (though that price may be an effort to clear out inventory ahead of the XM4C).

Alongside the XM4C, Sony released the next generation of two of its less-expensive midrange and entry-level headphone lines: the WH-CH730N and WH-CH530. They both get the same 10-band EQ upgrade and gaming EQ preset as the XM4C, and the CH730N will now fold up into a more compact form.

The entry-level CH530 come in six different colors. Image: Sony The $180 CH730N offer ANC with battery life up to 50 hours. Image: Sony

The two headphones also get a boost to battery life according to Sony: The CH730N get up to 50 hours with ANC, and the CH530 get up to 55 hours (there’s no ANC on the CH530). A new safe mode in the app allows a user to limit the max volume output of the headphones. It’s a nice addition for parents looking to protect their kids’ hearing, although there’s no way to lock the limit once it’s been set.

The WH-CH530 come in black, cobalt, mint green, white, pink, and coral and cost $70. For $180, you can get the WH-CN730N in black, blue, oat, white, or pink. Both headphones are available now.

The Hello Kitty headphones will be available in pink, of course. Image: Sony

Sony is also doing a partnership with Hello Kitty. Bundles include headphones — the WH-1000XM6, WH-CH730N, or WH-CH530 available in black or pink — a Hello Kitty-shaped carrying pouch, and Hello Kitty-branded bag. The bundles will be available in limited supply later this year on the Sony website only.

Tech.title: EcoFlow makes the miniature power station even smaller
Tech.content:
is a deputy editor and Verge co-founder with a passion for human-centric cities, e-bikes, and life as a digital nomad. He’s been a tech journalist for 20 years.

Posts from this author will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

If you’re in the market for a tiny power station that punches well above its size and weight then have a look at EcoFlow’s new fourth-generation River series.

The River 260 Gen4 features a 256Wh capacity battery while the 520 Gen4 packs in 512Wh — storing about 2.5x and 5x the energy of the largest airline-approved power banks, respectively. Better yet, the batteries are built using longer-lasting LFP chemistry that’s far less volatile. The River 260 Gen4 features four USB ports, and 300W of max continuous output delivered out its lone AC jack. The River 500 Gen4 features the same USB port selection but offers a pair of AC jacks good for 500W of continuous output.

Both of EcoFlow’s Gen4 power stations feature class-leading energy density that cuts both the weight and size, making these power stations lighter and more compact than similarly-specced competition. That makes them ideal for an overnight camping trip or photo shoot in the literal field. The EcoFlow 520 Gen4 is powerful enough to keep a standard US fridge running for about 4 hours during a blackout.

EcoFlow’s River 520 Gen4 can power a fridge much larger than the one pictured. Image: EcoFlow EcoFlow’s River 260 Gen4 has just one AC outlet with only 300W out, but all the same USB ports. Image: EcoFlow

Here’s a quick comparison to show just how much energy these remarkably small power stations are packing, starting with the River 520 Gen4:

Power Station Capacity (Wh) Dimensions (W × D × H) Volume (Liters) Weight Volumetric Energy Density (Wh/L) EcoFlow RIVER 520 Gen4 512 Wh 13.9 × 17.7 × 22.9 cm 5.63 L 4.6 kg (10.1 lbs) 90.9 Wh/L EcoFlow RIVER 2 Max 512 Wh 27.0 × 26.0 × 19.6 cm 13.76 L 6.1 kg (13.4 lbs) 37.2 Wh/L Anker 535 512 Wh 29.2 × 18.8 × 25.1 cm 13.78 L 7.6 kg (16.8 lbs) 37.2 Wh/L Bluetti AC50B 448 Wh 28.0 × 20.0 × 22.0 cm 12.32 L 6.7 kg (14.8 lbs) 36.4 Wh/L

And here’s how the River 260 Gen4 compares to some of the main competition:

Power Station Capacity (Wh) Dimensions (W × D × H) Volume (Liters) Weight Volumetric Energy Density (Wh/L) EcoFlow RIVER 260 Gen4 256 Wh 13.9 × 17.7 × 17.5 cm 4.30 L 3.0 kg (6.6 lbs) 59.5 Wh/L EcoFlow RIVER 2 256 Wh 24.5 × 21.4 × 14.2 cm 7.44 L 3.5 kg (7.7 lbs) 34.4 Wh/L Anker Solix C300 288 Wh 16.4 × 16.1 × 24.0 cm 6.34 L 4.1 kg (9.1 lbs) 45.4 Wh/L Bluetti EB3A 268.8 Wh 25.5 × 18.0 × 18.3 cm 8.40 L 4.6 kg (10.1 lbs) 32.0 Wh/L

Both models can serve as a UPS for your computer, with a cutover time of less than 10ms, and feature one state-of-the-art 140W USB-C PD3.1 port that’s bidirectional. That little trick lets these power stations eschew charging bricks in favor of direct DC charging from a 140W USB-C wall charger you might already own, or a portable USB-C solar panel EcoFlow will happily sell you.

EcoFlow has also addressed a common problem with all power stations that causes them to eventually die if left idling too long. By minimizing the energy spent converting stored DC to AC output, more watt-hours remain to charge your drone, bike computer, and phone, or to power your Starlink Mini and compact fridge.

The River 260 Gen4 will be available in Europe from Q4 2026, while the River 520 Gen4 will follow sometimes in Q1 2027. Pricing for both will be announced as we get closer to their global release dates.

Tech.title: The real reason your phone is getting more expensive
Tech.content:
When Apple debuts the next generation of iPhones this week, they’re likely to come with an unwanted change: a higher price tag. A price hike from the supply-chain powerhouse would be the clearest sign yet that soaring memory costs have become unavoidable — with no end to the memory crunch in sight.

Call it “chipflation” or “RAMageddon.” The shortage is reversing a decades-long decline in memory costs that helped make consumer electronics more powerful without making them dramatically more expensive. The terms “memory prices” and “memory shortage” appeared in 473 company transcripts last quarter, according to data provided by AlphaSense. The entire industry is seemingly working on the problem. And yet, we’re years away from seeing it fixed.

The common wisdom is that AI is at fault: The technology isn’t just contributing to higher energy prices and layoffs; it’s also helping drive up the cost of everything from smartphones to game consoles.

But the shortage was brewing well before ChatGPT took off — and was then amplified by AI’s unending hunger for RAM. The current market is the product of a complicated and very profitable reshuffling of the memory industry within a system that was already failing to keep up.

“We need to build more wafer capacity,” Manish Bhatia, president and COO of Micron — one of the three largest memory manufacturers — told The Verge. “[It’s] a very different challenge for the industry than it had been for many years before, where technology alone was able to keep up with the demand.”

Samsung HBM chips on a wafer at the Nano Korea expo, July 8th, 2026. Photo: SeongJoon Cho / Bloomberg via Getty Images

For years, memory manufacturers could increase production by fitting more chips onto each wafer. But those gains were shrinking and taking longer to achieve. In 2021, even as pandemic-era electronics demand surged, Micron concluded that the problem was more fundamental: Technological advances alone would no longer create enough capacity to keep pace with long-term demand. Manufacturers would have to process more wafers — and build enormous new facilities to do it.

Then the memory business collapsed. Pandemic-era purchases of computers, tablets, and phones had pulled demand forward; consumer spending weakened, and manufacturers were left with excess inventory. They lost money and slowed their expansion plans.

By the time the market began recovering, generative AI had unleashed a wave of demand far larger and more memory-intensive than manufacturers had ever anticipated.

The memory business is also extraordinarily concentrated. Three manufacturers account for about 90 percent of the market, according to Counterpoint, leaving the world dependent on a handful of companies to divide limited capacity between AI infrastructure and consumer devices. Counterpoint estimates that Samsung controlled 39 percent of the memory market in the second quarter of 2026, followed by SK Hynix at 26 percent and Micron at 25 percent.

The memory inside your phone or computer broadly falls into two buckets. DRAM, or dynamic random-access memory, temporarily holds the information a device needs while opening apps, loading webpages, or running software. NAND flash memory provides longer-term storage for things like photos and files.

“It’s not as simple as saying data centers are consuming RAM. The RAM is not the same.”

Inside AI data centers, specialized processors rely heavily on a form of DRAM called high-bandwidth memory, or HBM.

“It’s not as simple as saying data centers are consuming RAM,” David Naranjo, associate director at Counterpoint, told The Verge. “The RAM is not the same.”

By stacking memory chips together and using advanced connections and packaging, HBM can move enormous quantities of data to and from those processors much faster and more efficiently.

It’s more difficult to produce, but also more lucrative to sell. Deep-pocketed AI chipmakers like Nvidia and AMD and tech giants like Meta and Microsoft have an insatiable need for it to power their AI systems — and are more than happy to pay.

HBM also consumes significantly more manufacturing capacity than conventional DRAM. Memory chips are made many at a time on large, circular silicon wafers. Because a finished HBM product stacks multiple, larger chips together, it requires considerably more silicon. Micron estimates that producing a given amount of HBM requires roughly three times as many wafers as producing the same amount of conventional DRAM.

The incentives increasingly favor AI. Rather than guessing how many phones or laptops will sell a year from now, memory makers can lock in multiyear commitments from some of the world’s richest companies.

“We have been engaging in discussions with customers, prioritizing those who can guarantee committed future captive demand,” Jaejune Kim, Samsung’s executive vice president of memory, said on the company’s last earnings call.

AI is also increasing demand for conventional DRAM. Phone and PC makers want to run smaller AI models directly on their devices, requiring more sophisticated conventional memory — and more of it. Future models may need substantially more memory than their predecessors to support those capabilities.

“The three big memory guys, they’re just basically allocating the capacity that they have to these companies.”

“As AI spreads across various services such as search, coding, and productivity tools, the scope of demand is widening from a memory perspective,” said Song Hyun-jong, president of SK Hynix, another of the big three memory manufacturers, on the company’s most recent earnings call. “We are witnessing a structural shift in demand where both AI memory and conventional memory are growing together.”

Samsung and Micron have both said they remain committed to conventional DRAM. Micron’s Bhatia told The Verge that it still accounts for most of the company’s wafer capacity. But limited supply, surging demand, and AI customers willing to make long-term commitments have made it extraordinarily lucrative to cede space to HBM.

SK Hynix posted a record 76 percent operating margin last quarter, up from 41 percent a year earlier, while Micron’s adjusted gross margin hit a record 85 percent. Samsung’s semiconductor profits, meanwhile, jumped roughly 250-fold from a year earlier.

“It’s more profitable,” Naranjo said. “The three big memory guys, they’re just basically allocating the capacity that they have to these companies.”

Counterpoint estimates that DRAM prices for smartphones increased roughly 56 percent in the first quarter of 2026 compared to a quarter earlier, and grew around 83 percent in the second quarter.
